items.title: Melting glaciers in Dolomites reveal cache of first world war munitions
paragraphs: A significant cache of unexploded bombs from the first world war emerged this summer from rapidly retreating glaciers in the Dolomites, the Italian army has said.
The devices, which included Italian artillery shells and French mortar bombs, were removed and defused by the army’s Julia Alpine brigade, according to a statement.
The weapons originated from the white war, a battle between the Austro-Hungarian army and Italian troops across treacherous and bitterly cold terrain between 1915 and 1918.

More than a century later, hikers reported several sightings of bombs during the summer, mostly in the area of Canal San Bovo in the Primiero Valley in eastern Trentino. The soldiers then conducted an extensive sweep there and across other high-altitude and glacier locations in the Trentino Alto Adige region of the Dolomites.

They recovered and neutralised 250 explosives, including “18 Italian 75mm artillery shells and 37 Thevetot mortar shells – a French-made device that was also supplied to the Italian royal army during the first world war”, the Julia Alpine brigade.
It is not the first time that relics of the white war have emerged from melting glaciers, whose retreat has accelerated over more than decade.

“It is very much a consequence of global heating,” said Stefano Morosini, a professor at the University of Bergamo and the coordinator of heritage projects at Stelvio national park, where some of the explosives were also found.

“In recent years, at the end of each summer, these dangerous artefacts emerge and each year there is a higher number. They have been conserved by the ice for more than 100 years. Some had already exploded but many hadn’t, so now when they re-emerge, they are very, very dangerous.”
The advice to hikers and mountaineers is to “never touch any type of explosive device you might find, regardless of where it is located” and to promptly report any discovery to police.

Fought mainly in the Dolomites of Trentino Alto-Adige and the Alps of the Lombardy region, the white war was a period of history frozen in time until the 1990s, when global heating started to reveal an assortment of perfectly preserved relics, including weapons, sledges, letters and diaries.

A wooden barracks that had been dug into a cave on the top of Mount Scorluzzo, a 3,095-metre (10,154ft) peak overlooking the Stelvio pass, reappeared in 2015 after the ice which had sealed it off for almost a century completely melted.

The shelter had been hastily locked up when the first world war ended in November 1918, and the soldiers abandoned most of their belongings. Beds made of straw as well as clothes, lanterns, newspapers, postcards, coins, and tinned food were found well preserved inside.
A white war museum to host the relics is scheduled to open in Bormio in June 2027.
The white war is thought to have claimed more than a million lives, although the majority of soldiers were believed to have been killed by avalanches, falling down mountains or hypothermia.
Dozens of corpses, some still in their uniforms, have emerged from the melting ice over the past 15 years.
The relatives of an Italian soldier were able to bury him in 2017 after documents revealing his identity were found with his body on Presena glacier.
Morosini said the intense summer heat was making access to the glaciers in the Dolomites less safe. Eleven people died when a huge mass of the Marmolada glacier broke off in 2022.
“It is becoming more and more impossible to access the glaciers during the summer because of the very long heatwave at high altitude,” he said.
“If you come to the area, you can see how fast the glaciers are retreating and how strong the impact of climate change is.”

items.title: Asthma deaths reach decade-high levels and number of Australians dying of dementia grows
paragraphs: Dementia has accounted for more than 10% of all deaths for the first time, while the number of people dying from asthma is at decade-high levels, new data published by the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) reveals.

There were 188,421 deaths registered in 2025. Of these, 19,019 deaths were caused by dementia, including Alzheimer’s disease, the ABS deaths data released on Tuesday shows. It has been the leading cause of death in Australia since 2024.
The other leading causes of death in 2025 were ischaemic heart diseases, cerebrovascular diseases (such as stroke), lung cancer and chronic respiratory diseases.
Dementia Australia’s chief executive, Prof Tanya Buchanan, said there was an urgent need to act on dementia, given it was a leading public health issue.
“The data underlines the critical need for more recognition and funding to support people living with dementia, their families and carers,” Buchanan said.
There are an estimated 446,500 Australians currently living with dementia, and a further 1.7 million people involved in their care, she said.
“Despite the growing impact of dementia, investment in specific services, supports and prevention have not kept the same pace, and the stigma that surrounds dementia continues,” she said.
The data also revealed the highest number of asthma deaths recorded in a decade.
There were 484 Australians who died from asthma in 2025, up from 478 deaths in 2024.
Women account for almost two-thirds of asthma deaths, and almost two-thirds of all dementia deaths.
Asthma Australia’s CEO, Kate Miranda, said poorly controlled asthma increases the risk and is a preventable reason behind many asthma-related deaths.
“We have effective treatments and clear clinical guidelines, yet too many Australians are not getting the care they need to stay well,” she said.

Research has found the proportion of adults with well-controlled asthma has been falling, with many using little or no preventer treatment. Adherence among those using inhaled corticosteroids was also worsening, Miranda said.
Too many people only used asthma-reliever medications, and rely on it for their symptoms.
“But it doesn’t treat the underlying inflammation,” Miranda said.

“People, especially those with mild cases, think ‘it’s just asthma’, so they don’t get regular checkups and talk to their GP about their medication. People might take preventer medication on high pollen days or when they have a cold, but then they don’t take it otherwise.”
She said people should be aware that asthma guidelines have shifted to recommend anti-inflammatory reliever (Air) therapy, an anti-inflammatory that also treats symptoms.
“People, especially older Australians, are still using medications they had as a child without being aware guidelines have changed and better options exist,” Miranda said.
Drug-induced deaths also remained a public health issue in 2025, rising to 2,063 deaths from 2,007 deaths in 2024.

The ABS’s head of mortality statistics, Lauren Moran, said while opioids and benzodiazepines continue to be the most common drug classes involved in these deaths, there has been substantial growth in people dying after using stimulants, including methamphetamine.
Suicide remained the leading cause of premature death for both males and females in 2025, with men accounting for almost three-quarters of these deaths.
In Australia, support is available at Beyond Blue on 1300 22 4636, Lifeline on 13 11 14, and at MensLine on 1300 789 978

items.title: Rise in sales of radios and tinned foods, say retailers, after call to stock up
paragraphs: UK prepper stores see massive sales following government campaign
ByNicholas WattPolitical editor, Newsnight and Bernadette Kehoe
Some retailers have seen a dramatic increase in sales of essential goods after the government called for people to stock up in case of a crisis, according to figures obtained by Newsnight.
The Iceland supermarket chain said it was "clear" consumers had listened to warnings after it saw a 40% increase in sales of tinned products over the weekend.
The rise in sales came after Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said that people should stockpile goods to prepare for an emergency such as a cyber attack or an extreme weather event.
Robert Dyas reported a 160% increase in sales of radios compared with last week, while Maplin said sales had increased by 92% in radios, 284% in torches and 106% in power banks.
The Maplin figures cover the period since the government's announcement last week compared with the same period last month.

"Within hours of the Be Ready announcement we saw people reach for the basics - a torch, a wind-up radio, a power bank. Torch sales nearly quadrupled and radio sales almost doubled in three days," said Ollie Marshall, managing director at Maplin.
"These are simple, affordable products that keep a household connected and informed when the power goes out, and it's encouraging to see people taking the advice seriously."

On 22 October, Streeting said that people should ensure they have three litres of water per person per day; tinned goods in the cupboard; baby food; battery powered torches and mobile phone charging packs.
Many of the items cited by Streeting appeared in the list of goods gathered by Newsnight whose sales have shot up.

In response to the increase in retail sales of certain items, the defence secretary told Newsnight: "It's encouraging that people are taking practical steps to be ready. Having a few everyday essentials at home, from tinned food to torches, helps households prepare for disruption, whether that's flooding, power cuts or burst pipes. We can all play our part in making Britain more resilient."

An Iceland spokesperson told the BBC programme: "It's clear consumers have listened to the government's message as we have seen a 40% increase in sales of tinned products over the weekend and strong sales of bottled water too. Our supplies of these products remain healthy."
Sales of torches and radio have risen sharply for some UK retailers
Newsnight also spoke to independent retailers who reported a spike in sales of goods highlighted by the defence secretary.

Josh Pringle, from Sgt Prepper's online store, said his sales had increased tenfold: "We were a small outfit on Wednesday. And then the government launched the Be Ready campaign and we couldn't believe what we were seeing – order after order after order. Most of them were for a wind-up radio."

Lincoln Miles, founder of Preppers Shop UK, told Newsnight of a 650% increase in sales after the government announcement. "Everything about off grid seems to be the key of what people are buying for the minute."

items.title: Harry Kane becomes first Englishman in 25 years to win Ballon d'Or
paragraphs: England's soccer player Harry Kane wins the trophy for striker of the year during the Ballon d'Or ceremony at the London Palladium Theatre in London, England, Monday, Oct. 26, 2026 . Kin Cheung/AP hide caption
LONDON — Harry Kane became the first Englishman in 25 years to win the Ballon d'Or on Monday thanks to his prolific scoring last season.

Kane scored 73 goals for club and country last campaign — he was Europe's top scorer — and smashed scoring records in Germany for Bayern Munich and at the World Cup, where he captained England to a third-place finish.
The 33-year-old Kane says winning the prestigious individual award was built on so much more.

"Anything is possible with hard work, when no one else is watching, to go through the ups and downs, to learn through resilience, determination and self-belief," an emotional Kane said in a message to young players, after reflecting on his early career struggles.

"My journey wasn't straightforward. I wasn't the kid who went straight to the top. I had to experience the downs," he added. "I had to fight my way to be the very best right now. I hope that can give you inspiration as well."
Kane was followed in the voting by Kylian Mbappé, Lamine Yamal — voted best young talent for a third straight year — 2024 winner Rodri and record eight-time winner Lionel Messi.

Kane thanked his teammates, coaches, parents, children — "It's past your bedtime" — and wife Kate, " my best friend. We've been through ups and downs for sure. You're my biggest supporter. You always want the best for me."
Kane led Bayern to the Bundesliga and German Cup double, scoring a hat trick against Stuttgart in the cup final. Bayern also reached the Champions League semifinals.

At the World Cup, he scored six times to pass Gary Lineker as England's all-time leading World Cup scorer and placed himself among the all-time top five in tournament history. His lineup lost to Argentina in the semifinals but beat Mbappé's France for third place, England's best World Cup placing in 60 years.
An Englishman hadn't won the Ballon d'Or since Michael Owen in 2001.

"It's massive for England, for our country. (The ceremony) being here in London was a good omen for me," Kane said. "It's been too long. Certainly (there have been) incredible English players... To put us back on the map, to put us here with this trophy I'm extremely proud. Playing for England is my biggest honor, the thing I love to do the most."
England coach Thomas Tuchel told Kane the Three Lions are "lucky to have you as our leader."
"I ran out of superlatives to describe your performances a long time ago, but I'm delighted to see that you have now been formally recognized by the football world," Tuchel said.
Fans packed the streets and climbed light poles near the London Palladium, where the event was held, for a glimpse of the arriving athletes. Kane stopped to sign autographs on his way in.
They stayed through the ceremony and chanted Kane's name as he left the theater near Oxford Circus after midnight.
Kane planned to celebrate with family and friends, but just a little.
"We have a cup game on Wednesday so it can't get too messy," Kane said, noting he has an early Tuesday flight back to Munich in time for team training.
Monday's ceremony was held in London for the first time in recognition of the inaugural winner 70 years ago, England's Stanley Matthews in 1956.

Spain's London City Lionesses' Alexia Putellas wins the player of the year trophy during the Ballon d'Or ceremony at the London Palladium Theatre in London, England, Monday, Oct. 26, 2026 . Kin Cheung/AP hide caption
Earlier, Spain star Alexia Putellas won her record-equaling third women's Ballon d'Or after leading her former club Barcelona to multiple trophies last season including the Women's Champions League.
Putellas, who joined London City Lionesses in the offseason, also helped Spain win the Women's Nations League last December.
The 32-year-old midfielder ended Spain teammate Aitana Bonmati's three-year reign.

Putellas won the prestigious award in 2021 and 2022, tore her ACL and saw Bonmati rise to stardom. Bonmati, who completed her women's Ballon d'Or three-peat in 2025, was not on this year's shortlist after breaking her leg in December.
There wasn't a women's Ballon d'Or until 2018, when Ada Hegerberg won it.
Putellas urged young players to approach the sport with "love and passion."
"Believe in yourself, that's the most important thing," she said. "If you have a dream, go for it, even if at some point you have to start from zero."
Putellas had joined Barcelona in 2012 and called her time at the Catalan club "something special."
"I'm really grateful for having 14 seasons as a player (at Barcelona)," she said. "What I experienced last year was like a perfect story."

items.title: 'A way to escape': Fan excitement as new ACOTAR book hits shelves
paragraphs: Katie and Amy say they have been excited for the release of the newest ACOTAR book, A Court of Splintered Harmony
Torrential rain and high winds may not be what many would consider fantastical.
But it didn't stop about 30 hardcore fans turning out for the latest release of author Sarah J Maas’ romantasy series, A Court of Splintered Harmony, in Carrickfergus, County Antrim.
The sixth book in Maas's multi-million book selling series, A Court of Thorns and Roses (ACOTAR), was released at midnight on Tuesday after a five-year wait.
On Monday evening, a midnight release event was held in The Secret Bookshelf, an independent bookshop just off the town's main street.
Friends Katie Mccabrey and Amy Savage were among those who went along to try and get one of the first copies when the embargo broke.
Like many others, Katie and Amy love reading books as a way to unwind from the stresses and pressures of every day life.
"I just love reading these kinds of fantasy books because the real world is a little bit terrible and I love to escape into a fantasyland of fairies and anything other worldly," Amy says.
"We're all here tonight because we all share just needing to escape from everyday life in common and this is a great way to do it," Katie adds.
Some of those who were at the release party took part in activities like friendship bracelet making and felting

Among the activities lined up at The Secret Bookshelf to distract excited fans from clock-watching are felting, friendship bracelet making and a dedicated fan-chat area for readers to discuss their theories.
Some attending opt for comfy clothing, sporting pyjamas and slippers as they waited for the midnight drop.
The wait has almost been too much for Katie.
"I couldn't sleep, I've been so excited - I've been hyped up for two weeks straight," she says.
"I'm actually halfway through another book that I couldn't pay attention to because I've been so busy thinking about the characters from ACOTAR," Amy jokes.
"So I'm going to have to go back and re-read the book that I'm 300 pages deep in because I've been so busy and so excited for this new launch."

For those whose social media algorithms do not revolve around "BookTok", the literary discussion side of TikTok, A Court of Thorns and Roses - or ACOTAR for short - is a fantasy romance series, which gets its name from the first book.

It's set in the fictional world of Prythian, and without spoiling the now six-book series, fans have flocked to the story in their droves to read about the protagonist's dealings with love and the fae.
Maas is also credited with fuelling interest in the romantasy genre, which has skyrocketed in popularity due to its discussion on social media.
There have been five books published so far:
A Court of Thorns and Roses (ACOTAR) first came out in 2015
Maas announced the series' latest installment, A Court of Splintered Harmony, back in March.
And fans won't have to wait long for the follow-up, with the seventh book, A Court of Forgotten Melody, due to be released on 12 January 2027.
David Jeroen and Sami Patrick are hard to miss amongst the stacked shelves in The Secret Bookshelf - they've donned their finest mythical attire for the evening, with crowns and elf ears included.
The pair's love of reading prompted them to start an Instagram account dedicated to books, and they're spending their two-year "bookiversary" in an apt place.
And Sami's excited to spend the night talking about one of her favourite genres with likeminded people.
"I've always been a fantasy reader and it's just escapism really," she says.
David and Sami were the event's quiz hosts as attendees counted down to midnight

"I think it's all about escaping reality and going into a different world and dimension where you get to live through another character and experience new things that you wouldn't be able to in real life," he adds.
"You can't ride a dragon in real life so you can read about it."
While the evening will conclude with the newest ACOTAR release, Sami says the five-year wait has led her to some of Maas's other series, which she prefers.
Monday's midnight release event is the brainchild of Jo Zebedee, who runs The Secret Bookshelf alongside her husband, Chris.
Harkening back to her time helping to run the midnight launches of the Harry Potter books, Jo decided to bring the same magic for fans of the much loved romantasy series.
"We are a big fantasy shop, I'm a fantasy, sci-fi writer so it's in my blood, so we very much celebrate the world's that sometime can be difficult to find a space in mainstream books," she explains.
"There's something around the excitement of books and just that whole vibe of here's something to really celebrate.. we just wanted to bring that all together to make a fun night."
Jo Zebedee runs The Secret Bookshelf in Carrickfergus alongside her husband, Chris
Jo enlisted the help of not only local crafters for the event, but local businesses who gifted attendees treats for the late night.
She thinks its the place of independent bookshops, like hers, to foster the excitement amongst young people for reading.
"I think events is when a bookshop comes to life," she says.
"It's about a love of books and tonight is just such a love of books."

items.title: Tiny zebra-striped bee in West a 'huge surprise'
paragraphs: The species nests independently and relies on the saltmarsh plant called sea aster for food
A tiny zebra-striped bee, usually found along England's south and east coasts, has made an unexpected journey to the West Country.
The rare sea aster mining bee has been spotted at Steart Marshes in Somerset by naturalist Nigel Phillips, who said the find "was a huge surprise".
The Wildfowl and Wetlands Trust said saltmarsh restoration work at the nature reserve had helped create the perfect home for the newcomer.
The charity says the discovery shows how rare species and wildlife can thrive by restoring coastal habitats.
Steart Marshes are an example of how restoring saltmarshes can boost wildlife
The reserve supports a wide variety of coastal wildflowers, including plenty of sea aster, which is thought to have finally attracted the bees to the Steart peninsula.
"There were lots of them and several colonial nest areas in the dry sandy ground," said Phillips.
"At the time I thought they were only found in salt marsh areas around the Thames estuary."
The reserve hosts hundreds of animal species as well as many plants found in no other habitat
Of the 290 invertebrate species found in these habitats across the UK, 148 can only be found in saltmarshes.
Site manager Bay Alys Laver said: "People usually associate saltmarshes with huge flocks of wading birds, geese and ducks, but there is so much life here that goes unnoticed.
"Spotting such a rare species here is a testament to the brilliant work our staff do in maintaining the reserve in concert with local graziers.
"I was so happy to hear that we have been found by our first sea aster mining bees."

items.title: Albanese concedes $6m golf club grant in his electorate was not to contain ‘raw sewage’
paragraphs: Anthony Albanese has admitted he got it wrong after telling parliament a $6m grant to a golf club in his electorate was to stop “raw sewage” going into the nearby river.

The grant given to Marrickville golf club in Sydney’s inner-west is under scrutiny as part of a larger $560m invitation-only grants scheme, which transparency advocates say largely funded projects promised at the 2025 election in Labor-held seats.

Infrastructure department officials told a Senate estimates hearing on Monday afternoon the $6m grant given to the club in Albanese’s electorate did not fund works to prevent raw sewage from flowing into the nearby river, contrary to the prime minister’s claims.
“I can confirm that sewerage is not a component of this grant,” the department’s assistant secretary, Jacinta McDonald, said.
The assistant education minister, Anthony Chisholm, defended the prime minister’s response, saying the scope had changed since the local council’s original proposal.

“I think that was part of the original plan. But as often happens, as the scope of these sorts of announcements happen, the scope can change, and the New South Wales government, is my understanding, stepped in in support of the sewerage work,” Chisholm said.

First reported by the ABC, Albanese, who holds honorary social membership at the club, has swatted away any criticism that he influenced, or benefitted from, the decision, which was signed off by another minister.
In question time in early September, the prime minister told the house the money would go toward “an environmental project stopping raw sewage going into the Cooks River during flooding”.

“[The golf club] has existed for a long time, almost a 100 years, and they have a septic tank because it is on the floodplain, when it floods in Marrickville raw sewage flows into the Cooks River – that is what the funding is for,” Albanese said in another response to questions about his involvement in the decision-making process.

The prime minister was grilled repeatedly by the opposition about the grant in question time on Tuesday afternoon and the shadow energy minister, Dan Tehan, accused the prime minister of misleading the parliament, and urged him to correct the record.

In response, Albanese conceded “it was not correct” to say the funding was for sewerage works but said it was a matter for the infrastructure department, and noted the council was finalising the design of the project – including improvements to the clubhouse, stormwater harvesting, a new toilet and landscaping.
The NSW government committed in September 2025 to address sewerage infrastructure at the club, he said.

“I’m advised that the club, of course, has a long history. And indeed, in the media release announcing the project, it spoke about the venue’s last major remodel being in 1947. So this is a local club, owned by the council,” Albanese said.
“The [federal] funding was going to be for sewerage. The New South Wales government have stepped in, which is appropriate given that New South Wales run water and sewerage.”

items.title: ‘It’s the smell of freedom’: Belgrade cleans up after Student List triumph
paragraphs: Student List cleaned up at Serbia’s parliamentary elections. So it was only fitting that the morning after a night of raucous celebrations, the movement’s supporters were gathering, bin bags in hand, at Pioneers Park, opposite the national assembly building in Belgrade.

For the previous 18 months, this small patch of greenery – with its established trees and playground – had been a no-go zone. A pro-government camp known as Ćaciland had taken over the space with convicted criminals living there in white tents, happy to attack journalists, or anyone else who came too close. Police stood by but did nothing to prevent the violence.

On election night, it seemed that thuggery might be on the cards again. Half an hour before the polls closed, large numbers of masked, black-clad men started gathering in and around Pioneers Park. Their intimidating presence gave credence to pre-poll predictions that the governing Serbian Progressive party (SNS) would not hand over power without a struggle.

What happened next took almost everyone by surprise. Shortly after the polls closed – and before any projections of the results had been published – Aleksandar Vučić told supporters at SNS headquarters that they had suffered a comprehensive defeat to the Student List. As cheers rang around the heart of Belgrade, he added that he did “not want unrest” or “anything like that on the streets”.

The riot police stood aside and the barriers blocking access to the area around Pioneers Park were removed. The goon squad made a rapid exit – and Student List supporters joyfully ransacked Ćaciland, setting fire to some of the tents.

But this is not a movement that likes to leave a mess. Over the two years of anti-corruption protests that led to the Student List’s victory, participants have always cleaned up after themselves. So the call went out for volunteers to restore Pioneers Park to something approaching its previous state.

Hundreds of people answered the appeal and joined municipal workers to remove the remains of Ćaciland. Some dismantled the mangled white tents, while others painstakingly cleaned and disinfected the climbing frames, swings and slides in the children’s playground.

Radomir Dalic painstakingly combed over the grass to remove cigarette butts and other rubbish. Apparently relishing his labours, he said he was overjoyed that the park was finally rid of “criminals with violent intentions towards us”.
“Yesterday was a big victory, so today is the smell of freedom,” he added. “We are in garbage, but it’s the smell of freedom.”

Tamara Tomic wore yellow rubber gloves for the occasion – and radiated similar pride in taking part. “Gathering here and cleaning this place just shows that we want to live nicely,” she said. “We want to enjoy the city, enjoy a normal life without violence and without anyone torturing us.”

For now, nobody is asking too many questions about how the Student List will govern. In fact, Serbian voters have taken something of a leap into the unknown – because this is a movement that operates unlike a traditional political party. It has no hierarchy and no leader. Its candidates were chosen by a series of student assemblies, with nominations ranging from academics to athletes, economists to engineers.

The Student List did publish an 11-point plan. Most of these points deal with anti-corruption measures – ironically, the pitch that secured victory in 2012 for Vučić and the SNS. Other commitments include judicial reform, media freedom, affordable housing and improved access to healthcare, with the promise of “a doctor in every village”.

But beyond the domestic priorities – in essence, a clean-up for public institutions – little is clear. The Student List went into the elections without naming a candidate for prime minister, let alone a possible cabinet.

Kurt Bassuener, co-founder of the Democratization Policy Council, said he was concerned about what that might mean when the euphoria of victory died down, and the serious business of forming a government began.

The thinktank chief added: “I’m hoping that there is a dream scenario plan here – they have portfolios and people who have credibility in particular issue areas and they can hit the ground running. Because the danger of a broad coalition like this is that the fissures will show soon after victory.”

Ilija Srdanović, the candidate ranked first on the Student List, has played down the potential for strife. A cardiologist at the university in Novi Sad, the city where a deadly roof collapse sparked the student protests, he has protested alongside the students since the early days. However, he was keen to emphasise that his ranking on the list did not mean he would become prime minister.
“The student movement is fully democratic,” he said, adding that the aim was to buck Serbia’s history of “creating the cult of personality or leadership”.
The 250 candidates on the Student List were “equal subjects in this struggle”, Srdanović insisted, with “numerous candidates who can be chosen for the prime minister position or any other position”.

But his confidence does little to reassure those who have noticed that the broad spread of views held by Student List candidates could lead to trouble. Despite Vučić’s warnings that a Student List government would impose sanctions on Russia and recognise Kosovo’s unilateral declaration of independence, the movement’s foreign and regional policy remains opaque.
“We have not seen seas of EU flags at demonstrations by students or the marches across Serbia,” said Michael Davenport, a former EU and UK ambassador to the country.

“There are massive policy areas where there is no consensus among the Student List or those have been elected. The approach towards accession to the European Union is not clear, nor is the position with regard to regional issues like Bosnia and Herzegovina and, very particularly, Kosovo.”

Many people are happy to leave these concerns for another day. Vučić and the SNS have fallen – and the cacophony of car horns continued throughout Monday as drivers passed the clean-up crew in Pioneers Park.
One visible symbol of the old regime has been swept away. The Student List voters are hoping more will follow.

items.title: Musk slows down internet for Ukraine – level 1
paragraphs: A new report says that Elon Musk slows down the satellite internet for Ukraine. It is called Starlink. Ukraine uses Starlink to fight against Russia.

This makes it very hard for Ukrainian soldiers to use drones and stop rockets. Ukraine’s president says that the internet is still slow, but leaders are trying to fix it. Some people say that Musk talks to Donald Trump first. Others think that he does it alone.
American politicians are very angry. They want to find out what really happens. They believe that one rich man should not have so much power in a war.
Difficult words: fix (to make something work again), alone (without other people or help), power (when you can control or have an impact on what happens to other people).
You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Musk slows down internet for Ukraine – level 2
paragraphs: Reports show that Elon Musk ordered a slowdown of Starlink’s military internet service, which Ukraine relies on to defend itself from Russian attacks. The restriction made it much harder for Ukrainian forces to use drones and protect cities.

While some leaders think Musk acted completely on his own, others say he spoke with President Trump before making the decision. Ukrainian President Zelensky said that connection speeds are still limited, but officials are working to fix the problem.

The situation made many American politicians angry, and they are now demanding a full investigation. Many people believe that an ordinary person shouldn’t have the power to control military decisions or affect international war strategy.
Difficult words: slowdown (reducing the speed or activity of something), restriction (a rule which controls what can be done), limited (not working fully).
You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Musk slows down internet for Ukraine – level 3
paragraphs: Recent news reports reveal that Elon Musk personally authorized a slowdown of Starlink, the military-grade satellite network crucial to Ukraine’s defense against Russia.

The restriction severely hampered Ukrainian military operations, affected drone capabilities and missile interceptions. While some US officials suggest Musk acted on his own, other sources indicate he discussed the decision with President Trump and administration members. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed that Starlink service remains limited, though American officials promised to help resolve the issue.

The incident triggered strong outrage in Washington, and lawmakers call for a full investigation into potential contract violations and illegal interference. Commentators and politicians expressed deep concern over the dangerous concentration of geopolitical power in the hands of a single private citizen during wartime.

Difficult words: hamper (to delay something or prevent it from progressing), interception (stopping or catching something before it reaches its destination), violation (breaking a rule, law, or agreement).

items.title: MVRDV designs Essen Central Library as public "living room" in Germany
paragraphs: Red bookshelves fill the multipurpose interiors of this city library, created by Dutch studio MVRDV in a former department store in Essen, in collaboration with German studio Meyer Architekten.
Named Essen Central Library, the 11,000-square-metre civic building was designed as a “vibrant cultural and educational hub” for the German city and to offer more than a traditional archive.
MVRDV said this aims to ensure the building’s longevity and usefulness in the information age, while also providing opportunities for social interaction in Essen.
“Of all the building functions out there, the library is possibly the one that has had the biggest challenges to adapt to the new millennium”, said MVRDV partner Fokke Moerel.

“Essen Central Library offers a response to this challenge. The library remains an important civic building, yet it offers much more than just a place to find books – it becomes a living room that is open and inviting for all of Essen’s diverse citizens,” she continued.
“It offers a solution to the social atomisation and isolation that has also been growing in the past decades.”

Essen Central Library, which opened to the public on Saturday, relocates a former library to a more central location. It spans all six storeys of Boeckerhaus, the former department store on Kennedyplatz that it occupies.

MVRDV and Meyer Architekten said their design draws on a theory by sociologist Ray Oldenburg about third places, which are free and informal social environments for people to enjoy beyond their homes, schools and places of work.
As such, it is hoped the library can feel inclusive to everyone in the city, whether they are visiting “without a specific purpose” or looking for a specific collection.
Externally, the building is marked by large bands of glazing, allowing views of the library’s interior, including bands of study spaces on the perimeter of each floor.
MVRDV said this allows “the activities taking place within the library to become part of its expression towards the city”.
“The activated facade acts as an interface between the city and the library, connecting the public realm with the everyday experience of the library users,” said the studio.
“The different heights and uses create a lively view of people reading, working, talking, or relaxing, with visitors adding even more character to the space.”
Throughout the interior, bookshelves are used to define different spaces and combined in clusters on each floor, making collections “concentrated and identifiable”.

These clusters, named “media villages”, also define soft play spaces on the first floor, gaming pods on the second, and hobby zones on the third floor. They are all red in colour, but lighten in tone with each level.
The bookshelves are complemented by a palette of warm and natural wood finishes, plant pots and seating areas suited for socialising or focusing. Blue signage helps with wayfinding on each landing.

Completing the project is a ground-floor cafe intended to entice passersby and a rooftop events space with panoramic city views. There are also “makerspaces”, music rooms and areas to use technologies such as 3D printers, virtual reality and robotics.
MVRDV was founded in 1993 in Rotterdam. Its other recent projects include a proposal for a “new world wonder” in the Netherlands and a Bordeaux housing scheme with people-shaped portals.

Other libraries recently featured on Dezeen include a demountable timber structure in Amsterdam that was also conceived as “a living room for the neighbourhood” and a former commercial building in Norfolk that was overhauled and wrapped in a skin of cement shingles.
Photography by Daria Scagliola (unless stated otherwise)

items.title: Jay-Z picks himself to headline the Super Bowl halftime show in Southern California
paragraphs: FILE - Jay-Z gestures from the sidelines prior to the NFL Super Bowl 59 football game, Feb. 9, 2025, in New Orleans. Frank Franklin II/AP hide caption
LOS ANGELES — The man who has helped produce the Super Bowl halftime show is stepping into the spotlight: Jay-Z will headline the show himself.
The NFL, Apple Music and Roc Nation announced Monday night that Jay-Z will be the featured performer for the halftime festivities on Feb. 14 at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California.
NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell said he had one request when the league first reached an agreement with Roc Nation: that Jay-Z take the stage himself "whenever the moment felt right to him."

"From 'Reasonable Doubt' to standing on the Super Bowl halftime stage, this has been a journey," Jay-Z said in a statement. "Thirty years of music, work, and culture on the world's biggest stage. This run continues to be a dream come true."

After days of speculation, Jay-Z is set to return to the stadium where he closed his celebration of the 30th anniversary of "Reasonable Doubt," the mogul's 1996 debut album. The concerts included three sold-out shows at Yankee Stadium and sold-out performances in London and Paris ahead of a stop at SoFi Stadium over the weekend.

Jay-Z's Roc Nation has partnered with the NFL since 2019 to advise on and help produce the league's entertainment presentations, including the Super Bowl halftime show. At the time, Jay-Z said he had told Goodell, "If this is about me performing at the Super Bowl, then we can just end this conversation now."
Seven years later, Jay-Z is ready to perform after all.

Jay-Z, born Shawn Carter, has won 25 Grammy Awards and received 89 nominations, the second-most in history behind his wife, Beyoncé — who has performed at two Super Bowls. His catalog also includes the albums "The Blueprint" and "The Black Album," and hit songs such as "Hard Knock Life (Ghetto Anthem)," "99 Problems" and "Empire State of Mind," his collaboration with Alicia Keys.
Last year, "Reasonable Doubt" was inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame.

His recent concerts brought out a rotating cast of guests. At SoFi Stadium, his daughter Blue Ivy played piano on "The Story of O.J." and "Dead Presidents," while Scarface, John Legend and DJ Khaled joined him on opening night. Dr. Dre, Snoop Dogg and Too $hort appeared during Saturday's finale.
Earlier in the run, Beyoncé, Rihanna, Eminem and Nas were among the guests at Yankee Stadium.

Jay-Z has built a career as an executive and entrepreneur. The Brooklyn rapper co-founded Roc-A-Fella Records and founded Roc Nation in 2008, building it into an entertainment company that works with artists and athletes.
Jay-Z became the first rapper inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame in 2017 and joined the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2021. He is also a four-time Emmy winner.
Roc Nation will executive produce the halftime show, with Hamish Hamilton directing.

The halftime show has collected Emmys in recent years. Bad Bunny's performance in February won a record seven, including best variety special (live), while Kendrick Lamar's show last year won for music direction.

items.title: Brewers rout the Rays 10-1 to move within a win of their first World Series title
paragraphs: Milwaukee Brewers' Garrett Mitchell, left, celebrates past Tampa Bay Rays catcher Nick Fortes after scoring during the fifth inning of Game 3 of baseball's World Series, Monday, Oct. 26, 2026, in St. Petersburg, Fla., between the Milwaukee Brewers and the Tampa Bay Rays. Ashley Landis/AP hide caption
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — Jackson Chourio set the tone at the plate, Brice Turang sparked an historic offensive outburst and Robert Gasser shut the door on the mound.
The Milwaukee Brewers are one victory from their first World Series title after routing the Tampa Bay Rays 10-1 on Monday night thanks to a trio of young players who have shined in October.
Chourio bookended Milwaukee's eight-run fifth inning with two of his four hits, and Turang's two-run single opened a barrage of scoring with two outs.
"He was tremendous. Locked in. Gives us a big lift," Brewers manager Pat Murphy said about Chourio, who has eight hits in three Series games.

Gasser, a rookie left-hander, pitched one-hit ball and faced the minimum through six innings as Milwaukee rolled to a 3-0 lead in this Fall Classic. Game 4 is Tuesday night at Tropicana Field, where many Brewers fans showed up Monday and cheered from behind the visitors' dugout.
"It is really cool when you go on the road in such an intense atmosphere to have that support," Gasser said. "Normally it's 35,000 against nine, but tonight we had 20,000 people behind us."
Gasser allowed a line-drive single to Yandy Díaz leading off the bottom of the first and then retired 14 straight before Victor Mesa Jr. walked to begin the Tampa Bay sixth.

Tampa Bay Rays pitcher Cam Booser leaves the game during the fifth inning of Game 3 of baseball's World Series, Monday, Oct. 26, 2026, in St. Petersburg, Fla., between the Milwaukee Brewers and the Tampa Bay Rays. Ashley Landis/AP hide caption

With the help of a caught stealing and a double play, Gasser became the first starter to face the minimum 18 batters through six innings of a World Series game since Arizona's Curt Schilling in 2001 — and the first lefty to do it since Sandy Koufax for the Los Angeles Dodgers in 1965.

Chourio finished 4 for 5 with a double. Turang and William Contreras each went 3 for 5 as Milwaukee racked up 16 hits off "Fastball Freddy" Peralta and five relievers to win its eighth straight game — tying the record for a single postseason.

"I think that you could say this is one of my better games," Chourio said through a translator. "Really I was just taking every at-bat like it could be my last and trying to find any way I could to get on base."

Of the 43 previous major league teams to fall behind 3-0 in a best-of-seven postseason series, only the 2004 Boston Red Sox rallied to win four straight when they beat the New York Yankees in the American League Championship Series.

"It's kind of that chip and a chair mentality," Rays manager Kevin Cash said. "We've got a seat at the table. We've got to do something with the chip. Obviously the only thing we can do is win tomorrow."
Gasser became the first starter for Milwaukee to get an out in the sixth inning this postseason. He's allowed one run in 15 innings over three starts, all on the road.
Peralta, the MVP of the ALCS against Cleveland, ran out of gas against the Brewers. He was charged with five runs and seven hits in 4 2/3 innings against his former team.

"Just a little out of sync. I think he felt really good. Tried to power through it a little bit," Cash said. "Just inconsistencies in and out of the strike zone led to a bunch of really good at-bats by the Brewer lineup."
After a pair of tense, down-to-the-final-pitch, one-run games in Milwaukee, the Brewers put this one out of reach in the fifth with a postseason-record seven straight hits — all with two outs.
It was the first time in World Series history a team scored eight two-out runs in one inning.

"I was sitting in the dugout getting ready to go. There was two outs, and next thing you know, 40 minutes later, I have to go out on the field," Gasser said. "It was special. I had a smile on my face the whole time. It's just surreal when something like that happens."
Chourio began the rally with a one-out single and then stole second with two outs. Christian Yelich walked, and Peralta exited after Contreras' infield single loaded the bases.

The inning appeared to end when third baseman Junior Caminero fielded Contreras' bouncer and threw to second base for a forceout. But the call at second was overturned after a replay review, and Cam Booser entered.
Turang ripped a liner that shortstop Taylor Walls couldn't short hop. It bounced off his glove and rolled into shallow center field for a two-run single.
Garrett Mitchell followed with an RBI single, Cooper Pratt grounded a two-run double down the left-field line and Sal Frelick lined a run-scoring double to make it 8-0.
"It's definitely deflating," Cash said. "How could it not be?"

Milwaukee Brewers pitcher Brandon Woodruff celebrates their win with catcher Gary Sánchez in Game 3 of baseball's World Series, Monday, Oct. 26, 2026, in St. Petersburg, Fla., between the Milwaukee Brewers and the Tampa Bay Rays. Ashley Landis/AP hide caption

Cole Sulser replaced Booser and allowed an RBI single to David Hamilton and an RBI double to the 22-year-old Chourio, who became the second-youngest player with four hits and a stolen base in a World Series game behind Ty Cobb in 1908.
Murphy has compared Chourio to Pro Basketball Hall of Famer Kobe Bryant.

"Kobe was one of the best basketball players of all-time," Chourio said. "I had the opportunity to read his book, some of it at least, but the discipline he had, I think that's what you try to (take) from the great ones. You just take little things you can take from them and implement it into your own game. Hopefully I'm doing a little bit of that."

Brandon Woodruff pitched the ninth for the Brewers, allowing one run and two hits in his first appearance in 3 1/2 months. The two-time All-Star had been sidelined by a shoulder injury that originally was thought to require surgery.
Of the 25 previous teams that took a 3-0 lead in the World Series, 21 swept and four won in five games.

Originally the Seattle Pilots for one season in 1969, the franchise moved to Milwaukee and was renamed the Brewers in 1970. Their only other World Series trip came as an AL team and ended with a Game 7 loss to St. Louis in 1982.
Led by the 67-year-old Murphy, the Brewers need just one more win to end their championship drought.
The Rays led the AL with 98 wins in the regular season, swept the Yankees in three games in the Division Series and beat the Guardians in six games in the ALCS.
But they made uncharacteristic mistakes on the bases and defense during the first two games in Milwaukee, and completely unraveled at home.
Tampa Bay also has never won a World Series in 29 seasons. The Rays lost to the Phillies in five games in 2008 and to the Dodgers in six games in 2020.

Wearing their white Devil Rays uniforms, they were eager to play in front of their home fans at the quirky, cavernous Trop, which had its roof shredded by Hurricane Milton in October 2024 and needed major renovations.
But their cowbell-ringing, towel-waving fans among a sellout crowd of 40,388 couldn't lift them past the surging Brewers.

Milwaukee led the majors with 103 wins, beat the Padres in four games in their NLDS and swept the Dodgers in the NLCS. With a win in Game 4, the Brewers would become the first team to sweep an LCS and World Series since the 1976 Cincinnati Reds.
Griffin Jax is scheduled to start Game 4 for Tampa Bay. The Brewers hadn't announced a starter.
"We've been preparing for this day a lot," Chourio said. "We have one more to lock in for tomorrow to complete the mission."

items.title: Israel heads to polls for pivotal election defined by security and democracy
paragraphs: Israelis are heading to the polls for what many view as one of the most pivotal elections in the country's history.
Polling published on Friday suggests incumbent Benjamin Netanyahu is in a near neck-and-neck race with former military chief Gadi Eisenkot to become prime minister.
But neither of their political blocs are projected to win the 61 seats needed to form a majority government - meaning weeks or months of political wrangling may lie ahead.

The campaign has been shaped by the issue of security - with the opposition bloc hammering Netanyahu for the unprecedented security failure that led to the 7 October Hamas-led attacks on Israel, in which nearly 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken back to Gaza as hostages.
They have pushed for an independent commission of inquiry into the attacks - something Netanyahu has long resisted, insisting it would be biased against him.

Despite the opposition's attack lines, Netanyahu has once again framed himself as "Mr Security" - pointing to what he says are strategic victories in Israel's wars across the Middle East and his close relationship with US President Donald Trump.

Israel's proportional representation system means governments have always been coalitions - and the race to power can, and has, produced unexpected alliances. But this election looks especially tight - and lines in the sand have already been drawn.
Eisenkot, who leads the newly formed Yashar Party, is the main figure in the so-called "change bloc", a collection of parties who have ideological differences but share the goal of ousting Netanyahu.

Other leaders in the bloc include former prime minister Naftali Bennett and Avigdor Lieberman - both right-wingers who take hardline positions on security - and Yair Golan, a left-leaning former general.

For Netanyahu, a titan of Israeli politics who first served as prime minister in 1996, a return to power will hinge on another alliance with the far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties that make up his current governing coalition - the most right-wing in Israel's history.

There are two Arab party blocs in the running too, as about one-fifth of Israel's population is Arab - many of whom describe themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel. In theory, they could prove kingmakers. But all but one of the leading Jewish parties have ruled out working with them.
Eisenkot takes a broadly similar position to Netanyahu on Gaza, and has pledged to end Hamas rule in the territory within 18 months, through a US-led peace plan or, if necessary, military means.

Israel has continued to strike Gaza almost every day since a ceasefire was agreed last year, saying it is targeting Hamas operatives. The Israeli military has killed more than 74,000 people since the start of the war, according to Gaza's Hamas-run health ministry whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
Israel has faced growing international condemnation over its conduct in the war, and relations with its allies around the world have deteriorated.

Eisenkot largely supports Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank - which are illegal under international law - but wants to crack down on extremist Jewish settlers whose attacks are at an all-time high, according to UN figures. He has also spoken about creating the conditions for "autonomy or a state-minus" for Palestinians - under ultimate Israeli security control.
The two-state solution - the creation of an independent Palestinian state in peaceful coexistence alongside Israel - has all but disappeared from mainstream Israeli politics.

Though some have speculated the Arab parties may end up informally propping up an Eisenkot-led minority government - Lieberman, a key prospective member, has ruled out being part of such an arrangement.
Red lines like these mean the electoral arithmetic is complex - but it remains to be seen what kind of concessions, deals and U-turns can be reached once the results come in.
An unprecedented 70,000 people have reportedly flown home from abroad to vote, while half a million are set to cast ballots for the first time.
At 22:00 (20:00 GMT) on Tuesday, Israeli broadcasters will publish exit polls. These will give some indication of the direction of voting, but can vary significantly.
Up and down the country, Israelis will gather to watch the results trickle in, with Netanyahu's Likud meeting in Jerusalem and Eisenkot's Yashar - formed only last year - assembling in Tel Aviv.

Hundreds of thousands of Israeli soldiers and reservists will also cast ballots, but many of those votes will not begin being counted until Wednesday - meaning there may be a late boon for the right-wing parties who are thought to have strong support from that demographic.

Though often framed as a run-off between Eisenkot and Netanyahu, it is possible another leader could take power, if they were to withhold their party's support for a coalition unless given the top job.

An outcome dreaded by many is political deadlock - where no bloc is able to reach a majority, and a minority government cannot be formed. In that scenario, new elections would be called, with Netanyahu to remain as interim prime minister.
Between 2019 and 2022, Israel held five separate elections as parties struggled time and again to co-operate.

items.title: Local ceasefire brokered by Melania Trump starts in southern Ukraine
paragraphs: In this undated image from video provided by the Ukrainian 34th Separate Marine Brigade "Borysfen" on Sept. 22, 2026, smoke rises from a residential neighborhood in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in the Kherson region of Ukraine. Ukrainian 34th Separate Marine B/via AP hide caption

MYKOLAIV, Ukraine — A localized ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia took effect early Tuesday ahead of a humanitarian mission brokered by U.S. first lady Melania Trump, as missile attacks resumed in Kyiv.
The local pause in fighting started at 3 a.m. to allow an aid mission into the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky in southern Ukraine later this week.
According to her office, Melania Trump led talks with civilian negotiators from Russia and Ukraine after meeting with U.N. officials who briefed her on the situation in the town.
The aid mission is planned ahead of a new round of U.S.-brokered talks between Russia and Ukraine expected next month aimed at ending the war after more than 4½ years of fighting.
Up to 2,000 people are stranded in Oleshky with dwindling food and medicine. They are unable to leave because of explosive mines and drone attacks in the area, according to the U.N.
Russian and Ukrainian negotiators as well as the militaries of the two countries confirmed in separate statements that the ceasefire had begun.
The local ceasefire is due to last through Saturday, or longer, though deep mistrust between Russia and Ukraine has thwarted previous attempts at ceasefires.
Minutes after 3 a.m., multiple ballistic missile explosions shook Kyiv and air alerts sounded in multiple parts of the country.
Emergency workers clear debris and damaged road infrastructure near a destroyed car following a Russian overnight strike in Kyiv, Ukraine, Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026. Dan Bashakov/AP hide caption

Late Monday, the capital also came under attack, when Russian ballistic missiles damaged the grounds of a university in Kyiv, killing one person and leaving 10 injured, city officials said. In Kharkiv, Ukraine's second-largest city, authorities said attacks late Monday killed two people and injured four.
"It is important that the world sees that Russia is showing nothing but a desire to kill and continue waging war," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote in an online post shortly afterward.
Oleshky is in the partially occupied Kherson region, about 550 kilometers (340 miles) southeast of Kyiv, where the Dnipro River separates Russian and Ukrainian forces.
It was captured by Moscow's forces on the first day of their full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Further calamity struck in June 2023 when floodwaters inundated the town due to a dam collapse.

Oleshky sits across the Dnipro River from the city of Kherson, the region's administrative capital. Russian forces seized Kherson in the early stages of the 2022 invasion but retreated across the river several months later.
Negotiators involved in the aid mission said doctors, medicines, food supplies and water would be taken to Oleshky before evacuation corridors are opened.

items.title: Trump campaigns in Mississippi, highlighting Republicans' challenges
paragraphs: President Donald Trump arrives at a campaign rally at Crossroads Arena, in Corinth, Miss., Monday, Oct. 26, 2026. Jacquelyn Martin/AP hide caption

CORINTH, Miss. — President Donald Trump campaigned Monday in Mississippi, as he continued a closing midterm rally blitz that has highlighted Republicans' challenges ahead of an election that could drastically shift power in Washington and statehouses across the country.

"I'm here because Cindy's doing great, but I just got to make sure. I can't take a chance," Trump told the crowd, his voice audibly hoarse, as he worked to boost Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, who is facing a surprisingly stiff challenge from Democrat Scott Colom.

Colom was spotted at the rally site, too, creating the rare spectacle of Trump's staunchest supporters interacting directly with a figure the president would soon go on to denigrate as a "Marxist radical" and "fake" and "shameless phony who pretends to be a moderate" from the stage.

Mississippi, among the nation's most reliably Republican states, is not where the Republicans envisioned needing a late-October stop from the president. But Colom is one of many Democratic underdogs who have managed to expand the House and Senate battleground maps because of widespread voter discontent over inflation, the Iran war and other aspects of Trump's second presidency.
He said he had planned to go to the rally site to listen to what was on Trump supporters' minds.
"They actually deserve a senator that will listen to them, that actually cares about what they think, actually cares about what they're going through," Colom said ahead of the president's arrival.

Trump's event kicks off a week of aggressive campaigning that will include more stops in states he won comfortably in 2024, including Texas, South Carolina and Iowa. Trump also plans to hold a rally Saturday in Salina, Kansas, officials announced late Monday, marking his second visit to the state in less than two weeks.
Former Vice President Kamala Harris speaks at Women for Crowley event Monday, Oct. 26, 2026, in Milwaukee. Nam Y. Huh/AP hide caption

Top Democratic candidates and their surrogates were also greeting voters — more than 30 million of whom have already cast ballots, according to data collected by The Associated Press from election administrators across the country — as they try to end Republicans' threadbare majority in the House, reclaim control of the Senate and claw back power in state capitals.

Former Vice President Kamala Harris, Democrats' 2024 presidential candidate, campaigned in Wisconsin with Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, who faces Rep. Tom Tiffany, a Trump ally, in the governor's race. If elected, Crowley would be the first Black governor to lead the battleground state.
"This is a tight race because the stakes are so high," Harris said at an event billed as a "Women for Crowley" rally.
Meanwhile, in Michigan, Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed distanced himself from an ad created by a group called Rebellion PAC that blames high grocery prices on U.S. support for Israel.

"This ad is not affiliated in any way with the Abdul for Senate campaign," a spokesperson for El-Sayed, Roxie Richner, said in a statement about the spot, which features a couple discussing U.S. support for Israel as they shop for groceries.
"Apparently it's costing us a lot of money to drop bombs on Gaza," the woman says.
The ad had been condemned by U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens, who narrowly lost to El-Sayed in the Democratic primary.
The way to win Michigan "is not by blaming the high costs of our goods on the only Jewish homeland in the world," Stevens wrote on X.

El-Sayed, who would be the country's first Muslim senator, has denounced antisemitism while fiercely criticizing Israel for its military operations in Gaza — a position that has been a frequent point of attack for both Republicans and supporters of Israel in his party.

Vice President JD Vance reacts after speaking at a campaign rally at Bozeman Yellowstone International Airport, Monday, Oct. 26, 2026, in Belgrade, Mont. Finn Gomez//POOL Getty Images North America hide caption
Finn Gomez//POOL Getty Images North America

Vice President JD Vance returned to Kansas to stump for Sen. Roger Marshall, who finds himself in a tight contest with Democratic nominee and pastor Adam Hamilton. Hundreds of people were gathered inside the warehouse of a steel-fabricating company in north Topeka in a state where Democrats haven't won a Senate race since 1932.

Marshall, who has raised far less money than Hamilton, told the crowd that Trump is on the ballot, even if his name doesn't appear, because of how Democrats will thwart his agenda if they win control of Congress.
"Democrats are coming out like it's a presidential year," he said, calling on the GOP to match Democrats' energy.
Jace Sullivan, a 50-year-old electrician from Topeka who describes himself as "85% Republican," said Trump supporters need to "circle the wagons" and get out to vote.
Wearing a red "JD Vance for President 2028" shirt, he said he thinks Trump is rightly working to keep Iran from getting nuclear weapons.
"Gas prices are high and it does suck, but it's a means to an end," Sullivan said.
Trump, at the Mississippi rally, said he had, in fact, expected gas prices to rise even higher than they had.
"It worked out fine and it'll be over soon," he said of the war with Iran.

Earlier, Vance was in Belgrade, Montana, to campaign with Republican Aaron Flint, who is facing Democrat Sam Forstag in the race for the state's 1st Congressional District, and Republican Senate candidate Kurt Alme.

Despite the visits to ruby red states, Sen. Tim Scott, who serves as chairman of the National Republican Senatorial Committee, told The Associated Press Monday that GOP candidates are "closing very strongly" in races across the country, including South Carolina, which Trump is set to visit for the second time in as many weeks to stump for GOP Sen. Darline Graham.

"One of the reasons why we will be in the majority is because he has invested the time and the energy on the campaign trail," Scott said on the sidelines of U.S. Rep. Russell Fry's 3rd Annual Freedom Fry event.
But it's Trump's visit to Mississippi that perhaps brings the midterm landscape into the sharpest relief with just a week of campaigning left.
To be sure, Hyde-Smith, who is vying for her second full term, remains the favorite in a state Trump won three times by an average of nearly 20 percentage points.

But Colom, a local prosecutor who would make history as Mississippi's first Black senator since post-Civil War Reconstruction, is looking to parlay inflation, Trump's lagging popularity and Hyde-Smith's mistakes into an upset.

Senate Democrats' super PAC has been a late entry in the contest, with a $1.2 million investment. Mississippians have not chosen a new Democratic senator since 1947, and Democrats last won a Senate race there when that senator, the onetime segregationist John Stennis, won his last reelection in 1982.

In New York, meanwhile, one of the party's most vulnerable House members pulled from Trump's campaign playbook. Rep. Mike Lawler, who is in a tight race with Democrat Cait Conley in New York City's northern suburbs, manned a McDonald's drive-thru — mimicking something Trump did two years ago, even as Lawler has tried to emphasize his independence from the president.

items.title: Albanese promises ‘swift response’ on MP safety as he mulls panic buttons for politicians
paragraphs: Anthony Albanese has promised a “swift government response” to safety threats to MPs and floated the provision of duress alarms for electorate offices, saying politicians and their staff have put up with threats for too long.

The prime minister’s pledge to the Labor partyroom came hours after senator Fatima Payman again slammed her former government colleagues over the lack of staffing given to her office, controversially asking: “Is the prime minister waiting for something, like what happened to Dr Helen Haines, to occur to my office?”

MPs across the political divide have spoken forcefully of the need for more protection for their offices after the alleged attack on the Indi MP last week, raising alarm about threats and violence directed to their staff. Politicians are also revealing the scale of abuse, online and offline, directed toward them, including death and rape threats.

In the first Labor partyroom meeting since the alleged attack, Albanese gave a long address, saying this week “must be a turning point” for civil discourse and how threats are responded to. He also conceded there needed to be more investment in security and safety for politicians.
Albanese said MPs have had to “put up with the threat environment for too long”, that the government “need to do more”, and “more can and should be done”.
“You’ve all dedicated so much to the safety of others in the workplace. I’m determined to make sure we do everything for your safety and the safety of your staff as well,” he said.

Albanese did not give specifics, but promised a “swift government response” on safety, and noted numerous MPs had raised the prospect of receiving duress alarms, or panic buttons, to alert authorities of a safety incident. This was among a “series of options” under consideration.
The home affairs minister, Tony Burke, also told the meeting that the government was looking at safety at polling booths around election time.

Government sources said numerous changes were being considered, with a fulsome response and proposal likely to be revealed in coming days. MPs have raised a wide range of concerns, including greater security and hardening of their electoral offices, better communication with federal police, and resources for security at their private homes like CCTV and lighting – all options understood to be under consideration.
An ongoing review into commonwealth workplaces will also be expedited by Labor, with recommendations specifically about safety and security to be delivered soon.

The opposition leader, Angus Taylor, told his MPs in a Coalition partyroom meeting of ongoing conversations with the government about personal safety and the importance of getting it right, but did not raise any specific proposals.

Payman, who quit Labor in 2024 to sit on the crossbench, on Monday night lashed out at the prime minister for not responding to a request for additional staff in line with other independent political offices.

The prime minister has discretion over the allocation of personal staff, which are typically more senior advisers. All politicians receive electoral office staff, but Payman has zero advisers while 16 other crossbench MPs and senators shared 30 advisers, according to an internal document tabled in the hearing.

In a Senate estimates hearing, Payman questioned minister Don Farrell whether the staff allocation shortfall was due to Albanese having a personal gripe with her, claiming her staff were severely overworked.

“If [Albanese] cares so much about the welfare and wellbeing of people who work in this building, then I implore you [Farrell] and the prime minister to please look into the fact that my staff are burning out,” she said.
“Is the prime minister waiting for something, like what happened to Dr Helen Haines, to occur to my office? To me? For him to take our request seriously?”
Farrell and other Labor senators in the hearing strongly rejected the insinuation, but Payman refused to withdraw the comments when asked until her staffing request was dealt with.

Payman told Guardian Australia last week there had been a massive increase in the number of death threats and hate comments since 2024 when she defected from Labor. Payman said her office manager had opened mail last year containing human faeces, resulting in a biohazard team having to respond.

“We had all these people in hazmat suits come through [the office],” she said. “The trauma that that inflicts on my staff members is horrible. No office or no worker should ever have to deal with that kind of crap.”

items.title: Labor condemns One Nation cartoons depicting Penny Wong being murdered as Hanson says videos ‘not going anywhere’
paragraphs: Labor has accused Pauline Hanson of stoking division and violence in cartoons showing attacks on the foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, as One Nation defends its social media content, admitting it might not always be “in good taste”.
As parliament grapples with the safety of politicians in the wake of an alleged attack against Indi MP Helen Haines last week, cartoons produced by Hanson have come under increased scrutiny.

A 2022 episode of Hanson’s Please Explain series shows Wong being killed by the prime minister, Anthony Albanese. She is depicted slumped face-down over a desk, covered in blood and with a knife protruding from her back.

Scenes in Hanson’s Super Progressive Movie, released in February, show Wong being beheaded by Albanese, who believes he is killing Hanson with an axe. After Wong’s dismembered head drops to the floor, the One Nation leader quickly reveals herself to be hiding nearby.

On Sunday, the Australian federal police commissioner, Krissy Barrett, urged politicians to use respectful and cautious language, drawing a direct link between overheated political rhetoric including the Hanson cartoons and the rise in violent threats against politicians in Australia.
“It tells you everything about One Nation that they are happy to keep depicting this kind of violence,” she told Guardian Australia.
“Australians deserve elected representatives who are working to improve their lives, instead of promoting division, violence and personal attacks.”
A spokesperson for Hanson provided comments she made over the weekend, when she alleged Labor and Liberal “dirt units” were already back at work after the Haines attack.

“The Please Explain cartoons have nothing to do with the tragic attack on Helen Haines. They will not be going anywhere. Liberal and Labor politicians want our cartoons censored because they don’t like the scrutiny,” Hanson said.
On Monday, the creator of the cartoons, Mark Nicholson, refused to apologise for another episode making light of Tasmanian senator Jacqui Lambie’s health conditions.
That episode featured a depiction of Lambie saying: “I can’t laugh because of my prolapsed vagina.”
But Nicholson, who is also a candidate for One Nation at the upcoming Victorian state election, told the ABC he wanted to pick on people with public profiles.
“People who are powerful need to get a reality check,” he said.
“If you’re in the public realm, you open yourself up to praise, but you also open yourself up to parody. That’s the price you pay.”
One Nation’s Victorian leader, Warren Pickering, defended the cartoons on Tuesday, even as he agreed with calls to lower the temperature in Australia’s political discourse.
He said the Please Explain cartoons “absolutely” had not contributed to a deterioration, likening them to Looney Tunes characters Wile E Coyote and the Road Runner.
“Cartoons are an expression of freedom of speech,” he said.

“Now they’re not always going to be in good taste. They’re not always going to be defensible. But we used to be able to laugh at ourselves, and we use comedy as a medium to engage in broader dialogue within the political sphere on issues that otherwise a lot of people aren’t talking about, and realistically should be.”
Pickering said the Lambie cartoon “raises dialogue on broader issues”.
“I’d say those that do have a problem with a lot of the cartoons … make your own cartoon from the other side of politics. We know Labor’s a joke, but let’s see if they can do comedy.”

items.title: Jay-Z to perform at Super Bowl half-time show
paragraphs: Rapper Jay-Z will perform at the Super Bowl half-time show in February, the NFL has announced.
Jay-Z's company Roc Nation has produced the half-time show since 2019, and he plays a key role in selecting each year's performer but he has not performed before at the NFL championship game.
"Anticipation as to who Jay-Z might have guest star at halftime for the big game will now kick off," the NFL said in a statement. "Of course, his wife, Beyoncé, will be atop the list."
Next year's Super Bowl LXI will take place on 14 February near Los Angeles.
The hip-hop star will follow in the footsteps of other recent half-time performers including Bad Bunny, Kendrick Lamar, Usher, Rihanna and The Weeknd.
The musical performance draws global attention while the sport is watched by tens of millions of people in the US.
Kendrick Lamar's 2025 performance was the most watched Super Bowl half-time show in history and won the Emmy award for outstanding music direction.
The announcement was made after Jay-Z, whose real name is Shawn Carter, performed two shows last weekend at the Los Angeles stadium where the Super Bowl will be played.
The LA shows were part of a tour to celebrate the 30th anniversary of his debut album Reasonable Doubt.
"From 'Reasonable Doubt' to standing on the Super Bowl halftime stage, this has been a journey," said Jay-Z, whose real name is Shawn Carter.
"Thirty years of music, work, and culture on the world's biggest stage. This run continues to be a dream come true."
NFL commissioner Roger Goodell said he "couldn't be more excited for fans around the world to experience the artistry, creativity and cultural impact he will bring".
"When we first reached an agreement with Roc Nation to produce the show, I had just one request: that Jay-Z take the stage himself one day, whenever the moment felt right to him," Goodell said.
The star's accolades include being the first rapper inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame, 25 Grammy awards and being inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2021.

items.title: Our loos? They’re inspired by Milan’s Villa Necchi! The reborn planks-and-plasterboard theatre trouncing its flashy neighbours
paragraphs: Since the 2012 Olympics, the skyline of Hackney Wick in east London has bristled with cranes. The athletes may be long gone but the legacy of the sporting spectacle rolls on, as developers continue to extract profits from rising land values around the Olympic park. Across the canal, in this former industrial edgeland, there are more cranes than ever, busily hoisting prefabricated brick cladding panels into place, wrapping the latest loft-living concepts with a veneer of industrial chic. Where factories once stood, replicas of factories have risen, complete with sawtooth roofs and Crittall-esque windows, offering concierge-serviced views of the surrounding regeneration-scape.

But among all the crane towers, one is different from the rest. It stands still, now relieved of its duties, and encased in a silvery sheath of polycarbonate. Big red letters cling to the shimmering shaft, spelling out the new home of the Yard theatre. Once used to haul bits of buildings, the steel crane tower now serves as a beacon-cum-ventilation shaft, glowing by night while exhausting stale air from the theatre below.

It is one of many elements of this striking, low-budget building that have been cleverly reused and recycled, bringing economical pizzazz to the energetic young establishment. Founded in 2011 in a former printworks, the plucky warehouse theatre has come of age, with a £4m new building on the same site – and Ian McKellen set to star in the next show.

“We only expected it to last a few months,” says Jay Miller, founder and artistic director of the Yard, describing the theatre’s first incarnation. He cannily secured a cheap lease by pitching to the building’s owner that he could eliminate their security costs by occupying the vacant warehouse. He then hired the recent graduates of Practice Architecture to conjure an ad hoc auditorium on a shoestring. Their beguiling bricolage of butcher’s curtains, pink plasterboard and scavenged scaffolding planks lasted more than a decade and drew a loyal local crowd, staging shows that transferred to the National Theatre, became Bafta-winning television and won an Olivier award.

Miller, ever on the lookout for funding opportunities, saw a chance to expand when plans were mooted to redevelop the surrounding Queen’s Yard into a mixed-use district. That project never materialised, but Miller succeeded in leveraging £3m of CIL (Community Infrastructure Levy) from the London Legacy Development Corporation – the post-Olympic regeneration body – to fund the new theatre. In effect, the apartment blocks rising all around the Yard helped to pay for its existence.

The resulting project is far more than the usual “planning gain” token of community benefit. The work of Takero Shimazaki, a Tokyo-born Londoner who was shortlisted for the Stirling prize last year for an elegant timber and stone-roofed house, it is a tour de force of how to do a lot with a little. It reads like a collage of its context: a shed clad with corrugated fibre-cement sheeting, rising from graffiti-covered warehouse walls on one side and framed by a new brick gable end on the other. The bricks include subtle shades of blue, yellow and magenta, in a nod to the previous printworks, while the name of the theatre is spelt out in the brickwork, recalling the faded factory signs of the area.
