Kane's 12 goals for England last season - including six at the World Cup - take him up to a total of 73.
Only one player in history from Europe's top leagues has scored more in a season, Lionel Messi's 82 for Barcelona and Argentina in 2011-12.

Next on the list are Muller (72 in 1972-73), Cristiano Ronaldo (66 in both 2011-12 and 2014-15), former Brazil striker Ronaldo (66 in 1996-97), Erling Haaland (64 in 2022-23) and Luis Suarez (64 in 2015-16).
Former England striker Alan Shearer recently told BBC Sport: "The winner of the Ballon d'Or should be Harry Kane.
"His numbers for the last 12 to 18 months have been absolutely sensational for Bayern and for England. For that reason, he should get it."

Another ex-Three Lions player Danny Murphy added: "His goalscoring has been relentless, brilliant. He's had one of the best seasons of his career and it'll be a great reward for him if he gets the trophy.
"He's been brilliant at Bayern Munich since he's been there, adapted really well and he's been the best centre forward in the world for the last 12 months."
The Ballon d'Or was only available to European players from its formation in 1956 until 1995 when it was opened up to everyone.
Since then in four of the seven World Cup years, the Ballon d'Or has been awarded to a world champion - including Messi in 2023 (as the 2022 World Cup was in the winter).
However, that was the first time since 2006 it had happened, with Messi, Cristiano Ronaldo and Luka Modric all winning since then despite not winning the World Cup that year.

This is only the fifth time in the past 20 years that the Ballon d'Or has not gone to a player who has won either the World Cup, the Champions League or a European Championship/Copa America - with Kane joining Messi (three times) and Ronaldo.
Lamine Yamal, who won the World Cup with Spain, had been one of the favourites but lost out to Kane.
Last year, winning the Champions League helped PSG and France's Ousmane Dembele to the crown.
Kane may have just won the Ballon d'Or but some are already wondering if he is in a good place to retain it next year.
The striker has scored 10 goals in his opening 12 games for Bayern this season.
Throw in six goals in four Nations League games for England and that is a total of 16 in 16 matches so far.
Bayern are unbeaten in the Bundesliga and Champions League this season.
If they were to win a Treble - and Kane keeps scoring at about a goal a game - it would be tough to look past him, especially in a season with no World Cup, European Championship or Copa America.
The last player other than Messi or Ronaldo to win it two years in a row was Marco van Basten in 1988 and 1989.
However, Lamine Yamal will be hoping to make it third time lucky after finishing second twice in two years.
He has started the season in electric form, with 10 goals and 10 assists in 13 games for Barcelona in La Liga and the Champions League.
And Barca are currently favourites to win the Champions League, which could ultimately end up being a deciding factor.
He would be the youngest player to win the Ballon d'Or - aged 20 - if he does lift it next year.
Real Madrid's Kylian Mbappe will also fancy his chances of winning for the first time, with 14 goals in 13 appearances for club and country.
The youngest winner remains Brazilian Ronaldo, who was 21 when he won in 1997.
Arsenal, who have never had a Ballon d'Or winner, and Paris St-Germain are two of the other frontrunners to win the Champions League.

items.title: Chris Mason: Budget is imminent as tricky issues pile up for Burnham
paragraphs: In recent years, many but not all politicians have approached the issue of Brexit like you or I might approach an electric fence. Avoid getting too close and, if needs must, climb over it gingerly.
Burnham has no such reservations: he has repeatedly said in the last few weeks, let's talk about Brexit. He reckons the current deal between the UK and European Union isn't good enough.

Over the weekend he went further, suggesting he wanted an "honest discussion" about freedom of movement. Countries in the EU's single market have to sign up to freedom of movement, which lets people live and work in all the countries that are part of it. Given how big a deal immigration was for many in the EU referendum in 2016, even reopening the question of freedom of movement feels like a big deal.
On Monday morning, the prime minister appeared to add more detail, suggesting freedom of movement would only return in the UK having been sanctioned in a referendum.
Later, though, his team wouldn't repeat that, instead emphasising that Burnham wants to start a broad based conversation – without at this point committing to any possible outcome.

Some of his MPs felt this was a self-inflicted tangle he could have done without. Others see merit in Burnham's penchant for narrating his thoughts and possible direction publicly, thereby using his position to seek to dominate the political debate.

While the Labour Party's centre of gravity tilts towards a collective instinct that a closer relationship with the EU would be preferable to the status quo, there are differences of emphasis and indeed outright disagreements about how much closer and when would be wise.
Last week, Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh approved drilling in the Jackdaw field in the North Sea, about 150 miles east of Aberdeen.
This is principally a gas field and Fahnbulleh grounded her justification in providing the UK with greater energy security, at a time of war in Ukraine and in the Middle East.

The gas, she said, could be tapped into and serve British homes and businesses pretty much straight away, with the tax revenue put into an "energy wealth fund", with the aim being to invest in renewable and low carbon energy projects.
But what about the Rosebank field, 80 miles north west of the Shetland islands, with its focus on oil?

Labour figures in and outside government acknowledge this is a much, much harder sell to plenty in their own party and beyond. Some, who want to see the project go ahead, fear that the energy secretary is not likely to be convinced that it should.
It is in that context that we should see allies of the chancellor pointedly making it known that he is in favour of it.

His public language was quite telling on the day Jackdaw was approved, when he was talking about the Energy Wealth Fund: "It means the extra tax revenues that come from North Sea oil and gas can be directed into developing more clean energy projects for the future."
Note his reference to oil. Fahnbulleh said that Rosebank was "a different proposition" to Jackdaw.

Can those who worry, in particular, about the emissions from a new oil field, be won over by an argument grounded in this being a geopolitically pragmatic and environmentally credible part of transition to cleaner fuels?
Some Labour MPs hope so, but they know it's a tall order to persuade some, including some in government – which could, if it was approved, raise the question of ministerial resignations. Let's see.

items.title: New weather warnings as third storm set to hit Scotland
paragraphs: The Met Office said gusts of up to 65mph (105km/h) would hit coastal communities in the south-west on Monday evening and into the morning.
Forecasters added strong winds would be accompanied by heavy rain at certain points.
The latest weather system is unlikely to be as widely disruptive as Storm Boelo - or Storm Austen which came before it - and has so far not been named.
The next name on the storm list for the 2026/2027 season is Chloe.
Storm Boelo brought heavy flooding and wind gusts in some areas of up to 85mph (137km/h) on Monday.
A 60-year-old man died after being struck by a falling tree at Mid Kelton, near Castle Douglas, in Dumfries and Galloway on Sunday.
On Monday evening, Scottish and Southern Energy Networks (SSEN), which covers the north of Scotland, said work was ongoing to reconnect the supplies of about 15,000 homes that remained without power.

Meanwhile, Scottish Power Energy Networks (Spen) said all but a "very small number" of its 50,000 customers who lost power in Ayrshire and Dumfries and Galloway would have it restored by 02:00 on Tuesday.
Almost 100,000 homes had power restored in both areas across the weekend.
The Scottish Environment Protection Agency (Sepa) said it had put an amber risk of flooding in place for the northern and Western Isles and Caithness and Sutherland.
Sepa said areas of the southwest and Argyll, including the Solway Firth and Firth of Clyde, would experience volatile conditions, with large waves and strong winds.
They said flooding of low-lying land was likely.
Highland Council said flood gates on the mile-long Caol and Lochyside flood protection scheme, near Fort William, had been closed following a warning from Sepa.
Police Scotland said a high risk of disruption remained with poor weather conditions expected on Tuesday.

Police Scotland Assistant Chief Constable Mark Sutherland said that, although the amber weather warning was no longer in place, disruption was "likely well beyond that due to further poor weather, fallen trees and other damage caused by the storm".
Social Justice and Housing Secretary Shirley-Anne Somerville told BBC Scotland News there were "challenges ahead" due to the prolonged nature of the conditions.
She urged councils to review their readiness, adding authorities were working to ensure that "everything that can be done is being done".
Somerville also said that everyone can play a part by getting "households as resilient as we can, as well as looking after neighbours and friends".

items.title: Iraq's closure of Iran border crossing fuels protests
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Kurdi article.
Iraq's decision to close the al-Sheeb border crossing with Iran has triggered protests in the southern Maysan province and heightened tensions with Tehran.

The crossing was closed Wednesday, October 21, until further notice. Iraqi authorities cited technical and security concerns, but the decision has drawn growing opposition from influential Iran-aligned factions within Iraq's political establishment.
On Sunday, dozens of protesters blocked a main road leading to oil companies in Maysan, demanding the crossing reopen amid concerns about rising food prices and disrupted trade.

On Monday, an Iraqi court issued an arrest warrant for Mustafa Duair Abdulhassan, head of Maysan's provincial council, following a complaint from Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidii's office regarding Abdulhassan’s threats of civil disobedience. The prime minister also ordered an investigation into his remarks.

Abdulhassan warned Sunday that residents would "resort to civil disobedience and cut Maysan off from the rest of Iraq" unless the crossing reopened. He is affiliated with Sadiqoun, the political wing of the Iran-aligned Asaib Ahl al-Haq militia led by Qais al-Khazali.

The Islamic Resistance in Iraq, an umbrella organization of Iran-aligned armed factions, separately accused Baghdad of yielding to American "dictates and pressure" over restrictions on border crossings and Iranian flights.
Iranian state media reported that Tehran had received no advance notice of the closure. Iranian Interior Ministry spokesman Ali Zeinivand said the matter was under review.
VOA has reached out to the White House and State Department for comment on allegations of U.S. involvement in the closure but had not yet received a response at the time of publication.
Speaking to VOA, Abdul Amir Ta'iban, an adviser to Zaidi, accused Iran of facilitating smuggling activities that have damaged Iraq's economy and society.

"Iran has caused great harm to Iraq through the smuggling of drugs and counterfeit money," Ta'iban said, warning that narcotics trafficking has devastated Iraqi youth and counterfeit currency undermined confidence in the dinar.

He said Baghdad should close crossings where violations persist but acknowledged that broader closures would require a political decision by the government, backed by the ruling Coordination Framework coalition.
Iran's Embassy in Baghdad rejected the smuggling allegations, describing them as false.
A State Department spokesperson told VOA earlier this month that Iran has long exploited Iraqi resources and supported armed groups threatening Iraq's sovereignty.

"Our goal remains a sovereign, secure, and prosperous Iraq that prevents attacks in and from its territory, delivers for its people and the region, and stands as a strong U.S. partner," the spokesperson said.

Safwan Qusay, an economist close to the prime minister's office, said Iranian exporters sometimes convert Iraqi dinar earnings into dollars through informal markets, complicating Baghdad's financial controls.
According to Qusay, Iraq is exploring a mechanism allowing payments for certain Iranian humanitarian imports through an account in Oman, subject to U.S. approval.
Jamal Kocher, a member of Iraq's parliamentary Finance Committee, also did not rule out a sanctions connection, citing efforts to combat weapons trafficking, narcotics and counterfeit currency.

items.title: Australian politics live: Lambie awaiting Hanson apology over cartoon; security crackdown for nine MPs after alleged Haines attack
paragraphs: Farrer independent spent $1.7m on byelection campaign, electoral returns show
Former Rio Tinto boss to lead defence procurement watchdog
Lambie says Hanson hasn’t personally apologised over cartoon
Security reviews ramp up for MP offices over attack fears
Some politicians will receive security updates in their electorate offices after raising concerns about threats in the wake of the alleged attack on Helen Haines.
At least nine MPs will have security crackdowns accelerated for their electorate offices, the finance minister, Katy Gallagher, confirmed, after they raised concerns last week.
Security in Parliament House’s public places will also be stepped up.
Jacinda Ardern joins University of Sydney as lecturer and mentor

In news adjacent to federal politics, former New Zealand prime minister Jacinda Ardern has revealed she will lecture and mentor at the University of Sydney after moving to Australia earlier this year.
Based in the school of public health, she will host guest lectures and masterclasses and engage in mentoring.
Teal and regional independent backers were Farrer independent’s top donors

The top donor, Regional Voices Fund, backs independent candidates in regional seats while the second-highest donor, Keldoulis Investments, owned by Robert Keldoulis, is a major backer of Climate 200 – the funding vehicle that supports teal independents in getting elected.
Overall, Milthorpe spent $1,708,845 on her campaign, receiving $1,680,439 in donations and gifts.
Candidates endorsed by political parties, like Farley, are able to defer the campaign spending reports until February the following year when political party annual returns are published.
As a result, Farley’s electoral returns show he spent only $5,119 on his campaign and received no donations. This figure will likely be updated in February.

The independent candidate, Michelle Milthorpe, received almost $1.7m in donations from more than 5,000 donors in her campaign against One Nation in the seat of Farrer earlier this year, electoral returns show.

Milthorpe, backed by regional independents, including Helen Haines, ultimately lost the battle to One Nation’s David Farley in Sussan Ley’s former seat, 42.45% to Farley’s 57.55% on a two-party preferred basis.
The returns data, released by the Australian Electoral Commission yesterday, shows $670,653 of the total amount – or about 40% – donated was over the declaration threshold of $17,300.
Keldoulis Investments Pty Limited: $117,000
More respectful discourse is ‘what Helen Haines would want’: Richard Marles
The defence minister, Richard Marles, hopes politicians continue to show respect and civility for more than a day, following the outpouring of support for independent Helen Haines:
double quotation markI really hope that all of us can do better … we need to really try and collectively engage in bringing the temperature down, and have a much more respectful and civil discourse.
And I know that’s what Helen Haines would want.
Political debate should be ‘robust but respectful’: Ruston

A day after MPs addressed the House of Representatives paying tribute to independent Helen Haines, who was injured after an alleged attack in her electorate, Liberal senator Anne Ruston maintains that respect is necessary in political debate.
double quotation markWhat we do here sets the tone for what the rest of the nation thinks is acceptable.
There is a huge responsibility on politicians, not to shy away from robust debate. I don’t want anyone to think that we shouldn’t be having strong debate.
Governments need to be held to account for their decisions and that’s our job and we should keep doing it.
You can be robust and strong, but still be respectful.
Katy Gallagher calls for social media platforms to be held accountable for online abuse
Minister for women, Katy Gallagher, says the volume, scale and forcefulness of threats and abusive language has increased during her time in politics.
This follows reporting from the ABC that found almost 5,000 threats and violent comments were flagged on the social media accounts of 22 Labor politicians in three months by an AI tool.
double quotation markIt’s simply out of control in an online world and we’ve got to make the platforms accountable.
Facebook is the worst in terms of the platforms, Instagram and TikTok less so, but still bad.
The platforms have to help us here because, the way it’s going now, our accounts are just a place for people to come and abuse pretty vigorously.
Greens to announce plan for Victorian lobbyist register
The Victorian Greens will today announce an election commitment to establish a lobbyist register and ban political donations from “big corporate money”.
The party said there would be a legislated register for lobbyists and a ban on political donations from the gambling industry, fossil fuel companies and property developers.

Victoria has a $7,500 cap on donations but only foreign donations are banned. The state has a lobbyist register – but the only sanction available is the removal of a lobbyist from that register. Guardian Australia last year reported no lobbyist has been sanctioned in Victoria since the latest code of conduct was introduced by the Napthine government in 2013.
Victorian Greens leader, Ellen Sandell, says the state’s laws have allowed corporations to influence politics in the state:

double quotation markThese corporations don’t hand over thousands of dollars out of the goodness of their hearts. They expect something in return, and it’s everyday Victorians who end up paying the price.
Former mining boss Kellie Parker will lead the new defence agency overseeing the delivery of projects worth hundreds of billions of dollars.
The Albanese government will announce Parker, who used to run Rio Tinto’s Australian business, has been appointed to the role of national armaments director for five years.
She begins next month at the new independent defence delivery agency which was set up in response to cost blowouts and lacklustre project management.
Defence industry minister, Pat Conroy, pointed to Parker’s experience in bringing cultural change to the mining company after the destruction of the ancient Juukan Gorge rock shelters in 2020.
He said other senior female appointments including the first woman to lead the army, Lt Gen Susan Coyle, were merit-based.
double quotation markThey’ve both dealt with male-dominated industries with cultures that are pretty rough and challenging for women, and so they’re perfect people to lead that cultural journey.
Malicious actors using AI to find vulnerabilities, defence minister warns
The defence minister, Richard Marles, is doing the rounds this morning to address the Australian Signals Directorate’s (ASD) annual cyber threat report.

It warns Australians to prepare for more basic and important online services to go offline unexpectedly and urges businesses and critical infrastructure to use cutting-edge AI models to defend against digital threats.

double quotation markIf you’ve got an old system which is attached to the internet, it is effectively a gateway to a malicious actor. You’ve really got to prioritise hardening your system, even if that’s at the expense of access to it.
Malicious actors, are now able to use AI to find vulnerabilities in the systems of organisations and companies, and they’re doing that to exploit them.
Female and First Nations public servants facing ‘more egregious’ abuse online, parliament hears

A departmental boss has warned female public servants receive more “more egregious forms of abuse” on social media after complaints from bureaucrats about what they claim is selective clipping of evidence being posted online.
Last month, the Secretaries Board, which includes heads of departments, asked the government to introduce rules restricting testimony from being uploaded to X and Instagram.
They argued the clips were exposing public servants to ridicule and abuse, but their bid has been dismissed as an attempt to limit public accountability.
Steven Kennedy, secretary of the department of the prime minister and cabinet, told a parliamentary hearing yesterday:.

double quotation markI would note that secretaries have observed that it is often female public servants and those from First Nations … backgrounds who experience the more egregious forms of abuse on social media.
Thanks, Martin Farrer! I’ll steer us through politics for the rest of the morning.
Liberal candidate’s husband allegedly assaulted in Melbourne confrontation
The husband of a Victorian Liberal party candidate has allegedly been assaulted during a confrontation over election signs.
A Liberal party spokesperson on Monday evening confirmed the husband of their candidate for Yan Yean, Amanda Dow, was involved in an alleged incident in Mernda yesterday afternoon.
double quotation markWe understand Ms Dow’s husband approached a member of the public who was removing Liberal party campaign signage and was allegedly assaulted.
He suffered facial injuries and was taken to hospital and was discharged today.

Police confirmed a 59-year-old Mernda man had been charged with recklessly causing injury, criminal damage and unlawful assault over the incident, which they alleged occurred near Abundant Avenue and Bridge Inn Road at about 2pm yesterday.
double quotation markPolice have been told the victim attended an address to retrieve political campaign signage when he was [allegedly] assaulted.
They said the man has been bailed to appear before Heidelberg magistrates’ court on 1 February 2027.

Independent senator Jacqui Lambie says the One Nation leader, Pauline Hanson, has yet to personally apologise to her over her party’s “Please Explain” cartoon that poked fun at her medical condition, as the candidate behind the cartoon refuses to apologise.
Hanson publicly apologised for the cartoon that depicted Lambie saying “I can’t laugh because of my prolapsed vagina” and the video was subsequently removed from online platforms.
However, Lambie told ABC’s 7.30 last night that Hanson “hasn’t emailed, messaged, even sent me a nice little card and said, ‘I’m really sorry for doing that’”.

Mark Nicholson – who is running in the Victorian state election for One Nation and is cofounder of Stepmates Studio which makes the cartoons – told 7.30 it was his job to “pick on people in the public realm” and he would not apologise:
double quotation markNot right now. If I do anything that is apology-worthy, I’ll apologise.
Nicholson claimed he had “drawn quite a lot of attention” to the medical issue, rather than trivialising it.
Lambie said Nicholson should drop out of the election.
Good morning and welcome to our live news blog. I’m Martin Farrer with the top overnight stories and then it will be Kat Wong with the main action.

items.title: Busted's James Bourne says 'hero' brother saved his life with kidney donation
paragraphs: James Bourne: "I can't believe how much better I'm starting to feel already."
Busted star James Bourne has said his brother "saved my life" by donating a kidney, after doctors had given him "a few years left to live".
The guitarist, 43, dropped out of an arena tour featuring his band and fellow punk-pop favourites McFly in September 2025, just a day before it began.
He blamed health problems and was replaced by his younger brother Chris.
James later said he needed major surgery to "extend my life", and has now thanked his "hero" Chris and said they are both recovering from their transplant operations.
Bourne with his Busted bandmates Charlie Simpson and Matt Willis in 2023
"Wow, what the hell happened?" James wrote on Monday. "One minute you're heading out on tour, the next thing you know you're on the bench and out of the game.
"My condition was serious and the doctors told me I had a few years left to live.
"I'm happy to share now that my youngest brother, Chris, who stepped in for me on tour last year, has saved my life yet again. This time quite literally by donating me one of his kidneys."
Chris Bourne went on tour with Busted after his brother was forced to drop out
James continued: "I can't believe how much better I'm starting to feel already.
"I'm still going to need some time, but I wanted you to know that we're both recovering from surgery just fine. My brother is a hero."
Chris posted his own message on X saying simply: "We did it brother."
Bourne has not given any more details of his condition.
Busted had eight top 10 hits in the UK between 2002 and 2004

The guitarist, vocalist and songwriter shot to fame with Charlie Simpson and Matt Willis in Busted in the early 2000s, and the trio had hits including What I Go To School For, Year 3000 and Crashed the Wedding.
They scored four number one singles in the UK before splitting up in 2005. In 2013, Bourne and Willis teamed up with McFly to make McBusted, before Simpson rejoined Busted for a full reunion in 2015.
Bourne has written songs for McFly and 5 Seconds of Summer, and also fronted his own band, Son of Dork. He recently released the music from his stage musical Murder at the Gates.

items.title: Brazil: defeated Flávio Bolsonaro ordered to surrender passports
paragraphs: The far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro was banned from leaving Brazil and ordered to surrender his passports just hours after his dramatic loss in the presidential election to the leftist president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.
The ruling was issued by supreme court justice Alexandre de Moraes, the same justice who oversaw the trial of the senator’s father, the former president Jair Bolsonaro, for attempting a coup.
Bolsonaro posted a video saying the decision was based on an interview his brother, Eduardo Bolsonaro, gave last Friday urging his brother to leave Brazil if he lost the election.

The brief ruling, however, only refers to a criminal case in which the federal police are investigating Flávio Bolsonaro over his possible involvement in a money-laundering scheme. The ruling orders him not to have any contact with his friend Willer Tomaz, a lawyer linked to betting companies that police suspect were being used to launder about £680m.
It also cancelled all of Bolsonaro’s passports, including the diplomatic one he holds as a congressman, and ordered him to hand them over within 24 hours.
Bolsonaro was the first to speak publicly about the matter, before Brazilian media were even aware of the judge’s decision.

In a video posted on social media, he said he had just left a visit to his father, who is under house arrest in Brasília, when “Lula’s federal police were at his door and in the middle of the street, and I was served with an order to hand over my passports and I am also prohibited from leaving the country”.
He added that, although his brother – who is in self-imposed exile in the US – told a US podcast on Friday that he favoured the senator leaving Brazil if he lost the election, “I never said that”.
When his Senate term ends early next year, Bolsonaro will be out of public office for the first time in 24 years, and therefore without the special jurisdiction afforded to officeholders.

He is under investigation in another criminal case, too, over what happened to the £20m he was captured on tape asking a disgraced banker accused of corruption to provide for a biopic about his father.
Like Jair Bolsonaro four years ago, the senator has still not conceded defeat to Lula.

The Folha de S.Paulo newspaper also reported that Flávio Bolsonaro had been persuaded to drop his plan to seek to annul the election, which he had announced after the result was declared on Sunday night.

Bolsonaro had claimed that the two-hour extension of voting – intended to allow voters who had been unable to access the mandatory free public transport to cast their ballots – had harmed the election, despite the fact that his own campaign had also argued for an extension.
According to the newspaper, allies and lawyers told him his argument was legally weak.

Bolsonaro had still not publicly reversed his demand for an annulment, and in the same video he said he would file another case to have Lula’s ticket disqualified over alleged abuse of economic power, a similar case to others his legal team brought during the campaign.

items.title: Samsung’s Switch 2-ready MicroSD Express card is on sale for less than $50
paragraphs: Samsung’s discounted memory cards can store dozens of games, depending on their size.
Samsung’s discounted memory cards can store dozens of games, depending on their size.
is a tech journalist and commerce writer based out of Portland, Oregon. He’s contributed to sites like Digital Trends, Business Insider, and WIRED.

Running out of space on your Nintendo Switch 2? Thankfully, Samsung’s P9 MicroSD Express card is discounted at multiple retailers, with the 256GB version going for $47.99 (Amazon, B&H Photo) and the 512GB version $99 (Amazon, B&H Photo). The smaller card typically sells for around $80, and the larger option usually sells between $150 and $200, though both are higher than their original launch prices, likely because of the ongoing memory shortage.

The P9 is great if you need more storage for your Nintendo Switch 2. The microSD Express card offers sequential read speeds of up to 800MB/s, but only gadgets with a microSD Express card slot can take full advantage of the highest speeds. That includes certain cameras, tablets, and drones with a microSD USH-I slot.

First-party Switch 2 games generally run between 10 and 30 gigabytes each — the upcoming The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake is 27GB, for example — while third-party games can take up even more space (Cyberpunk 2077 is 60GB). Until recently, the Switch 2 was one of the few devices that could take advantage of the faster MicroSD Express standard, but this year’s Asus ROG Ally X20 also added support for MicroSD Express. While expensive, the latter is an impressive gaming handheld that runs Windows 11, giving it a versatility that’s hard to find elsewhere.

items.title: Macklemore begins Free Palestine tour after Ed Sheeran fallout
paragraphs: Macklemore has begun his Free Palestine tour in Dublin after Ed Sheeran's controversial decision to drop the rapper from his tour last month.
The American star is playing to a crowd of up to 13,000 at the city's 3Arena - and, hours before the sell-out show, had promised "many incredible surprise guests".
The artist - whose real name is Benjamin Haggerty - announced the tour days after being dropped from Sheeran's Loop Tour following pro-Palestinian comments he made onstage.

He was criticised by Jewish groups after saying "free Palestine" at two concerts and making political speeches, including referring to the death toll from Israel's military action in Gaza as a genocide - a claim that Israel rejects.
Sheeran later stressed that the decision to drop Macklemore was made by his promoter, not by himself.
Among the acts on the bill at Macklemore's Dublin show were singer-songwriter Hozier, rap trio Kneecap and folk band Beoga, who had also performed on Sheeran's tour.
Macklemore has said that proceeds from his Free Palestine tour will go to organisations supporting Palestinians.
He will perform in Paris on Thursday and in London on Friday.

The Israeli military launched a campaign in Gaza in response to an unprecedented Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 were taken hostage.
During Israel's military campaign in Gaza more than 70,000 people have been killed, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
Israel says its troops conduct self-defence operations in Gaza and the occupied West Bank in accordance with international law.

The controversy began when Macklemore, performing as the opening act for Sheeran at a concert in New Jersey in early September, said: "A big part of the reason why I wanted to do this tour in the first place is so that I could stand up in stadiums like this and say two words that are very, very dear to my heart: Free Palestine."
The Thrift Shop rapper then performed a song dedicated to pro-Palestinian protesters at Columbia University in the US.
The lyrics are critical of Israel's military actions in Gaza after the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attack.
After he was taken off the tour on 14 September, Macklemore accused stadium owners of rallying together to push him out.
He was also accused by billionaire stadium owner Robert Kraft of hate speech and antisemitic rhetoric surrounding Israel and Gaza.
Sheeran said that the decision to drop Macklemore from his tour was made by concert promoter Messina Touring Group.
His early remarks led to all of his support acts to drop out of the tour in solidarity with Macklemore, and fans to express frustration.
Sheeran then addressed the controversy during the start of a gig in Philadelphia.
He said he had made "mistakes" handling the fallout, apologising to fans and taking a stand on the Israel-Gaza conflict, which he said was "a humanitarian issue".
He described the 7 October 2023 attacks as "horrific" and also called the situation in Gaza "unjustifiable and disproportionate".

items.title: Anthropic is burning gas to feed the AI boom
paragraphs: As it prepares to go public, Anthropic’s S-1 filing makes generative AI’s methane dependency glaringly obvious.
“Competition for access to electrical supply and data center locations with adequate power availability is intense.”

In documents filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission Monday, Anthropic acknowledges that data centers are becoming increasingly reliant on “natural gas” — the fossil fuel industry’s marketing term for what is primarily methane — leaving the company’s AI data center buildout vulnerable to rising fuel costs and existing supply chain constraints. And in a possible catch-22, Anthropic admits that rising global temperatures — a symptom of burning fossil fuels — will increase the company’s operating costs.

“Competition for access to electrical supply and data center locations with adequate power availability is intense,” Anthropic says, adding that some of its planned data centers rely on electricity generated by natural gas turbines on-site. Anthropic leases capacity from hyperscalers, but it announced a $50 billion dollar plan last year to expand data centers in Texas and New York.

The US, the epicenter for data centers globally, is planning to build more fossil fuel generation capacity than it has in a decade as data centers demand more electricity. Donald Trump’s administration has sought to kill renewable energy projects while tilting the regulatory landscape in favor of fossil fuels, which Trump claims is a more important energy source for powering data centers around the clock than solar and wind farms that generate power intermittently.

Now, a shortage of gas turbines is slowing data center construction. Some developers are installing gas engines on-site as a way to avoid long wait times to connect to power grids. Developers are also turning to more simple turbine technology at these sites as they face backlogs from turbine manufacturers, making on-site power generation less efficient and more polluting as a result.

Data center electricity demand could wipe out decades of gains in air quality over the next five years, one recent Texas-based study found — raising levels of soot, smog-forming pollutants, and planet-heating carbon dioxide. Even as data centers create more greenhouse gas pollution, Anthropic’s S-1 points to climate change as a risk to its bottom line. It will have to pay more for electricity and water to cool servers at data centers as temperatures climb.

Nevertheless, Anthropic expects increased competition for natural gas and pipeline capacity from hyperscalers and cloud service providers rushing to build their own data centers. “This competition could drive up the price of natural gas,” the company notes.

Gas makes up the biggest chunk of the US electricity mix, 40 percent of the nation’s power generation. And Americans are already feeling the pain of rising costs as utilities scramble to upgrade energy infrastructure and meet rising power demand.

Pissed-off residents have successfully blocked dozens of proposed data centers across the US. Anthropic acknowledges that the specter of ballooning utility bills is enough to interfere with a data center project. “If our efforts to secure electrical power are perceived to affect other utility customers and the broader grid, regulators may impose conditions, standby charges, or other requirements intended to address such impacts,” it says.

If regulators push data center developers to shoulder more of the costs for new energy infrastructure, Anthropic says that could also raise its operating costs. And without a secure gas supply and the pipelines to transport the fuel, the company says, it might need to delay or abandon planned data center projects altogether.
Ultimately, these challenges could stunt Anthropic’s growth:

Any failure to secure access to adequate electrical power, any legal, regulatory, or other administrative action or change limiting the availability of electricity, or any significant increase in energy or compliance costs, could adversely affect our cost structure and limit our ability to scale our compute infrastructure, develop and deploy our models, and service our customers.

items.title: Pentagon designates Confucius Institute in US as national security threat
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Mandarin article.
The Department of War has designated Chinese-funded Confucius Institutes on American university campuses as a national security threat.
China's Foreign Ministry responded Monday, saying it opposed what it called “smears and stigmatization” targeting the institutes.

In a video address Friday, Secretary of War Hegseth described Confucius Institutes as “Chinese government-backed propaganda cultural programs” that had infiltrated universities in nearly every U.S. state. He said Congress had banned the institutes several years ago, but they had returned in new forms under different names.

“It turns out that 80 new propaganda cells across 30 universities had popped up using different names and different charters, but with the same mission: to steal intellectual property and to infiltrate the minds of American students,” he said.

He said the Pentagon had added those organizations to its list of institutions threatening national security and had “systematically dismantled every single one of these organizations” over the past two months.
Hegseth did not identify a specific instance of intellectual property theft involving a Confucius Institute in his remarks.

Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said at a news conference Monday that China opposed what he described as “smears and stigmatization targeting Confucius Institutes.”“Educational exchanges and cooperation between China and the United States help deepen mutual understanding between the peoples of both countries. They are two-way, mutually and win-win, and should not be disrupted or undermined,” he said.
Days before Hegseth’s remarks, the Department of War announced October 19 that it had successfully completed initial research security audits at 30 universities across the United States.

The Pentagon said all 30 universities covered by its initial audits had addressed identified relationships with foreign entities on the National Defense Authorization Act’s Section 1286 list of entities of concern.

According to the Department of War, the audits resulted in more than 80 “termination-related actions.” Those included ending relationships with listed entities, as well as precautionary terminations involving entities not specifically on the list

items.title: Pakistan defends attacks on Afghanistan, denies civilian casualties
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Pashto article.

Pakistan’s government has defended its attacks on Afghanistan as an act of “self-defense” and rejected killing Afghan civilians. Pakistan’s Foreign Affairs Ministry, in a statement Monday posted on X, said that its attacks are “directed against terrorists and their logistical support based in Afghanistan,” and rejected the civilian casualties “attributed” to the attacks.

Pakistani forces and the Afghan Taliban have recently clashed along the border, and Pakistan also has carried out airstrikes in Afghanistan. The Afghan Taliban called Pakistan’s airstrikes in Afghanistan “an act of aggression and crime in violation of all accepted principles.”
The United Nations Mission in Afghanistan said in September that it had documented more than 1,100 civilian deaths and injuries from cross-border attacks in Afghanistan so far in 2026.
Pakistan accuses the Taliban of sheltering the militant group Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan, or TTP, which has taken responsibility for attacks inside Pakistan.
The Afghan Taliban publicly deny harboring any militant group, but a U.N. report, released in August, said that the Taliban continue to support TTP.
A spokesperson for the U.S. State Department told VOA in an email statement in July that Pakistan has the “right to defend against terrorist attacks.”
“The Pakistani people have suffered greatly at the hands of terrorists,” the unnamed spokesperson said at the time.
The U.N. said that the Pakistani Taliban’s attacks inside Pakistan have increased.
Pakistan has said that the attacks inside Pakistan have resulted in more than 3,500 casualties so far in 2026.

Ismail Khan, an editor at Pakistan’s Dawn newspaper, told VOA that both sides blame each other, and relations between the two countries have deteriorated. “Borders are closed [between the two countries]. There is no trade and no negotiation is underway,” he said.
Khan added that some countries, including China, Turkey and Qatar, have tried to get Pakistan and the Afghan Taliban to resume negotiations, but those efforts have not yielded results.
“In the end, both countries have to negotiate and find a way out,” he said.
But Khan said the situation is likely to continue for now because both “Pakistan and Afghanistan are not ready to negotiate.”

items.title: Afghanistan sees drop in men’s university enrollment as women remain barred
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Dari article.

University enrollment among men in Afghanistan in 2026 has fallen nearly one-third from levels before the Taliban’s takeover, while women’s enrollment has remained at zero for the third consecutive year.

A new U.N. report says enrollment at public and private universities in Afghanistan totaled approximately 208,000 students, all men, in 2026, down from about 430,000 students, including 124,000 women, in 2020.

“Women remain excluded from formal participation, male enrollment is substantially lower than in 2019, the academic workforce has shrunk, and private institutions face continuing financial pressure,” the report said.
The Taliban barred women from university education in December 2022 and from medical training institutes, which offer diplomas in nursing, midwifery and other health fields December 2024.
Since seizing power in 2021, the Taliban have placed sweeping restrictions on women’s rights and freedom.

Under the Taliban, women and girls are not allowed to get an education beyond 6th grade. They are barred from working with government and non-government organizations, going to parks, gyms, public baths, and beauty salons.
The group has issued more than 100 decrees that curb women’s and girls’ rights and freedoms, including their right to get an education.

Meanwhile, the Taliban have tightened their control over men’s higher education by imposing numerous restrictions, such as conducting new oral exams on religious topics, dress codes, removing hundreds of books and other learning materials, and discontinuing over a dozen subjects related to human rights, democracy, gender, governance and other social science fields, according to the U.N.
Farid, a university student in Kabul, told VOA that students have few incentives to pursue higher education.
“There are only a few opportunities for graduates. This makes people not be motivated to continue their studies,” said Farid, who did not want his full name disclosed for security reasons.
He added that most of the students also face financial problems, forcing them to discontinue their studies.
“The economic situation has worsened. Students are not even able to pay for commuting to the university daily,” he said.
Farid added that students are also worried about their job prospects after graduation.
Mohammad Asif Nang, former deputy minister for education in Afghanistan, told VOA that the future of higher education in Afghanistan is uncertain.
“For example, a young man loses hope of a better future when he cannot find himself in a system based on competition, merit and professional qualifications,” he said.
“These trends affect not only higher education itself but also the future supply of qualified professionals across Afghanistan’s education, health and wider service sector,” the U.N. report said.

items.title: Protest leaders urge French pupils to keep barricading their schools
paragraphs: French children should continue to barricade their schools and take part in street protests, a student union said on Monday after the government announced a package of education measures to try to stem the crisis.

“Today we’re at the negotiating table, we’re able to negotiate with the government,” Pierre Sourzat of Les Lycéens told France Info television. “We’re in a power struggle and we still need to call for continued mobilisation to meet a maximum of our demands.”
The government told high school student representatives it would cap some class sizes and review the university application system. But Sourzat said: “We want measures, not half measures.”

More than five weeks after the start of high school blockades in September, the government made the proposals to address the demands of what has become the biggest youth protest movement in years. It has been joined by trade unions and cost-of-living protesters in regular mass street demonstrations on Saturdays.

High school pupils had demanded an end to teacher and staff shortages and for repairs to decrepit school buildings that had collapsing ceilings, mould, broken toilets, a lack of chairs and windows that did not shut.
The education minister, Édouard Geffray, said some schools were so dilapidated they were “not fit” for teaching. He announced a government loan of €4bn to regional authorities to begin repairs.

Responding to complaints of overcrowded classes, Geffray said class sizes for 15-year-olds in the first year of high school would be capped at 28 in the 50% of schools in the lowest-income areas, increasing to all high schools next year. He said more teaching posts would be created and there would be a review of the French baccalaureate system.

The university application platform, Parcoursup, which has been described as opaque and unfair, will be changed in 2027 and replaced by a new system in 2028, according to the government. Parliament will hold a debate on the issue on Wednesday.
The higher education minister, Philippe Baptiste, said 15,000 extra student places would be created in higher education, focusing on vocational courses.

Louis Letoublon, who attended a meeting with the prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, on behalf of Les Lycéens, said: “Bravo to the high school students who have demonstrated. We’ve got something: the government is afraid and knows it must do something and listen to us. “Not all our demands were ⁠met. We’ll go on for as long as it takes.”
Baptiste said the government’s door was “open” for more discussions.
Several children have been maimed or seriously injured in the protests, allegedly by police explosive weapons. Hundreds of children have been arrested and held in police custody.

The authorities have increased security measures and placed restrictions on demonstrations after France saw its worst day of violence in years on 17 October, with looting, fires and vandalism of state buildings. Curfews have been put in place in certain cities, alongside protest bans. Protest routes were pushed to the outskirts of cities on Saturday when demonstrations passed off largely peacefully.

The interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, said there had been a new phenomenon in cities such as Nice and Montpellier at the weekend with ultra-right groups arriving in “organised formations” and targeting protesters. Eleven suspects are to face charges.
In a visit to Marseille on Monday, Emmanuel Macron said nationwide street protests were likely continue, and that the next day of street demonstrations on 31 October would also be a “day of risk”.

The French president said the looting and vandalism seen on 17 October should never happen again. Speaking to members of the police, he said it was “not normal” for the country to be in “such a state of turmoil” six months before a presidential election.
Macron steps down next spring and the far-right leader Marine Le Pen is leading the polls.

Macron said: “We will continue to hold the line. If we all do our jobs well, this movement will subside – because we will address legitimate expectations, and because order will be maintained. But nothing is a foregone conclusion.”
Authorities have admitted to security and intelligence failures that paved the way for the clashes on 17 October.

items.title: Oscar-winning producer says BBC gave her £400,000 payout after she raised antisemitism concerns
paragraphs: An Oscar-winning executive producer claims she received a £400,000 payout from the BBC after alleging she faced antisemitic remarks from colleagues at the corporation.

Lucie Kon, who worked as a commissioning editor overseeing several documentaries, including Mr Nobody Against Putin, told The Telegraph, external that BBC colleagues said Zionists like her were "evil" following the 7 October attacks.
Kon's post was made redundant as part of a BBC restructure. She said the payment she received was for redundancy back pay and settlement for personal injury caused by the process.
The BBC says it did not uphold any of the allegations of antisemitism but accepted there were "shortcomings" in how it treated Kon, which had a "personal impact" on her.
The corporation did not specify what the shortcomings were.
Kon says she raised a number of concerns about how she was treated following the Hamas-led 7 October attacks.
"I really did feel like I had Jew stamped on my forehead. I became a problem. And anytime I tried to mention anything, it was like, 'Oh God, there she goes again.'
"I became a proper pain. They didn't know what else to do with me."
Kon also claimed she was told by a colleague that "if you want to call Hamas terrorists then you have to call Israel terrorists, too".
She helped lead a group representing Jewish staff in the corporation and raised issues with the then-director general, Tim Davie.
Kon told The Telegraph that her religion had not been an issue during her many years working for the BBC until the October 7 attacks.
She later told LBC that the BBC was "not institutionally antisemitic".
The BBC said it was grateful that Kon acknowledged the BBC is not institutionally antisemitic, adding that she was a "valued member of staff with many years of dedicated service" to the corporation.

items.title: When an invasive fish is also tasty, Maryland schoolkids can help 'eat the problem'
paragraphs: Invasive blue catfish are a problem in the Chesapeake Bay and its tributaries, preying on native seafood like the blue crab. To help keep them in check, local schoolchildren are eating catfish for lunch. Ryan Kellman/NPR hide caption

PRESTON, Md. — It's lunchtime at Preston Elementary School, on Maryland's Eastern Shore. Kids file in, get dollops of food on their segmented trays, and maybe grab a chocolate milk. But one option on today's menu is special, served alongside grapes and broccoli.
"I got a catfish sandwich!" announces Ben Rochon, a second-grader. Between mouthfuls, he tells me how it is: "It's yummy."
He's eating a catfish cake, also known by its nickname, the "catty patty." Some kids like it with ketchup or mayo. Fifth-grader Teagan Donovan goes minimal.
"I like it by itself with no toppings, because it's pretty good by itself," she says. In Teagan's case, "by itself" is literal: "I ignore the bun."
At Preston Elementary School on Maryland's Eastern Shore, catfish sandwiches are a highlight of a local food initiative. Ryan Kellman/NPR hide caption

Not everyone's into the fish cake — after all, this sunny Friday is also pizza day at Preston, and cheese slices are tough competition. But more kids have been trying catfish when it's served a couple of times a month. That's good news to Beth Brewster, who oversees food services for Caroline County Public Schools.
"It tastes great. It's great for you," she says of the fish cake.

It has another benefit: It's made with blue catfish. Since spreading to the Chesapeake Bay in recent decades, the fish has become an apex predator. It can grow to more than 100 pounds; its voracious appetite is fueling worries that it's eating too many native species.
"It tastes so good because it eats everything we love — crabs and rockfish, and all kinds of things that we love to eat," Brewster says.
Beth Brewster led her chefs in developing a catfish cake known as the "catty patty." Brewster is the supervisor of food services for Caroline County Public Schools. Ryan Kellman/NPR hide caption
State officials first asked Brewster to help tackle this problem about eight years ago.

"I was like, 'Beth, we have this invasive species. It tastes pretty good, is what we've been hearing. Can you do something about it?'" says Karen Fedor, administrator of the Farm and Food Programs at the Maryland Department of Agriculture.

Fedor describes Brewster as an "out-of-the-box thinker" who'd be up for the challenge of experimenting with recipes that appeal to kids — and also conform with federal dietary requirements. That's how Brewster's team landed on a crabcake-like dish made of blue catfish.
"It was kind of fun for my chefs to play with the recipe," she says, adding that because they have USDA approval, the cakes can be served anywhere in the U.S.

The pandemic initially slowed the effort down, Brewster says. But then she heard that Virginia was partnering with a California-based program called Bay2Tray to connect seafood with schools. Brewster got in touch with a simple message: "I have a fish for you."

Now, other school districts in both Maryland and Virginia are serving blue catfish. In Preston, a rural community near the Choptank River, kids are excited to do their part by chowing down on the catty patty.
"It kind of tastes like crabs, but in a fish way," says fifth-grader Raelynn Truitt. "It's like, really really good."

Fifth-grader Teagan Donovan, at left, doesn't go for ketchup, mustard or mayo on her catfish sandwich. Classmate Raelynn Truitt is also a fan: "It kind of tastes like crabs, but in a fish way," she says. Ryan Kellman/NPR hide caption

To Brewster, the blue catfish presents a bad news-good news proposition. It's invasive — and its white, flaky meat is tasty, in part because it's not a bottom feeder. It was first brought to rivers in Virginia in the 1970s for recreational fishing.
"Blue catfish are a large freshwater catfish native to the Midwest," says Branson Williams, manager of the Invasive Fishes Program for the Maryland Department of Natural Resources.
The idea, he says, was that people would catch the fish in a few rivers feeding into the Chesapeake. But brackish water in the bay would keep them from spreading.
"They're a freshwater fish; they should stay in those freshwater portions of the river," Williams says. But, it turns out, "they can handle some salinity."

Zach Swann sorts through the day's catch of blue catfish at a dock on the lower Potomac River. The species was first brought to rivers in Virginia in the 1970s for recreational fishing. It's spread to every tidal tributary of the Chesapeake Bay in Maryland. Ryan Kellman/NPR hide caption

You could even say those officials got catfished. Because in 2018, when Virginia and Maryland had record rainfall, the blue catfish used all that fresh water to leave those rivers and find new habitats.
"They now occur in every tidal tributary of Maryland. They occur in the Chesapeake Bay proper," Williams says.

In some spots, blue catfish make up about 70% of the fish biomass, or total weight, Williams says. Virginia officials have also been raising the alarm, saying the fish is out of control and threatening the seafood industry that relies on traditional species such as flounder.
Blue catfish reproduce quickly and eat important forage fish like menhaden. They also gobble up young crabs and fish, adding to stress on those populations.
If the Chesapeake Bay has fewer blue crabs, it would be a huge economic and cultural blow to Maryland. So the state is turning to the only predator the blue catfish really has: people.

It joins other states trying to tap humans' role as apex predators to combat invasive species. They include Kentucky and Illinois targeting the Asian carp, and Maine and Washington state's battle against invasive green crabs.
Rocky Rice likes to average at least 1,200 pounds of blue catfish on each outing on the lower Potomac River. The invasive fish is now his primary target. Ryan Kellman/NPR hide caption

On a recent sunny morning on the lower Potomac River, Rocky Rice is bringing his catch back to the dock. He's a fourth-generation Maryland waterman. But instead of crabs, his boat is full of blue catfish. He tosses them into ice tubs, sorting them by size.
"Right at a thousand," he says, as he slings a fat catfish into a crowded tub. "It's usually about a hundred pounds to a tub."
That's actually a little light. Rice wants to average about 1,200 to 1,500 pounds. He goes out three days a week, pulling catfish from hoop pots that trap them in their nets.

Rice, at right, and Swann, his first mate, sort blue catfish by size and weight. Rice says the fish doesn't bring the high prices of some other seafood, but it provides a steady income for his small operation. Ryan Kellman/NPR hide caption
He started fishing for blue catfish 14 years ago to stay busy when he wasn't crabbing.

Now that's all flipped around. The market for blue catfish doesn't bring the high prices of other seafood, but Rice says the market and steady volume of his catch are strong enough to sustain his small operation.
"What I started off as just something to do to fill in, in between other seasons, actually has turned into my primary job now."
And Rice can fish for blue catfish year-round. Because they're invasive, there is no season or size limit.
"You can catch as many of them as you want," says Maryland Department of Natural Resources' Williams. "And you don't have to throw the little ones back. Please keep them all."
Before we leave the dock, I ask Rice if he eats blue catfish himself.
"Oh yeah!" he answers. "They're good. It's a snow white, mild fillet."

The lack of a "fishy" flavor means blue catfish is good for fish tacos, Rice says. But he has his own preference: "You know, I'm from the country. So, if we can, we want to deep-fry everything, like nuggets and fried fillets."
Students at Preston Elementary select their lunches, including a catfish cake sandwich. On a recent visit, the school also offered fillets. Ryan Kellman/NPR hide caption
By early afternoon, Rice's catch will be on its way to a processor. And that's where things hit a bit of a bottleneck. Catfish is the only U.S. fish that's required to have a USDA inspection.

The rule is meant to protect the U.S. market from cheap imports. But it takes money and time for a seafood processor to have a USDA inspector on site. As a result, only four processors in Maryland are able to handle processing blue catfish, according to Williams — even with grants and other help.

Still, the fish is making its way to grocery stores and restaurants around the country; in Maryland, it's also in schools and food banks. After all, it's an affordable protein that comes from a sustainable fish. That makes it a good fit for Bay2Tray, which focuses on developing new markets for bycatch and invasive fish.
"Just yesterday, I shipped a pallet of the blue catfish to a university in Texas," says Jenn Lovewell, chief nutrition officer for Real Good Fish, the company that runs Bay2Tray.
Rice secures his boat before heading back to his fish house in Maryland. Ryan Kellman/NPR hide caption
Both Lovewell and Brewster, the school official, say millions of pounds of the fish need to be harvested, just to maintain the status quo.
"It'll never be eradicated," says Brewster.
So she urges people to seek out the fish in markets and restaurants.
Or as Lovewell puts it, "Eat the problem and save the bay."
Newly harvested blue catfish are quickly put on ice, ready to be sent to a seafood processor. Ryan Kellman/NPR hide caption

items.title: Will the public change its mind about Meghan?
paragraphs: Meghan, who recently moved back to the UK with Prince Harry and their children, has frequently been accused of cutting off those once close to her.
Her treatment of her father was seen as a prime example.
"She ditched her family, ditched her dad, ditched most of her old friends, split Harry from William," wrote one commentator in 2020.
"Get on a plane and go see the poor man before it's too late," she was told on social media about her father.
All of that might need to be viewed in a different and more sympathetic light.
By 2019, Meghan had received disturbing allegations about Thomas Markle, in a letter from her father's first wife, Roslyn Loveless.
She says it is why she kept her distance and also why she didn't bring her children to him, including when she moved to the United States with her family.

That letter was shared with Meghan by the police, at a time when she was classified as a working royal. It's not clear who else knew about the letter, including Palace officials, but it must have been a sensitive matter for her.
And according to the Sussexes' spokesman, Meghan believed an investigation into the allegations was going ahead, presumably at a time when she was on official trips and having to put on a brave face.
There was also criticism levelled at Meghan in December 2025 when her father was in hospital in the Philippines, undergoing the amputation of his leg.
"I don't want to die estranged from Meghan. I want to meet my grandkids. It might be nice to meet her husband too," Markle told the Mail on Sunday at the time.
There was a media storm about whether Meghan was going to reach out to her father, culminating in a letter being delivered from her to her father, which at the time was assumed to be well-wishes.
But that whole episode now looks different with the benefit of hindsight. That letter was a much more fraught affair. It revealed that Meghan knew about the allegations against her father.
We now understand that Meghan was telling him he would never see his grandchildren.
Thomas Markle has strongly denied all the allegations against him, saying they are "sick lies" which are trying to destroy his reputation.
His daughter Samantha Markle has also rejected the claims, saying the stories are "fake news" and "clickbait".

"There will be no legal action against my dad with no evidence in so many flimsy stories and my dad never had access to any such content and was in the hospital most of the time that he was there," she wrote on X on Sunday.

Samantha also challenges the credibility of the letter written by her mother, Roslyn Loveless, which was shared with Meghan in 2019 and contained details of allegations of sexual abuse against Thomas Markle.
When you look through photos of Meghan at events over the last seven years, you wonder what was going on behind the familiar smile.
Those years have seen Netflix films, a tell-all memoir by Prince Harry, cookery series, podcasts and TV interviews. But a hidden narrative has been running in the background.
Meghan's supporters have pointed to other factors in how she has been treated, with racism and sexism part of that toxic mix.
But maybe there was also a sense of not knowing the authentic person behind the polished Brand Meghan.
On Instagram, she has curated her life to look idyllic, but perhaps she'll get a more generous hearing now that her back story is as messy and imperfect as everyone else's.
It could still be an uphill struggle to become more popular, beyond her own vocal, core group of supporters.
A survey from YouGov earlier this month found 22% of people had a positive view of Meghan, compared with 49% who dislike her.
That suggests there is still some way to go before Meghan fully wins the trust of the public. Fascination, yes. But affection, not always.
For the British public, Californian Meghan hasn't always translated well.
But perhaps this complex, still developing story - and the light it sheds on previous years - might mean there's a more rounded view of her in the future.

items.title: Surprising things we have learnt from Anthropic's blockbuster share listing
paragraphs: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has become a key figure in the current AI era.
Artificial intelligence (AI) firm Anthropic just released the required paperwork ahead of its long-anticipated debut on the US stock market.
The 335-page document included fresh details of how the Claude chatbot owner makes money, what it spends that money on and who it is controlled by.
Anthropic also detailed some of the the risks it claimed AI technology poses, including how it could take human lives. That information sat alongside the many purported benefits of the technology.
Here are five key points worth highlighting from the filing.
Every public company has to tell potential investors how things could go wrong.
Anthropic's "risk factors" were unique, also disclosing how the AI technology it is developing could doom humanity as a whole.

"Sufficiently advanced AI systems could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity," Anthropic said.

It noted that less than a year ago, a hacking group Anthropic believed to be sponsored by China "manipulated" Claude to successfully intrude on a number of institutions, including large technology companies, financial institutions, chemical manufacturing companies and government agencies.
But Anthropic said its success is dependent on its ability to constantly "develop, improve, and deploy the most advanced, capable, and useful AI models".

One of the most significant risks to that ability is Anthropic's access to infrastructure it needs, including computer chips and data centres, to build, train and operate the models that underpin its technology.
Anthropic has yet to disclose a target share price for its stock listing.

The company is widely expected to debut with a market valuation of $2 trillion or more, making it the largest stock listing in history. But the figure will be heavily influenced by its financial performance.
Anthropic lost $80.7bn (£60bn) in the first half of this year, double what it lost across 2025 altogether.
The company's overall revenue was $16.2bn billion for the six-month period. Revenues are rising rapidly, but the firm has a long way to go before it breaks even.

Troy Hooper, co-head of equity capital markets at Mergermarket, said Anthropic's revenue growth is "exceptional". But investors are "less forgiving" of tech companies promising huge future returns than they were even months ago, he added.
Anthropic's debt picture is also unclear given it has a huge amount of accounting charges related to certain forms of investment.
"As a result, investors do not yet have a clear view of Anthropic's underlying profitability or whether its rate of cash generation is sufficient to support the business as it scales," Hooper added.
Despite losing money, Anthropic has heaps of cash lying about.
At $131.6bn, almost all of its cash in hand is defined as "working capital", meaning it can use the money to fund its operations day-to-day.
Currently, Anthropic has more cash on hand than Meta and Google combined.
Anthropic's costs could rise as it faces fierce competition for top staff and computing power from other AI giants.
The leasing of data centres alone is costing the company $321.4bn so far this year.
Hooper said such large costs are expected to grow. Even with this kind of cash, it won't be enough to maintain its business growth.
Any investors in Anthropic "will be paying for future dominance, not present-day economics", he said.
Anthropic sees boundless ways it can sell its technology to customers.
A large portion of its current business comes from just 250 major enterprise customers, which it says have paid it at least $10mn in the past year.
An even smaller number, just five enterprise customers, make up a quarter of its current business.
Michael Monaghan, portfolio manager of Founder ETF, pointed out that "many top Anthropic customers have no long-term contract".
The company's level of business concentration leaves Anthropic dependent on a small fraction of its paying customers to support its growth, with no guarantee it will continue.

Anthropic also has enterprise relationships with the likes of Google and Amazon, both of which are also investors in the company "and competitors", creating potential business conflicts in the future, Monaghan noted.
Anthropic said its overall enterprise customer base has grown rapidly, going from roughly 1,500 customers last year to almost 12,000 this year.
Part of its growth strategy is offering Claude tools for free before working to "convert these users into paying customers over time".
The strategy has led to Claude seeing "the fastest enterprise adoption of any technology in history", the company claimed.
For all of the risks Anthropic has said AI poses, it also reiterated its claim AI will produce an "extraordinary" amount of good.
"Achieving our mission means the world gains the enormous benefits of frontier AI while mitigating the most significant risks," the company said.
That mission is defined as: "The responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity."
"We do not pursue projects based on commercial opportunity or research novelty alone; our efforts must advance our mission. "

Such hypothetical benefits include progress in healthcare, like the development of bespoke treatments for illnesses and improved disease detection, tailored education and legal advice and making more efficient power grids and batteries.
Decades of scientific progress could be condensed into years, accelerating drug discovery, disease detection, and the delivery of personalized therapy.

Anthropic said AI could provide individually tailored education and expert financial and legal advice, advance power grids and battery design for greater efficiency and reliability and help the "developing world" build more technological capabilities.
"Ultimately, we believe frontier AI will help drive global economic growth," the company said.

items.title: iPhone Duo now supports Apple Pencil with iOS 27.2
paragraphs: The latest iOS update also adds dual-camera use in group FaceTime calls.
The latest iOS update also adds dual-camera use in group FaceTime calls.
Photo: Amelia Holowaty Krales / The Verge
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Apple has just released iOS 27.2, bringing Apple Pencil support to the iPhone Duo. The software update also includes an “Edge Light” feature for the iPhone Duo that’s intended to illuminate your face during video calls.

Apple previously said the iPhone Duo would add support for the Apple Pencil “later this year.” The company’s first foldable comes with revamped iOS 27 controls designed to work across the device’s 7.6-inch inner display and 5.4-inch outer screen. Many major apps, like Netflix, Prime Video, and Microsoft Outlook, already support the Duo’s extra screen real estate, but some still need some work.

The iOS 27.2 update also allows Siri AI to take suggested actions in Messages, while adding support for Siri AI in more languages, including French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish. Apple is rolling out support for Google’s SynthID AI watermark in Photos and Image Playground, too, according to 9to5Mac.

Other smaller but notable updates include user profiles on the Apple TV app on iPhone. The Apple Podcasts app is also replacing its “Up Next” queue with a list of “New Episodes,” along with a “Continue Playing” section just beneath it. You’ll also see the new Apple Music logo. And group calls on FaceTime now support dual capture so you can show both what’s visible from your selfie cam and your back cameras.
Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates.
