items.title: ‘Extremely disappointed’: WA government seeks reimbursement from Deloitte over flawed university report
paragraphs: The Western Australian government has said it is “extremely disappointed” and is seeking an “expedited” cost recovery from Deloitte after errors were discovered in a report about a potential university merger, including AI-hallucinated references and hundreds of millions of dollars in cost discrepancies.
The government paid Deloitte $166,000 for a feasibility study on merging the University of Western Australia, Curtin University and Murdoch University.
Deloitte considered three merger options between the three universities, with “low”, “mid” and “high” cost scenarios, and broke down the calculations of those costs in the report’s appendix.

Under the “high” cost scenario of a merger between Curtin and UWA, the report calculates the “total costs to day 1” as $514m, and “post day 1” over five years at $145m. The total cost of those two payments is $659m but the report wrote $399m – a $260m discrepancy.

Prof Stephen Bartos, an expert in public sector governance at the University of Canberra, said the errors discredited the report. “In my view, they’re so extensive that you probably need a new report, or at the very least someone to go through that material from the ground up and rework it manually without the use of AI,” he said.
“Any errors in a report like this, especially on something controversial like a university merger, discredits the report, and Deloitte shouldn’t have had these errors.”

Under a “low” cost merger scenario between Curtin, UWA and Murdoch, the total costs to day one are $396m and total post day one over five years are $116m. That total would be $512m but the report calculates the two numbers to $823m – a $311m discrepancy.
Deloitte is already under pressure after it was revealed in the media this month that the same report contained hallucinated AI references, leading the state opposition to label it “AI slop”.

The consultancy firm admits in its report it used generative AI to “support the collation of research, synthesis of information and editorial proofing” and had earlier dismissed the errors as “minor”.
A spokesperson for the WA government told Guardian Australia that the Department of Energy and Economic Diversification had written to Deloitte to expedite the cost recovery process for the report.
“We are extremely disappointed these errors are being found now,” the spokesperson said.
“We are advised they do not affect the modelling in the report or its findings, but any errors will be corrected as part of a review by Deloitte which will re-issue the report.
“All available data, along with new information, will be interrogated by the university reform business case.”
The WA tertiary education minister, Tony Buti, described them as “typos”, though a day later said he was angry and disappointed with Deloitte.
Guardian Australia has found that one of the references to a World Health Organization report has a ChatGPT metadata tag on the URL, indicating that the link was directly sourced from the chatbot.

In the report, Curtin University is referred to repeatedly as the Curtin University of Technology – a name the institution has not used since 2010, and that was changed under an act of state parliament in 2017.
Bartos said the numbers diverging so significantly was cause for concern. “Unless the numbers add up, a government might not want to do it,” he said.

Prof Christian Downie, from the Australian National University’s school of regulation and global governance, who has previously examined submissions to government that contained AI hallucinations, said human errors happened and mistakes in reports could be expected and, although Deloitte outlined broadly its use of AI in the report, there was a lack of transparency.

“We need much more detail about how [AI is] being used and for what parts of the report writing process,” he said. “If they’re going to use it for data collection and if there’s concerns about the data, then that needs to be detailed in the report.”
Downie said without transparency it was hard to have confidence in the report. He said broadly as AI use increases, governments need to reassess their contracts with consultancy firms.

“All levels of government, both state and federal, need to be recalibrating their contractual relationship arrangements when they outsource work to consulting firms to ensure that the proper incentives and penalties are in place in those contracts,” he said.

The WA government has that argued the merger is a “once-in-a-generation” opportunity. Buti told the ABC on Tuesday: “I want to commit to it if the business case stacks up, and then it’s a government decision.”

It was not supported by Murdoch University, whose vice-chancellor, Prof Andrew Deeks, criticised the report and penned an op-ed on the university’s website arguing that “all that a university merger will do for WA is cost a lot of time, money and energy, while reducing choices for students and alienating alumni”.
“That the Western Australian government continues to be taken in by this nonsense is extraordinary,” he wrote. “Another fail for Deloitte.”
Deloitte did not respond to questions from Guardian Australia.

items.title: Neighbours is being recut into a microdrama focused on Margot Robbie – and her co-stars aren’t happy
paragraphs: The long-running Australian soap opera Neighbours is being recut with AI into a microdrama designed to be watched on phones, sparking a debate among the show’s actors and the industry over the wider implications of television archives being mined for new content.

RoseBerry Media, which specialises in making “vertical television” for phones, has repurposed original episodes of Neighbours for distribution on its Epis platform, using an AI-assisted production tool called RedSnapper.

The microdrama made from the footage will initially focus on Margot Robbie’s character, Donna Freedman, whom she played from 2008 to 2011. Two of Robbie’s storylines will be recut into vertical micro-episodes, creating about 150 minutes of content.

The Neighbours star Stefan Dennis has voiced concerns over the project, telling the Herald Sun it was “unbelievably invasive, morally and legally wrong and somehow it appears we can’t do anything about it”.

“I’ve got my agent [on it],” he said. “I imagine everyone else on Neighbours is doing the same thing, as well as the MEAA [Media, Entertainment and Arts Alliance] and Australian Writers’ Guild. Whether they can stop it is another thing. We’re dealing with a very big machine.”
Dennis’s agent told Guardian Australia he would not be commenting further.

A former Neighbours cast member, Matthew Werkmeister, who played Zeke Kinski from 2005 to 2011 and appeared alongside Robbie in a love-triangle storyline, told Guardian Australia that he only learned about the deal when he was approached for comment.
“I find it extremely concerning,” Werkmeister said. “Not from any money-making point of view, but from my image being used through AI and a platform I did not consent to.”

Werkmeister said he had received no notification from the Neighbours producer, Fremantle, or RoseBerry Media regarding whether residuals would be paid to actors in the vertical series. Guardian Australia understands that any residuals will be paid to writers and actors based on their agreements for the series, as per normal process.

“When I signed my original contracts, I was 13,” he said. “In all honestly I can’t remember exactly every line point, but AI and streaming platforms, let alone vertical streaming platforms, didn’t exist and was not a consideration.”
Werkmeister dismissed claims that the vertical format would introduce the classic soap to younger audiences and called the venture a “money grab for Fremantle”.

“They’re just trying to dump their existing library to make a quick buck,” he said. “I’d be intrigued to know if they reached out to the wonderful Margot Robbie, since her star power is likely a main motivator for this venture.”
Guardian Australia has contacted Robbie for comment.
Mattie Webb, the agent for the actor Sam Clark – who played Donna’s partner, Ringo Brown – said Clark was waiting to hear from US actors’ union Sag-Aftra before commenting.

But Webb, an LA-based manager with 27 years’ experience, said AI was rapidly disrupting the entire industry. “All week I’ve been dealing with deepfake videos and AI,” he said. “It’s a whole new world.”

The Neighbours microdrama arrives amid a boom in vertical serials, which are usually made up of episodes around just one-minute long and tailored for mobile phone viewing. The microdrama market, which originated in China, was estimated to be worth up to $15bn (A$21.4bn) globally last year.

Some verticals are entirely original and shot for the format, while others are cut from existing material; in 2023, Paramount Pictures released Mean Girls on TikTok as 23 episodes. Others are entirely unofficial, with fans recutting their favourite shows into snippets for millions of viewers on social media.

In this era, Neighbours is a goldmine, having broadcast more than 9,300 episodes between its launch in 1985 and end in 2025. The soap also served as a launchpad for several international stars, including Robbie, Guy Pearce, Kylie Minogue, Jason Donovan, Dichen Lachman, Natalie Imbruglia, Liam Hemsworth and Jesse Spencer.

In comments reported by Variety last month, Fremantle’s commercial and international chief executive, Jens Richter, described the project as “an exciting example of how technology and creative thinking can unlock new value from our diverse catalog and content library”.
Fremantle defended the microdrama when contacted by Guardian Australia, saying that it will only use “original, previously broadcast footage, dialogue and performances”.
RedSnapper, the AI technology, “does not generate new scenes or performances, alter actors’ faces or likenesses, or use synthetic voices”, a spokesperson told Guardian Australia.
RedSnapper was used to help with “catalogue analysis, editing and vertical reframing, with a human editor reviewing and approving every stage of the editing process”.
A RoseBerry Media spokesperson said the company was aligned with Fremantle’s response and had “nothing further to add”.
Australia’s largest union for actors, the Media, Entertainment and Arts Alliance, confirmed it was assisting Neighbours cast members and their representatives after the announcement.

The MEAA acting chief executive, Adam Portelli, said anyone involved in Neighbours could contact the union “to ensure their work is not exploited without their knowledge, consent or fair compensation”.

Portelli called on the Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, and parliament to legislate to protect the creative sector by ensuring workers “are fairly and directly compensated when their work is exploited by AI”.
A spokesperson for the Australian Writers’ Guild told Guardian Australia it was “in discussions with Fremantle and hopes to reach a fair resolution soon”.
Werkmeister also backed legislative intervention, warning that the project would set a precedent that would reach far beyond Ramsay Street.
“Converting existing work via AI without proper consultation or fair compensation sets a concerning precedent,” he said.
“We urgently need way more robust AI regulations, guardrails and proper consent mechanisms in place.”

items.title: Uh oh, the iPhone Duo complaints have begun
paragraphs: There was a lot of pressure on Apple to get things right with the iPhone Duo. It's been seven years since the first Samsung Galaxy Fold came out in 2019, and three years since Google released the first Pixel Fold. The refrain is that Apple does things late, but it does them better, learning from rivals' mistakes to put out something that feels more functional, more premium and 'just works'.
The iPhone Duo selling out until January suggested that people were buying into that idea with Apple's first foldable. Now the early reviews and feedback are starting to raise questions.
Dang these iPhone Duo screens can't be fixed til January! 😂💀💀💀 https://t.co/ZsZX5l42mpOctober 24, 2026

One of the most concerning issues coming from real-world feedback involves breaks concentrated around the hinge of the phone, including vertical cracks down the centre, dead pixels or lines across one side of the screen. And because of the scarcity of stock, some people have been told they'll have to wait until January for a replacement.
iPhone Duo Review: 10,000 Folds Later... - YouTube
While clearly not ideal, the extent of the issue is unclear. There's no evidence yet of a widespread manufacturing or design defect.

A lot of iPhone Duo testing posted on social media has focused precisely on the hinge and crease given that it's a potential source of weakness (and that the invisibility of the crease has been touted as one of the features making the Duo superior to other foldables.

In the video by Tim Pan above, the crease does become visibly deeper after 500 manual folds and palpably deeper after 10,000, easily within the range of a few months of real use, but Tim generally finds the hinge to hold up well.
But another test, by HTX Studio (below), finds that the crease became deeper than that of two other foldables after just 3,000 folds and also notes that the screen around the crease is softer.
iPhone Duo Review: After 3,000 Folds, Here’s What We Found - YouTube

Was on the fence with iPhone Duo. But will definitely pass on the $2,000 phone after it failed: ▫️dirt test (gets stuck in hinge and magnetic closing doesn’t work) ▫️lighter test (inner screen can’t handle 10 seconds of direct flame) ▫️bend test (OLED screen gets line defect) https://t.co/zOKK6pztL8October 24, 2026

Some have been subjecting to the poor Duo to harsher treatment. Trung Peng decides to pass on the device after finding the crease to be a magnet for dust and dirty. He also finds that the screen gets marked if you hold a naked flame to it. So, yeah, maybe don't do that.

I had two complaints about the iPhone Duo’s design that Apple responded to directly. Both are in my newsletter: 1) It gets warm. During FaceTime calls, while using the camera and sometimes just using other apps, the Duo can get quite warm. Apple says that’s the new thermal design working as intended, moving heat away from the chip. Glad the chip is cool. My hand isn’t. 2) Touch ID pushes my buttons. Instead of just using Face ID on the phone screen, Apple told me it wanted to keep unlocking consistent whether the phone is open or closed. But I’m mostly unlocking it in phone mode. Why not give me Face ID on the outside and Touch ID on the inside? I’d take convenience over consistency. Read the full review here—gift link: https://t.co/03Z58J2GxtOctober 21, 2026

Speaking of heat, other early tests have raised concerns about the phone running warm without being intentionally singed. Joanna Stern was concerned enough to end a FaceTime call during her testing because it felt too hot.

Apple responded that this points to the cooling system working correctly. The Duo's vapor chamber is slimmer than the one in the iPhone 18 Pro, and there's a flexible graphite heat pipe around the hinge to compensate. This helps transfer heat between the two halves of the device, increasing the surface area to dissipate heat but potentially making the whole device warmer to the touch.
iPhone Duo Review: First Generation Fun! - YouTube

Another common gripe with the Duo involves the optimisation of some apps (or lack of). Some apps designed for iOS 26 or 27 present a smaller layout surrounded by black bars. Some behave the same as iPhone-only apps on an iPad: presenting a tiny version of the app in the middle of the display, which is blurry when resized.
But apps that have already been redesigned for the iPhone Duo appear to work very well. It's not ideal for the Duo to launch before a lot of apps are ready for it, but developers will catch up.

Others have cited buggy transition animations and apps that get the camera orientation wrong. Sometimes Apple's own software seems to get confused show the wrong orientation. Again, this is something that can probably be fixed.

For Stefan Van Der Merwe, the lack of Face ID is a deal breaker. I don't think this will be such a decisive factor for everyone, but I can see how it can be disappointing for a phone designed with multitasking in mind. That said, as a foldable, the Duo really needs two hands.

We haven't completed our own review of the Duo yet, and I've not yet seen anything that should massively change people's decision on whether to buy the Duo or not. It was already clear that it's not one of the best camera phones, and it's not presented as such.

You might want to wait a few months for some of the software problems to be ironed out for a smoother initial experience of the Duo – but then you might have no choice with preorders backed up until the end the year. And by that point, you might feel you have enough patience to wait another nine months for the Duo 2.

items.title: "If I start at 8am, I feel I've lost the day already," manga artist Yé Wei shows us his obsessively organised art studio
paragraphs: Yé Wei (aka Esquissewei) is a French mangaka and the author of Astral. He founded Manga Dojo, an online drawing school, and is currently working on his second book. In this feature, he takes us on a tour of his art studio as part of our Artist in Residence series.

My studio is about 30 square metres, and it has a slightly odd history: it used to be two bedrooms – mine and my older brother’s – in my parents’ house just outside Paris, until we knocked the wall through. My brother’s bed is still in here, and I’ll come back to why that matters.

The space is split in two. On one side, everything digital: a Wacom Cintiq Pro 24 hooked up to a MacBook Pro M2 Max, running Clip Studio Paint [see the best digital art software – ed]. For manga specifically, nothing else comes close – the pen stabilisation, the panel tools, the screentones, it’s all built for exactly what I do.

All three screens are running my own drawings. When I’m working on my new manga I want my previous pages permanently in front of me, so I’m always referencing myself rather than hunting through folders.

The desk itself is custom-built: two and a half metres of solid wood worktop weighing around 100kg, which is not something you move on a whim. It's rated for 300kg of load. I had it built to carry everything at once: Mac, PC, drawing setup and the full streaming rig, without a single wobble.

I built the computer myself, and I’d be lying if I said it was purely for work – I’m a lifelong geek and gamer. The water-cooling loop was a project in itself. When I need to reset my eye before going back to a page, this is where I go.

On the other side, everything traditional, and this is where things get out of hand. I own more than 3,000 markers. Not a typo. Plus dozens and dozens of nibs, pencils and screentone sheets. I’m an ambassador for a few art brands, including Clairefontaine and Graph’it, so material arrives constantly and I ran out of places to put it.

This is my second desk, dedicated entirely to traditional work, with the marker and liner wall standing right in front of it. Everything is arranged so I can reach any colour without standing up or breaking concentration – that’s the whole point. I sit down here and just sink into the drawing. After a morning of screens, the smell of alcohol markers is what tells my brain it’s time to make something with my hands

Everything now lives in labelled boxes, because otherwise I’d never find anything again. There’s a third layer to the room too: I’ve been shooting photo and video since 2011, and I still use that gear every day.

A Sony FX30, a Sennheiser MKH 416 shotgun mic and big continuous softboxes – the proper studio kind – because I film courses and live critique sessions for my drawing school, and for the 550,000 people who follow the channel.
I sit on an HBADA X7, which has built-in massage, heating and ventilation – it sounds ridiculous until you’ve spent six straight hours inking a page.

Next to me is a manga library of over a thousand volumes that I raid constantly for reference, plus copies of my own manga, Astral. My day is very rigid. Up at 5:30, sport at 6, at my desk by 7. If I start at 8 I feel like I’ve already lost the day – which is ridiculous, but there it is. I work until noon, then my energy collapses, so I sleep from 2pm to 3:30pm.

That’s what the bed is for. It’s the single most important piece of furniture in the room. Cutting the day in half is non negotiable. Back at it until 6 or 7pm, then in bed by 10. I’m obsessively organised. Clean desk, batteries charged, every pen where it should be, or I feel half-lost before I’ve started.

The biggest lesson? For years I called myself a mangaka online and quietly felt like a fraud, because I was teaching manga without having published one. Then Astral came out in 2025 and the impostor syndrome simply vanished. I’m on my second book now.
Astral is the story of Nejma, a young woman searching for meaning, and Elane, a druidess, who are bound by Merlin’s lost grimoire as ancient Celtic legends come to life.
I was 40 when it came out, and I’d spent years teaching manga online while quietly wondering whether I had the right to – this book is what settled that question, for good.
This is an illustration of Sana, a character from the Astral universe, drawn in Clip Studio Paint.

I'm a serious figure collector: 12 large-scale statues and a small army of smaller ones. Owning them is a childhood dream made literal – as a kid these were completely out of reach, and now I get to work inside the universe that made me want to draw in the first place. They’re also genuinely useful for lighting and anatomy reference.

Gohan is my favourite character in all of manga. He’s the kid who inherits enormous potential and has to decide what to do with it, and every single day he pushes me to go and build my own version of that.
Nami is on my desk because we share one very specific trait: an excellent sense of direction. Whenever I travel with friends, I’m always the one navigating – nobody else even tries anymore.
Apprendre à Dessiner des Mangas is a practical guide book designed for those who truly want to learn to draw – not just watch tutorials, but pick up a pencil and get started.
You can see more of Yé's work on his website.

items.title: Flight disruption and thousands without electricity after Storm Boelo
paragraphs: Thousands of homes across the island of Ireland are without power after Storm Boelo.
Northern Ireland Electricity (NIE) said 7,000 customers have been affected, while about 41,000 homes, farms and businesses across the Republic of Ireland are without electricity on Sunday morning.
The worst impacted areas in Northern Ireland include Springfield in County Fermanagh and Bushmills in County Antrim, where more than 1,000 homes near each village are without power.
Flights have also been cancelled at Belfast City, Belfast International and Dublin Airports due to the storm.

An NIE spokesperson said high winds and severe weather conditions during Saturday night and into the early hours of Sunday morning resulted in a "level of damage to the electricity network, leading to power outages for some customers".
NIE said customers can check estimated restoration times using its Powercheck tool, external.
A spokesperson for the Republic of Ireland's ESB Networks said properties in the north west of the country are primarily affected.
"As Met Éireann weather warnings remain in place, there may be further power outages this morning," they said.
Among the villages worst affected in the Republic of Ireland is Milford in County Donegal with more 1,600 homes without power and Aghagad in County Sligo with over 1,200 homes impacted.
ESB Networks said crews have been deployed to all impacted areas and they "expect the vast majority of impacted customers to have their supply restored by this evening".
A yellow weather warning for all of Northern Ireland is in place until midday while a yellow wind warning is also in place in County Donegal until 15:00 local time on Sunday.
At Belfast City Airport, flights departing to Edinburgh, Cardiff, Manchester and Kirkwall on Sunday morning have been cancelled.
Meanwhile, flights arriving from Edinburgh, Leeds Bradford, Cardiff, Manchester, Birmingham and Inverness have also been cancelled.
At Belfast International Airport, 17 flights have been cancelled this morning.
"Storm Boelo continues to cause some disruption to flights today. Please check with your airline for latest flight information as delays can be expected," a spokesperson said.
At Dublin Airport, strong winds continue to have an impact on flight operations on Sunday.
"Mainly due to weather issues in other countries, airlines have so far cancelled 12 inbound and 12 outbound flights," Graeme McQueen from the airport's operator daa has said.
He advised passengers to travel to the airport as normal and keep in contact with their airline, adding that further disruption is possible due to the wind warnings.
An amber warning across parts of County Antrim and County Londonderry ended at 10:00 GMT on Sunday.
On Saturday, Northern Ireland's strongest gust of wind reached 78mph and was recorded in Orlock Head, County Down.
Magilligan in County Londonderry recorded 73mph and Castlederg in County Tyrone recorded a wind gust of 70mph.
Westerly winds will continue to gust close to 70mph in exposed coastal areas until well into the afternoon.
Generally, though winds will gradually ease through the afternoon with a significant reduction this evening.
An orange wind warning ended in County Donegal at 09:00 local time on Sunday.
On Saturday, Malin Head in Donegal had gusts of 83mph recorded.
The last 24 hours also brought notable amounts of rain with Castlederg and Lough Fea in the Sperrins recording almost 40mm.
Over 30mm has been recorded at Killylane in the Antrim Glens and 30mm at Stormont in Belfast.
Sunday is due to be a drier day but still very windy with some sunshine and occasional passing showers.
The disturbed weather pattern will continue into the half term week as another deep area of low pressure will bring more strong winds later on Monday and through to Tuesday.
The Met Office has issued a yellow wind warning across parts of Northern Ireland for this system which may be updated later on Sunday.
The second half of the new week, however, looks somewhat quieter, drier, and less windy.

items.title: Arup creates arrow-shaped viewpoint for Fehmarnbelt Tunnel project
paragraphs: A zigzagging path tops the demountable Pilen viewpoint in Denmark, created by engineering firm Arup to give the public views of the construction of the vast Fehmarnbelt Tunnel.

Fehmarnbelt Tunnel is an 18-kilometre-long road-and-rail tunnel being built underwater between Rødbyhavn in Denmark and Puttgarden in Germany to improve links between continental Europe and Scandinavia.
Pilen, whose name means “the arrow” in Danish, offers views of its construction site to help the public gain an understanding of its scale.
According to Arup, its design is intended to symbolise travel, evoking an arrow or compass needle, and it points to the site where the tunnel emerges in Germany to orient users.
The ramped structure measures 217 metres in length, reflecting the size of each of the 89 individual concrete elements that will form the tunnel, which will be the longest of its kind.

“The arrow-shaped design points towards the location where the Fehmarnbelt tunnel emerges on the German side, acting as a large compass needle for visitors,” project architect Kristian Winther told Dezeen.
“At 217 metres long, the viewpoint also reflects the length of one of the tunnel elements,” Winther continued.

“We hope the viewpoint will create a closer connection between the tunnel project, the local community, and visitors, giving people an opportunity to experience the scale of the project more directly.”
Pilen was designed for contractors Femern, which is overseeing the tunnel’s construction and wanted to open up the construction site to the public.
The site was chosen for its proximity to the tunnel portal, maximising views of construction work, but also for the expansive views of the coastal landscape beyond.
Pilen’s structure is built from landfill timber and steel and designed to be demounted once the tunnel is complete.

To facilitate this, all the components, including the foundations, are engineered to be easily reused in other projects, “helping to give the materials a life beyond the viewpoint itself”, Winther said.
The main deck is formed from timber and landscaped with greenery and local vegetation, through which a fully accessible landscaped walkway zigzags as it rises 24 metres above sea level.
Fehmarnbelt tunnel is scheduled for completion in 2029. It is expected to reduce journey times between Hamburg and Copenhagen to 2.5 hours by train.
We recently reported on a 300,000 square metres land reclamation scheme in Denmark created as part of the project, which will be landscaped with ponds and planting.
Other viewpoints recently featured on Dezeen include the Titlis Tower in the Swiss Alps by Herzog & de Meuron and Lech Mountain Mirror in the Austrian Alps by Snøhetta.

items.title: When a teen posts a selfie, how much filter is 'too much' filter?
paragraphs: How much filter is too much filter for kids and teens posting selfies on social media?

That is the question state attorneys general across the country are grappling with following a landmark settlement with Meta this summer. As part of the agreement, the social media giant agreed to block some digital beauty filters for minors — specifically those mimicking extreme transformations like cosmetic procedures or heavy makeup.
Now, the burden falls on state officials to tell Meta where to draw the line. But defining where harmless fun ends and harmful manipulation begins is far from straightforward.

For teenagers navigating the digital landscape, the pressure of online perfection is a daily reality. Much of that pressure has been driven by online beauty trends like "Instagram face." Coined in 2019 by The New Yorker writer Jia Tolentino, the phrase refers to a look characterized by a small button nose, high cheekbones and pouty lips. While traditionally only achievable in real life through plastic surgery or extreme makeup, it can be applied instantly online using beauty filters.

Mia Lerner, a 17-year-old high school senior in California and a youth body image activist, knows the toll these digital tools can take. She told NPR experimenting with beauty filters contributed to her eating disorder and left her struggling with her self-image.

"I've even tried to fix my nose with AI," Lerner said. "My face looks a lot better, I think, in [the] photo that I manipulated with these beauty filters. But I'm still living with this nose that I see in the mirror."
Lerner welcomes the aspect of the Meta settlement that aims to restrict beauty filters for minors. "It's a very important step in the right direction," Lerner said.
However, the agreement reached in August between Meta and 47 U.S. states — plus Washington D.C. and three territories — does not institute a blanket ban on all digital effects.

Filters that transform users into playful characters, like elves or puppies, will remain available for young people. But so will filters offering subtle beautification effects — such as smoothing skin tone or adding a slight eye glow.
It is this category of relatively minor editing that particularly concerns Lerner.

"When I see something that has been so obviously AI-generated, it's very easy for me to logically say, 'Well, that's obviously been manipulated so I can't compare myself to that,'" Lerner said. "But when I see these videos of people who are just slightly edited, it's a lot easier for me to go down that comparison path."
Meta has previously implemented measures to manage beauty filters, which are increasingly powered by artificial intelligence.

The tech giant has already banned filters that explicitly promote cosmetic surgery, such as those overlaying pre-surgery marker lines onto skin. It has also shut down its platform for third-party creators of these tools, introduced mandatory labels for AI-generated content, and deployed automated AI detection systems. Despite these systems, harmful aesthetic filters and features that keep children trapped in an endless cycle of scrolling, clicking, and staying online persistently slipped past these guardrails, as a federal judge wrote in a summary judgement denying Meta's defense this summer.

Meta is not the only tech company grappling with teen access to beauty filters. TikTok also restricts users under the age of 18 from using them. Snapchat does not restrict teen access to filters. Neither company responded to NPR's request for comment. YouTube told NPR it does not have any filters. But there's nothing stopping users from posting images or videos made with third party filters to the platform — or onto TikTok and Instagram, for that matter.

Meanwhile, state attorneys general are reaching the end of a two-month window they set themselves to provide Meta with guidance in the form of a letter on what constitutes a bannable filter — and what does not.
They face a moving target, as digital beauty standards evolve rapidly.

"If the states want to define what is a beauty filter, they should define what is beauty," said Florencia Solari, a creative technologist who has spent years developing AI and augmented reality experiences for global brands.

Solari noted that trend cycles move quickly. "Instagram face" is already falling out of favor. "People are starting to move away from that because it's starting to look a bit clownish," Solari said. "Now it's going towards extreme thinness. So that's another problem."

As a result, the tools that are used to achieve the latest look are therefore also changing. So what might be branded by lawmakers as an "extreme" beauty filter in 2026 will likely be different in 2027.
While beauty standards are changing quickly, so is technology.

Instead of sitting in boardrooms debating pixel thresholds for cheekbones, Kelly Frasier, the co-author of a recent study highlighting the negative impacts of social media on body issues in adolescents, said legislators should consider the fact that teens will soon be able to use AI to create entire fake universes around themselves, not just change the way they look. So they should focus on broader AI regulation for minors.

"I think that legislators are asking the wrong question if they're asking where to draw the line for beauty filters," said Frasier. "And to be honest, filters will probably become completely obsolete within the next few years."

On top of the technological and cultural challenges, legal experts warn that individual states may struggle to reach a consensus on what does and does not constitute what the settlement agreement describes as a "cosmetic procedure filter."

"What we don't really have a sense of is what happens if the states disagree with each other?" said David Greene, senior counsel at the Electronic Frontier Foundation. "What if one state finds, you know, eyebrow lifting to be completely acceptable and another one thinks it's awful?"

NPR reached out to the attorneys general offices in all four plaintiff states that led the trial — California, Colorado, Kentucky, and New Jersey — for an update on the guidelines. But officials either declined to comment or did not respond.
Beyond the U.S., some international regulators are hoping to avoid discussions around beauty filter definitions entirely.
In Europe, the proposed KIDS Act — designed to regulate youth social media usage — takes a sweeping approach.

In that plan, "Beauty filters – not extreme beauty filters; beauty filters full stop – are forbidden for minors," said European Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier. Regnier said EU legislators are closely watching the implementation of the U.S. settlement. "We want child-friendly services for our children. A beauty filter has nothing to do with a child-friendly service," Regnier said.
Meta says that it plans to enforce the ban on "cosmetic procedure filters" by early next year.

For youth activists like Lerner, the hope is that tech companies and regulators will include teens in these discussions. "So often it's just the government or these companies in these conversations," Lerner said. "The company should be asking us for our actual perspectives, like 'Are people actually using these extreme AI filters or is that not going to make a difference?' 'Do we need to target something else?'"
Meta said the company has partnered with teens over the years, but did not respond to NPR's question asking if it is doing so currently.

items.title: Five uncanny venues where guests are treated to frightfully unique interiors
paragraphs: With spooky season in full swing and Halloween rapidly approaching, this lookbook rounds up five venues featuring unusual decor, including faux body parts, dead insects and slaughterhouse machinery.
A London pub, a brewery in Copenhagen and a bar in Shanghai are among the selected projects.

This is the latest in our lookbooks series, which provides visual inspiration from Dezeen’s archive. For more inspiration, see previous lookbooks featuring billiard tables, wooden staircases and bookmaxxed interiors.
The owner of this Shanghai bar is interested in insects – local studio Atelier XY honoured this through the addition of over 1,000 preserved specimens.

A wooden grid covering the back wall and ceiling of the bar area features thousands of beetles housed in individual recesses, while a glass-brick wall containing 42 preserved Thai Black tarantulas acts as a partition. Pull-out drawers, containing yet more taxidermied creatures, double as slim side tables.
The atmosphere of being inside an oven was recreated in this Valencia nightclub by Spanish firm Clap Studio.
Red lighting, stainless steel, glowing ceiling grids and burnt-looking alpi wood cladding come together to create a blisteringly immersive interior.
Bar Far, Italy, by Clementine Keith-Roach and Christopher Page
Human legs support tables, disembodied hands hold candlesticks and torsos emerge from walls in this unsettlingly cave-like bar by artists Clementine Keith-Roach and Christopher Page.
The space, which was open on a temporary basis during early 2026, was described as being “at once church and tomb, prophecy and ruin, heaven and hell” by installation curator Vittoria Bonifati.
Dark wood panelling and chairs upholstered in tartan set the mood for The Scottish Room, which inhabits the third floor of The Audley, a pub in London’s Mayfair neighbourhood.

Designed by architecture studio Laplace, this room belies the rest of the comparatively playful interior, being dominated by a sprawling chandelier made from deer antlers hanging above a nine-metre-long oaken table.
A former butchery in Copenhagen’s Meatpacking District has been converted into a lofty brewery by local studio Pihlmann Architects, with an interior partitioned using translucent curtains.
The studio elected to retain the original system of hanging rails, which the abattoir would have once used to suspend up to 980 animal carcasses.

items.title: Just Eat's AI apocalypse raises a glaring question
paragraphs: Lots of gastronomy businesses have gone all in on unappetising AI food imagery, but surely even the most enthusiastic slop purveyor would baulk at the Just Eat AI fail. The food delivery app's implementation of very literal text-to-image generation saw restaurants' menus filled with grotesque fantasy creations.
Just Eat has apologised and said it was removing the images. But what was it thinking?

As reported by the BBC, images spotted on the Just Eat app in the UK include a bacon and egg soda bread cocktail at a Northern Ireland cafe and a 'jacket potato' represented by an actual jacket with pictures of baked potatoes on it.

Other gems included a plain garlic bread shaped like a plane because of a typo, a bowl of tiger cubs (tiger prawns, apparently), a literal toad in the hole and a 'lighter' breakfast depicted as a cigarette lighter.

If I found out a particular restaurant was using AI to create images for its food, I just wouldn't eat there. Actually, even the fact @JustEatUK are trialling this out is already making me think of avoiding the app from now on. #JustEat #AI #food https://t.co/5OV94zwUzKOctober 21, 2026

Just Eat is really late to this party. Its rival Uber Eats went through this embarrassment almost three years ago. The technology has advanced massively since then, but somehow Just Eat managed to roll out an even worse implementation. On social media, people have been asking how a $4bn company managed to mess up so badly and how it could roll out such a risky feature without properly testing it.

But there's also an even more obvious question: why? Even if the AI 'worked' as intended and generated an image of the perfect Platonic ideal of each dish, using fake product photography for food seems like a guaranteed way to cause disappointment and complaints from customers.

Users have already been sharing screenshots on social media, showing 'AI vs reality' comparisons, with some complaining that Just Eat has refused to issue refunds despite the actual product ordered not even remotely resembling the AI hallucination.

That's not the fault of the business making the food when the false impression was created by an AI image foisted on it by the app. They join the growing list of businesses suffering because of automatic AI-generated images pushed on their products on platforms as varied as Amazon and Reddit.
