items.title: Musk says SpaceX restricted Ukraine's Starlink connection as service restored
paragraphs: Elon Musk has said his company SpaceX restricted Ukraine's Starlink internet service, after Ukrainian officials said connectivity issues appeared to have been resolved.

The tech billionaire accused Ukraine of violating its terms of service by using it for military activity - but denied being responsible for a simultaneous issue with its US-run, military-grade counterpart Starshield.
Kyiv has not officially commented on Musk's latest claim but Ukrainian presidential adviser Serhii Beskrestnov said his post was "very strange".
Musk had earlier denied deliberately throttling Ukraine's connection, which it says hampered its ability to conduct defensive operations for more than a week.
The issue first emerged last week during a broader row between Washington and Kyiv over Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil infrastructure.

Musk's latest comments, and the seeming restoration of the service, came after US President Donald Trump said he had told the Tesla and X owner to "put it back", having repeatedly denied instructing him to limit the service.
"Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be," Musk wrote on X on Saturday.
"Ukraine['s] military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week."

He went on to say that SpaceX had "done more to defend Ukraine than any private company on Earth" and reiterated his stipulation that Starshield was a different system and controlled by the US government, adding: "What they decide to do is up to them."
He added in a later post: "[Starlink] can be used for infrastructure that is military, but it cannot be used for unequivocally offensive strikes that make it fair game to be struck back."
Reacting to Musk's post, Beskrestnov wrote on Telegram that Starlink terminals operating in Ukraine have a speed restriction of 70-90km/h and do not work on Russian territory.
"Therefore, we physically cannot use commercial Starlink for deep strikes and medium-range strikes," he said.
"It is very strange that Elon Musk is not aware of Starlink restrictions in Ukraine."
There was no immediate comment from Ukraine's defence ministry.

Ukraine uses both the civilian service Starlink and the more secure Starshield, depending on what communications are needed, both of which run on networks of low Earth orbit satellites launched by SpaceX.

Starlink allows military units to co-ordinate, particularly in remote areas on the battlefield, while Starshield allows Ukrainian drone operators to see targets in real time, as well as operate interceptor drones.
Russia is not authorised to use Starlink, so when Ukraine sends long-range missiles or drones deep into Russia to hit oil refineries, the network does not work.

Ukraine's Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara said earlier on Saturday that the military was now recording a "stable connection", with drones now able to reach speeds in excess of 400km/h (249mph). Kyiv previously said the connection would cut out above 161km/h.
"The speeds are now where they need to be," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky wrote on Telegram.
Musk did not disclose in his post why SpaceX had chosen to make the change to its service last week, when Ukraine's extensive use of Starlink had been known for several years.
The connection issues coincided with a tense diplomatic standoff between Zelensky and Trump over Ukrainian strikes on oil infrastructure within Russia.
Trump said the strikes on Russian oil refineries, which Kyiv says are crucial to stemming the main revenue source for Moscow's war effort, have pushed global prices higher.
While the attacks have had an impact on global fuel prices, rises seen this year have primarily been due to the Iran war.

Faced with midterm elections next month and domestic displeasure with rising fuel prices, Trump has waived some sanctions on Russia and agreed a deal with Moscow - criticised by European allies as funding Russia's war machine - to supply Russian diesel to the US and the global market.

Zelensky initially agreed to cease strikes targeting Russian oil facilities on the proviso that Moscow cease striking Ukraine's energy infrastructure, before restarting the strikes after several instances of Russia disregarding this.

The Ukrainian leader said that, as well as seemingly limiting Starlink capability in Ukraine, the US had also threatened to withdraw intelligence sharing if the strikes did not stop, something Trump also denied.
Fighting and aerial attacks continue to be exchanged between Russia and Ukraine overnight.
Ukraine's emergency services said three people were killed and 15 others injured, including an 11-year-old girl, in attacks on the Dnipropetrovsk region, in the south east.
Another six people were injured when a Russian drone struck an apartment block in the central city of Vinnytsia, it said.

The Russian defence ministry said on Sunday that it had struck a cargo vessel it claimed was being used to supply the Ukrainian army while it was en route to the Black Sea port of Chornomorsk overnight.
It also said Russian forces hit a logistics centre, a distribution centre and a logistics terminal in the Ukrainian city of Kharkiv.

Ukraine's defence ministry earlier said it struck a facility in the Russian city of Oryol run by a sanctioned heavy machinery manufacturer. Russian authorities said three people were killed in the strike.

items.title: Why do AI platforms want humans to design their branding?
paragraphs: If you ever feel like the world has stopped making sense, you're not alone. Here's the latest thing to baffle my brain. The very AI companies that seem to be hell-bent on putting human designers out of work also keep hiring human designers to create their brand identities.

In 2026, my inbox has been full of PR emails about these kind of developments. How&How rebranding AI image generator Ideogram. Lazarev crafting the identity for AI video app Elva. Together giving AI audit firm Clusia a four-petal mark. Meta asking lettering artist Jessica Hische to draw the new logo for its new AI platform, Muse.

So why do the companies who seem most invested in machine-made creativity keep reaching for the human kind? And should creatives whose livelihoods AI threatens be helping them? The more I think about these conundrums, the more confused I seem to get.

The first question is, if we accept that AI can make nice looking images, why wouldn't AI companies want to use them for their own branding? It's a simple question, and actually there's a simple answer too. Branding has never been about making things look nice. It’s about making people believe you.
As I noted in my recent article about attempts to rebrand AI slop, it's pretty clear that AI companies have a credibility problem right now. Not just with designers, but with the general public too.

I've lost track of how many times I've heard people without a creative bone in their body calling out AI images, whether they're on Facebook, a dodgy gig poster hanging up in the pub, or the cover of their nephew’s self-published fantasy novel.

So it might seem like a paradox, yet it makes perfect sense that AI companies are putting humans front and centre when it comes to their own branding. But it's no surprise, too, that the backlash from some creatives has been noisy.

When Jessica announced her Muse work, for example, she was hammered on Threads, despite explaining that the $12,500 fee would help her keep two small shops and their staff afloat. Her critics argued, though, that we shouldn't be lending our craft and credibility to the thing that’s eroding demand for it.
I understand the logic and I understand the anger. But one has to wonder how much refusing such commissions would actually change anything.

Capitalists are investing literal billions of dollars in generative AI, and ultimately if Jessica had turned down the Muse job, it's not like they'd have turned on their heels and gone home. They'd just have found someone else. There are lot of capable designers out there, and even if they'd hired a bad one and the logo hadn't been any good, it hardly would have brought the AI juggernaut to halt.

On a more positive note, the very fact these companies are keen to hire humans is surely something we can hang on to. As Jessica said in an interview for Wired: “Isn’t this ultimately the future that we want? Large companies hiring independent artists to do things?”
In short, if AI companies want to pay humans to make them look human, surely it's best we take the money, do brilliant work and remind everyone why they asked in the first place?

Tom May is an award-winning journalist specialising in art, design, photography and technology. He is the author of the books The 50 Greatest Designers (Arcturus) and Great TED Talks: Creativity (Pavilion). Tom was previously editor of Professional Photography magazine, associate editor at Creative Bloq, and deputy editor at net magazine.

items.title: Cookie theft: how fraudsters get the digital key to your accounts
paragraphs: You’ve had a busy morning of life admin, logging into various accounts to check balances and make payments. At the end of a productive few hours you close your laptop and move on to your next job.

What you don’t know is that fraudsters have hijacked your session with the bank and are now able to access your account. You are the victim of cookie theft, which belongs to a type of fraud known as “session hijacking”.

“Cookies have become the primary target for hackers,” says Marijus Briedis, chief technology officer at cyber security company NordVPN. In the year to June it identified 52bn cookies in stolen data circulating online.

When you log into a website, such as your bank’s, you are given a unique cookie that sits on your device and stores your data temporarily. This means you can move from page to page without repeatedly being asked for your login details. It’s called a “session cookie” – or key – and as soon as you log out, it stops being of use.
But while the session is open – and that will last beyond your activity if you choose to be remembered on a website, or if you do not properly close it – you could be vulnerable to cookie theft.

Briedis says: “Think of a session cookie as a digital key that’s already turned in the lock. When you stay logged into a site, that cookie is what keeps the door open for you. If a hacker steals that active cookie, they essentially become you.
“They don’t need your password, they don’t trigger a login alert, and they can often bypass your multifactor authentication (MFA).”
The cookies are stolen from your device. The theft is usually a result of you having inadvertently downloaded malware.

“Once that malware is on your device, it goes straight for your browser’s database, grabs all those active session cookies, and sends them back to the hacker,” says Briedis. “They’re essentially reaching into your digital pocket and grabbing your keys while you’re not looking.”
It looks like a regular session on the web. At some point you will have logged in and given your password, and maybe used MFA to prove it’s you.
You may not realise that you are a victim until you later find that someone has used the session cookie to hack your account.

If it’s a social media or email account you may discover it’s been used by scammers to trick other people. If it’s your bank they could access your account, or they could use details they find to perpetrate an impersonation scam.
And if you were shopping online, the fraudsters could change and redirect your order and charge it to your saved payment details.
You may be alerted by a security alert from a site, for example, a message asking if you have tried to change any details.
Be really careful about the extensions and software you download, because that’s where infostealer malware will usually be hidden.

Look out for signs that your laptop or phone has been infected with malware. Briedis says red flags include your device suddenly struggling with simple tasks, a battery that drains faster than it should, frequent crashes, or a browser that starts behaving oddly with redirects, pop-ups, or a changed homepage.
Do not use insecure public wifi for sites that require you to log in. The chance of cookies being stolen through this channel is low, but you should always be cautious.
Get into the habit of logging out of accounts. “Just closing a tab doesn’t end the session,” says Briedis. ”You need to manually log out to invalidate that cookie and make it useless to a thief.”
He suggests moving passwords out of your browser and into a dedicated password manager.
Clearing your cookies regularly will reduce what’s available to be stolen.
If you suspect you have been compromised, run an antivirus scan. Also log out of your accounts on every device and change your passwords.
Use MFA on accounts, as it does still offer more protection than a simple password.
Alert your bank if you notice any suspicious payments.

items.title: Collectible furniture meets cultural critique at Dutch Design Week’s Table of Power
paragraphs: Show Not Show has put a twist on a classic project documenting the echelons of power with an exhibition of the design collective’s furniture at Dutch Design Week.
Held at the Kruisruimte exhibition space in Eindhoven, The Table of Power exhibition takes inspiration from Jacqueline Hassink’s 1990s photo series of the same name.
This saw the photographer document the boardrooms of Fortune 500 companies, empty of people.
As in those photographs, The Table of Power has a long table at its centre as a symbol of institutional authority.
In this case, the table seems to stretch eternally into the horizon, thanks to the mirror placed at the far end.

Designed especially for the exhibition by collective members Frank Penders and Luuk van Laarhoven, the table is made from sheet metal, cut and bent into a brutalist form, with brushed textures and chromatic gradients adding allure.

Around it, collectible furniture, lighting and textile pieces from fellow members Lucas Zito, Marc Meeuwissen, Mokko and Studio Fabius Clovis as well as guest exhibitors Aleksandra Adamchyk, Kilian Vos and Pablo Octavio fill the room with a mix of raw wood, glossy lacquer, sculptural metal and translucent glowing bioplastic.
The idea for the exhibition came after Show Not Show were invited to host Dutch Design Week’s official press dinner.

“Our exhibition space isn’t that big,” said Penders. “So we decided to do something quite simple: instead of fitting a dinner into our exhibition, we made the dinner the starting point for the exhibition.”
In Show Not Show’s vision, the press represents a site of power in the design industry, influencing what gets seen, discussed and remembered, and their presence completes the exhibition’s concept.
Guests at the dinner were encouraged to get up from the table from time to time to “share the power”, but Dezeen observed that few journalists ever got up.
Penders told Dezeen that The Table of Power continues Show Not Show’s practice of using exhibitions to explore aspects of the design world that are not commonly seen.

“Each exhibition offers a glimpse into our world as designers, revealing something that visitors might not normally see or consider,” Penders told Dezeen. “In 2024, we showed our experiments and prototypes. In 2025, we focused on the ideas and concepts behind our work.”

“This year, the subject is visibility. Being seen, becoming known and finding recognition for what you create. It is about the relationship between designers, their work and the media that bring it to a wider audience.”

In addition to the table, Octavio’s curtain-like brushed aluminium room dividers are given a symbolic role to play in the exhibition. Their height allows those sitting down greater oversight of the room than their standing peers, adding to the sense of power imbalance.

Key pieces in the exhibition include a new series of angular wooden stools called Barricada, designed by Meewissen to match the dining table seating. Like all of his works, they are made with just one tool and one material.

There is also characterful plywood furniture by Studio Fabius Clovis, its uneven surface highlighted with high-gloss lacquer, and totemic pendant lights by Lucas Zito, 3D printed from bioplastic and playing with the spatial effects of unexpected scale.

Guest exhibitors Adamchyk, Vos and Octavio continue the elemental mood, bringing their sculptural zigzagging Waveform drawer, geological Future Fossils rugs and stone-like but squishy Lapis lounge chair respectively.

Show Not Show launched in 2024 and has exhibited at the Kruisruimte each year since. It has also taken its shows abroad with presentations at the Design Biennale Rotterdam, Collectible Brussels and Milan design week.

Elsewhere at Dutch Design Week, Boris Acket and Maison the Faux have staged the moody and maximalist installation Everything Moist Seems Alive at the MU Hybrid Art House, complete with performances from the Dutch National Opera and Ballet.
Dutch Design Week 2026 takes place from 17 to 25 October 2026 at various locations across Eindhoven, the Netherlands. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

items.title: Rosebank: Life on the oil field at the centre of a political storm
paragraphs: Scotland editorReporting fromRosebank oil field
When we landed by helicopter at Rosebank, this oil field was at the centre of a political storm - and set to be in the path of a real one.
We arrived on Wednesday morning, just a few hours after the UK government had granted consent for the production of gas from the Jackdaw field in the North Sea.
But already attention was shifting to this wild and windy patch of the North Atlantic – the next big decision for Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh.
Rosebank is bigger than Jackdaw, it would generate higher greenhouse gas emissions, and it could be far more lucrative for its owners, Adura and Ithaca.
Nicola Boyd loves her job on the Petrojarl Rosebank vessel
This summer, along with a camera crew, I travelled to Jackdaw, 150 miles east of Aberdeen.
Now we were the first journalists to visit Rosebank.

We came here - days before Storm Boelo arrived with strong winds and heavy rain - to scrutinise a controversial project which is at the heart of a national debate about climate change, energy policy and the economy.
But we also hoped for a rare glimpse into life offshore.
"It's good fun, it's interesting, every day can change," said Nicola Boyd, who runs the helideck, and greeted us as we struggled out of our lifejackets and survival suits.
Boyd has worked offshore for nearly a decade, including a year on Rosebank - where she spends two weeks at a time followed by three weeks' leave.
The Petrojarl Rosebank is moored in the North Atlantic waiting to see if production gets the go-ahead from the UK government
It's also a job that calls for steady legs and a strong stomach.
Unlike the fixed Jackdaw platform, this installation – 80 miles north west of Shetland – is a large ship, a floating production, storage and offloading vessel (FPSO) named the Petrojarl Rosebank.
It's been chartered by the field's owners from Aberdeen-based Altera and, during my 48 hours on board, it was constantly but gently rolling on the North Atlantic swell.
With the understatement typical of an Orkney islander, lead mechanical technician Ewan Leonard told me the winter weather could be "a bit of a challenge."
"Last week we had a 30m heave coming through," he said, referring to the swell, "so we'll probably suffer more of that as the winter goes on."
Altera CEO Chris Brett told me that in the industry the environment west of Shetland is considered "as harsh as you get anywhere in the world."
Whatever your view on that industry, the sheer scale of what humans have achieved in such conditions is impressive.
Ewan Leonard says the winter weather can be "a bit of a challenge"
The deep reserves of skill, ingenuity and engineering prowess among the 122 people on board are obvious.
The jobs are well-paid and, according to Ewan Leonard, the facilities are excellent.
"We have single-man cabins, there's good gym facilities, there's a lot of rec rooms here."
Douglas Hogge, a production supervisor in charge of a team responsible for the safe extraction of oil and gas, agrees.
"There's the gym, the sauna," he said, adding "you can obviously go and get some fresh air. There's plenty of fresh air out there."
Food on board the ship was described as "fantastic"
"As you've seen yourself, the food is fantastic on board, so no complaints." added Leonard.
Everyone we spoke to agreed with that, praising the talented chefs who sent out all sorts of delicious dishes, from braised ox cheek to mackerel to pork loin, day and night.
As dusk gathers and the nightshift get ready for work with a strange breakfast of fillet steak and chocolate brownie pudding, the vessel begins to glow in the gloom.
It is a strange sight, the decks criss-crossed by a bewilderingly complex array of pipes, valves and bright yellow steelwork.
The ship is an array of pipes, valves and bright yellow steelwork
The ship doesn't move far, rotating around a fixed central point called the turret to face into the weather, making life a little easier for those on board.
If production is approved, oil and gas will be pumped up through the turret from wells in the field below, which contains an estimated 300m to 500m barrels, enough for perhaps 25 years.
"For myself and a lot of the guys, that would see us out to retirement," said Douglas Hogge.
"We need to see this approved," he added.
Environmental campaigners strongly disagree. They've been trying to stop Rosebank for years, with some success.
"The future of the energy sector in the UK is renewable energy," said Tessa Khan, executive director of the campaigning group Uplift.
Consent for production at Rosebank was first granted under the Conservative government in 2023.

But in 2025, after a challenge by Greenpeace and Uplift, the Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled the approvals of the UK's largest known untapped oil field and Jackdaw were unlawful because they had failed to take into account the climate impact of actually burning the fossil fuels in cars, homes and factories.

The judge, Lord Ericht, said the fields' developers could carry on with work short of producing oil and gas while they provided more detailed environmental assessments for the government and regulators to consider.

"We think Rosebank would be a disastrous decision and a terrible deal for ordinary people across this country," said Khan, urging prime minister Andy Burnham to prioritise renewables in his quest to re-industrialise the nation.
"If the government's interested in building investor confidence, giving the green light to a major new oil field is going to do the opposite," she argued.
Whatever happens with Rosebank and Jackdaw, the long-term trend for the industry is clear and it is one of decline.

It's a quarter of a century since oil production peaked and in recent years jobs in oil and gas have been disappearing much faster than they're being created in renewable energy such as wind and solar power.
The oil from Rosebank would be loaded onto tankers via a gigantic hose and nozzle, which looks like the super-sized pump of an enormous floating filling station.
From there it would be sold on the international market and, most likely, taken to continental Europe for refining.
Opponents say that proves the project is of little benefit to the UK and should be rejected.
Supporters argue that's not the case because UK and European energy markets are co-dependent, adding that Rosebank will generate millions in tax for the Treasury.
Neil McCulloch, chief executive of Adura – which owns 80% of Rosebank and is a joint venture between Shell and the Norwegian state energy firm, Equinor – is optimistic.

He points out that Rosebank contains not just oil but gas which would be piped to Shetland and on to the St Fergus terminal in Aberdeenshire, with the potential to heat 500,000 British homes at peak production.
Approval of this project, argues McCulloch, could pave the way for four more Jackdaw-sized gas developments in the waters west of Shetland – Tornado, Tornado East, Tobermory and Suilven.
"We would like to proceed with them," he said.
A surge in fossil fuel production if Rosebank is approved is exactly what campaigners fear.

It would, argues Tessa Khan, exacerbate the deadly and damaging impact of climate change for British teachers, nurses, firefighters and families worried about their children while making "huge profits for companies that are already incredibly profitable".
The oil from Rosebank would be loaded onto tankers via a gigantic hose and nozzle
When it comes to the impending UK government decision – which sources have told BBC News should come before Christmas – there is a strange mood at Rosebank.
The decision in favour of Jackdaw has clearly encouraged many on board but it has also highlighted the jeopardy they are facing.

For now, most workers we spoke to said they were just focusing on the job, with its strange rhythms and unusual restrictions – no ability to pop to the shops, no alcohol, a lot of special occasions missed.
And for some on board, very particular cravings.
For steward Liam Davidson, it is a desire to see his French bulldog, Bailey, at the end of his fortnight on board.
"My wee dog's at the heliport when I arrive," he said, "I do miss her."
It is hoped the decision on Rosebank will be made in the next few weeks
For Nicola Boyd, it's her double bed and a pizza delivery.
"I love seeing the family, but for me, it's the pizza," she told me.
But this time there might be a delay in delivering Boyd herself.
She is coming to the end of her fortnight but, as she helped us into our survival suits, the Met Office issued an amber weather warning for much of Scotland.
For Rosebank, it seems, there are stormy seas ahead, one way or the another.

items.title: Why the charts are full of old songs - and so are your playlists
paragraphs: One of 2026's biggest hits is Zara Larsson's Lush Life, originally released in 2015
More music is being created than at any other time in human history. Every day, more than 100,000 songs, external are being submitted to streaming services.

And despite the deluge of AI music, external - Spotify says it has removed 75 million "spammy tracks" from its catalogue - real music still makes up most of our listening. The streaming service Deezer says AI accounts for just 0.5% of streams on its platform.
The problem for all those artists creating new music is that our listening habits increasingly show a love for nostalgia.
Luminate, an independent entertainment data and analytics company that tracks music, film, and television consumption first started tracking music streaming in 2008.
This year, it recorded that the streaming of current music (released less than 18 months ago) was significantly dwarfed by older music in both the UK and US.
In the first half of 2026, almost two thirds of the music played (about 60%) was released five or more years ago.
So, if we're stuck in a streaming rut, what's to blame?
In the UK, most of us seem to be shunning new songs.
Eighteen of the year's top 20 bestselling songs, external were released 12 months ago, or earlier.
The year's eighth biggest hit is Zara Larsson's Lush Life, which originally came out in June 2015. Michael Jackson's Billie Jean (1983) is in 22nd place. Fleetwood Mac's Dreams (1977) is 30th.

It's a sign that, with practically every song ever recorded available at the press of a button, people are increasingly seeking out the classics - or what the music industry categorises as "deep catalogue".
There, in the two most-played genres, R&B and Hip-Hop, external, about 60% of streams are old-school catalogue hits.
Even when current songs do break out, they themselves dominate streaming for weeks and even months.
Sam Fender and Olivia Dean's duet Rein Me In recently made UK chart history, spending a record-breaking 23 non-consecutive weeks at number one.
Olivia Dean and Sam Fender have broken chart history with Rein Me In, after 19 non-consecutive weeks at the top of the UK singles chart

Even after a song has gone viral, some musicians say it can be hard to promote subsequent releases and sustain a career. A platform like TikTok isn't set up to boost artists, it's there to create viral moments around a single song.
"It's easier [today] for folks to be passive fans," noted J Erving, the founder of Raye's distribution company, Human Re Sources, in a recent interview with Billboard, external.
"For you to consider yourself broken [as a mainstream artist], people need to care about you beyond the song. Where is the connectivity? Are people really dialled in in a deeper way?"
It's a problem the music industry is keen to tackle.
Oliver Schusser, the Head of Apple Music, says his streaming service is working to champion "tomorrow's artists" in its curation.
"You know, we do the Super Bowl halftime show, we need to make sure that we still have performers in 10, 20, 30 years," he tells BBC News.
"Because if you look back at the performers we had in the last four years, they all started somewhere before they got to the world's biggest stage."
Other organisations like Sofar Sounds work exclusively with grassroots musicians, putting on intimate pop-up gigs in cities across the globe.
This October, its Shoreditch Sofar Fringe festival showcased a whole host of artists like East London rapper J Casa.
Rapper J Casa is one of thousands of grassroots artists trying to cut through the noise on streaming platforms
In an age of content oversaturation, Casa thinks there's something unique about a live performance.
Rather than hearing more of what they already know, Casa says audiences form "a lasting connection" with a new artist and their music.
Sofar is also launching its Human Discovery Movement, external campaign that aims to put music curation and discovery "back into human hands."
Music lovers can now text a "mystery number" and receive voice notes from Sofar's tastemakers with recommendations for new music worldwide.
Artificial intelligence (AI) may also be playing its part in the so-called death of new music.

Spotify, and its competitors like Apple Music and Amazon Music, are driving the trend in AI-assisted curation, allowing premium subscribers to automatically generate playlists through text prompts to fit a mood, vibe or occasion.
Musicologist Anna-Kaisa Kaila thinks "there absolutely is potential for bias" with AI-generative playlist technology.

"With AI systems, the bias can either come from the data or from the system itself. If there's not enough training data in a particular style that is perhaps not so commercially dominant, it will be that much harder for the system to pull up tracks in that style."
Others fear an algorithmic streaming bubble is to the detriment of genuine music, its discovery and creatives' livelihoods.

As Tim Garcia, London-based DJ and curator puts it: "They're based on everyone's listening behaviour and data, right? So, you're probably going to get given a very similar recommendation to an artist you're already listening to."
Dan Mackta, managing director at Qobuz, an online music platform that maintains a strict human-first approach to curation, agrees the technology "is never going to want to throw a curve ball at you".
London-based artist Chiminyo performs at his ongoing jazz-electronic NRG project

Chiminyo, a London-based independent artist, believes that auto-generated playlists are also misleading people into thinking they're listening to "hand-picked" tunes from bona fide artists - as opposed to digitally mass-produced sound-alikes created to catch streams.

Scrolling through a "relaxing jazz piano playlist" with over 370,000 saves on Spotify, he spots that top featured artists that rack up hundreds of thousands of monthly listens have unverified accounts.
Little - if anything - can be found about them online, he says.
To his trained ear, Chiminyo also says the different artists' tracks sound near identical, reason enough to conclude the compositions have been synthetically mass-produced.
"Its all the same: the same piano feel, the same microphone placement, the same tape machine, has been used on every single one of these tracks."

When asked, Spotify said it had rolled out platform-wide policies, external against impersonation and is working to the improve filtering out of AI-related issues on its platform. But it acknowledges AI's use in music production sits on a spectrum with some artists choosing to use it to varying degrees.
New music may not be dying out, but it's clear it has a lot to contend with in 2026.

items.title: ‘Synthetic twin’: Why Socceroo Cristian Volpato is the latest footballer to license his AI clone
paragraphs: The Socceroos star stares at the camera as he strides through an enormous atrium, the sound of his football boots on polished concrete echoing around him. Suddenly, he spawns four digital clones that peel off out of view to re-emerge in different settings around the world.

This scene from a social media video is fake and generated by artificial intelligence. But it has been authorised by the very real 22-year-old footballer, Cristian Volpato, the latest professional athlete to licence and monetise his AI likeness.

Draped in a white linen suit with his feet on the sand, Volpato’s “synthetic twin” turns towards a photographer as the limestone stacks of the Twelve Apostles tower behind him. Another dominates a large digital billboard wearing a football jersey. One smiles into a mirror while adjusting a sharp grey suit.

This video was produced by a new company that acts as an AI licensing agent for professional athletes. Experts believe it is one small part of a nascent online industry that could transform the future of image rights and sports content.
As bookmakers, broadcasters and brands increasingly use athletes’ images in AI generated content without their permission, some players are fighting back.
In mid-September, Volpato, who plays for Italian Serie A club, Sassuolo, struck a deal with the California-based company Callandor to license his AI image.

As part of the deal, Callandor was given exclusive rights to Volpato’s digital likeness, voice, biometric profiles and performance data. The company will monetise his AI image by landing brand deals, taking a cut, and help restrict content that does not have his approval.
From Los Angeles, Callandor’s co-founder, Michael Fisk, tells Guardian Australia he’s in the business of making “synthetic twins”.

“Cristian is constantly training,” Fisk says. “He’s constantly out there playing. If he has any free time whatsoever, he’ll probably want to spend it with family and friends, so he loses on a lot of opportunities on brand placements.
“A synthetic twin could be used 24-7, year-round by brands. Assuming it’s approved, right?”

Founded in February, Callandor has a small stable of athletes, including Brazilian footballer Jorginho and American sailor Chris Poole. Its campaigns are only in the pilot phase, but Callandor is pursuing an array of opportunities beyond traditional advertising.

Fisk, a former executive at Sony Pictures and MGM, talks of creating AI-generated book voiceovers with foreign language editions. His team is also plotting apps that offer fans a personal relationship with a synthetic twin.
“Ultimately, the holy grail of an athlete is to have that one-on-one interaction with fans,” Fisk says.
He raises the prospect of creating an app that monitors how people play football. A digital clone of Volpato would give real-time instructions.
“He’s realising I’m not handling the ball well [so] his synthetic twin can tell me, ‘Hey, you should be doing this and this and this’,” says Fisk.
“Volpato would never be able to do that one-on-one with [them].”

Volpato’s deal with Callandor is at the cutting edge of AI rights deals, but he isn’t the first to embrace the technology. In June, Brazilian superstar Neymar licensed his AI likeness to a Chinese-owned entertainment platform that created short videos published during the FIFA World Cup.
These projects are being launched as governments across the world consider basic regulation of AI. At the moment, player contracts with major Australian sporting leagues make no mention of AI.
But technology isn’t waiting for regulation to catch up and Fisk says his synthetic twin clients are blurring the lines between real and fake.
“It’s becoming almost impossible to detect, that look and feel, the difference, particularly when you see it on a mobile device,” he says.

William Saunders leads a small Sydney based start-up, Hyperknown, that’s trying to cut similar deals. He says athletes are beginning to realise that if they don’t monetise their AI image, others will.

Earlier this month, the AFL told its gambling partner Sportsbet to stop using AI images of players without their consent. This was prompted by a complaint from the players’ union, which is considering whether stricter rules should be negotiated.
“Sportsbet shows us what happens when companies and technology get ahead of consent,” Saunders says.
“Volpato represents the counter-move: people establishing their rights before others start making decisions about their identities.
“We’re watching a race between what technology can do and what people have actually authorised.”
Many in the Australian sports industry, including content creators, bookmakers, broadcasters and athletes themselves, have started embracing the technology.

Earlier this month, Australian cricketer Travis Head personally appeared in an ad for the broadcaster Kayo. He joked that his AI clone had already finished filming the ad, before throwing to vision of him riding a flying kookaburra.

Brand deals and endorsements have become major money makers for athletes, with some securing multimillion dollar contracts. It remains unclear whether brands will be willing to pay as much for an AI clone, as opposed to the real deal.
But Saunders, whose company has only just launched, says the opportunities are enormous. He talks of AI clones selling products in foreign languages in nations athletes have never visited.
“The next trust signal won’t just say ‘made with AI’,” he says, referencing a tag often used by social media companies. “It will say ‘made with this person’s permission’.
“AI can make content abundant. It can’t manufacture someone’s permission. That’s becoming a new commercial requirement.”
Jonathan Harlen, an expert in intellectual property law at Southern Cross University, says the rise of AI brokers is “the obvious next step” in a “supercharged global market”.
From a legal perspective, he says this new industry presents “a tangle of different interests and rights” that need to be carefully negotiated.

“While copyright already subsists in voice recordings, artistic works and cinematographic images, it is only recognised where there has been human authorship, as well as a degree of independent or creative human effort involved in the making of the work,” Harlen says.

Celebrities and athletes do have some protection against AI-generated content using their image and voice without consent. But these “passing off” laws only apply when public figures can prove they have suffered an economic loss.
This has not slowed an explosion of deepfakes generated by increasingly sophisticated off-the-shelf software.

In the UK last month, a campaign was launched by some the world’s top footballers, including Cole Palmer and Lucy Bronze, which highlighted their concerns about deepfakes and the inability for regulation to slow their explosion. This campaign was backed by the global player union, Fifpro.
One offshore casino used a deepfake video of Manchester United player Bruno Fernandes in advertising earlier this year.
Not all unauthorised deepfakes will be unwanted, however. Fisk says a heavy-handed crackdown on “fan art” using AI tools might be counterproductive.
“You don’t want fans to use your image and put you in [content] using brands that you don’t use, or saying something that you would never say,” he says.
“Obviously, anything with religion and drugs, or whatever it might be, you have to be very, very careful. So it does complicate things a bit, but the opportunities are phenomenal.”
But in this emerging realm, the consequences may be hard to predict.

items.title: Ste Marie imbues Monos Vancouver office with "residential quality"
paragraphs: Canadian interiors studio Ste Marie has designed the Vancouver headquarters of luggage brand Monos to emphasise simplicity and shift mood throughout the day.
Located in the city’s Mount Pleasant neighbourhood, the Monos office was created to reflect the brand’s development to date and provide space for continued growth.

Ste Marie was presented with an open-ended brief, allowing the studio to develop a “flexible framework” for a company that is “still exploring what it could become” and would allow its team to collaborate, experiment and host.
“Monos is a brand grounded in design, mindfulness, human connection, and we understood this as an opportunity to create a place where those values could be put into practice,” said Ste Marie.
“A place where their people could come together to work, create, exchange ideas, test new things, host events and gather as an extended community.”
The studio, which previously designed the interiors for a Monos store in Toronto, approached the workplace like a residential project and organised the spaces into three overlapping areas.
“Like an apartment, it accommodates everyday activity as naturally as moments of hosting,” said the studio. “The residential quality also supports Monos’ culture of openness.”
The first area features low, soft modular sofas for lounging and conversation, and enclosed banquettes below conical pendant lights that facilitate personal exchanges, small meetings or shared meals.
An elongated communal table at the centre of the open plan provides a flexible surface for meetings, product development, testing, dining and gathering.
Here, the custom millwork is arranged in perpendicular planes that form vertical supports and horizontal overhead light boxes.
At the back is a kitchen and tea room with solid-surface counters and handleless cabinets, continuing the minimalist schema that runs throughout.
“These areas can expand and contract as needed: a meeting can become a meal, a work surface can become a display, and a lounge can transform into an event space,” Ste Marie said.
The hardness of the polished concrete flooring and rift-cut timber millwork is offset by soft furnishings, natural-fibre rugs and sheer curtains.
Dimmable lighting enables the mood to shift from early morning focused work to more casual afternoon meetings and then evening events.
“The result is a workplace that feels considered but not overly designed, with the warmth and informality of a personal space and the flexibility of a creative studio,” said Ste Marie.
Ste Marie was founded by Craig Stanghetta and has developed a reputation for its cinematic hospitality spaces across North America.

Other recent projects by the studio include a trio of venues in Edmonton, a series of amenity spaces within a renovated 1960s tower in Chicago and a Vancouver restaurant influenced by Hong Kong’s “love motels”.

items.title: The rise of new black spaces in music
paragraphs: African diaspora is finding new audiences in a city celebrated for its musical heritage
A new sound is taking Bristol's dancefloors by storm.

Driven by rolling log drums, syncopated rhythms and infectious melodies, amapiano and other electronic sounds from across the African diaspora are finding new audiences in a city celebrated for its musical heritage.
Behind these parties is a new generation of black promoters passionate about creating spaces where black people can hear their music, celebrate their cultures and feel like they belong.
But for some, building these spaces has also meant confronting the familiar challenge of finding spaces where black music and the communities around it are welcomed and not feared.
Unkle Mykel started hosting events to connect to different cultures
Bristol-based promoter Unkle Mykel's journey into events began in his own back garden after he moved to Bristol in 2017.
What started as garden barbecues gradually grew into a way of bringing people together, particularly members of Bristol's black, Asian and minority ethnic communities.
"It's about celebrating our cultures, bringing people into that fold and connecting," says the 32-year-old, who hosts Bristol Barbecue Family and The Aux Social.
Originally from Kenya, Mykel moved to the UK in 2005. Since then, he has witnessed changes in the visibility of African music.

"There was no Afrobeats on the airwaves," he laughs, recalling his early years in the country, when he says Caribbean reggae, dancehall and soca were more prominent in the musical landscape he encountered.
Now, he sees the growing popularity of genres such as amapiano - a popular South African house music subgenre - as an opportunity to broaden the scene.
"We don't need to pretend to be nobody else, we're just us. It just took a while to get there."
DJ and promoter Khiah Lou runs amapiano event called Khaya Nights
For 30-year-old DJ and promoter Khiah Lou, representation, she says, is central to her work.
Last year she launched Khaya Nights, an event dedicated to amapiano and other African Caribbean electronic dance music.
Having performed internationally, she had seen how other cities had developed a wider range of events celebrating these sounds. Bristol, she felt, was lagging behind.
Rather than wait for the scene to develop, Khiah decided to help build it herself.
"If we don't do it, who else is going to do it?" she says.
"Young black people are starting to make a way for themselves because I don't think we have a choice."
Khiah says these nights provide a place where people can connect with their identities and see their cultures reflected in the city around them.
"At first it seems like it's just a party, but it's so much more than that," she says.
"It's really important for your own self-identity. If your community doesn't have events, where do you feel you can go?"
"At first it seems like just a party, but it's so much more than that,' says Khiah
Tazmin Samuels, who DJs as Azumei, shares those concerns about representation.
As part of Rushtown, a black-led music collective, Tazmin wants to champion sounds and subcultures from across Africa, Latin America and the Caribbean.

"My main motivation for getting together with people and starting Rushtown came from seeing the lack of representation of black music that black people are currently listening to within the city," says Tazmin.
She sees encouraging signs, with more black music-focused brands emerging in Bristol. But she believes the wider music industry has yet to recognise the value of what these promoters are building.
Tazmin says the wider music industry must recognise the value of black promoters
But creating these spaces is not always straightforward.

Khiah says she has struggled to find venues willing to host nights aimed at black audiences. Although she considers Bristol an inclusive city, her experience as a promoter has revealed a different side of its nightlife.
"I've had some venue owners straight up tell me they're worried about having a black event," she says.
"I feel like black crowds are kind of met with fear, and that's really disheartening."
Mykel describes similar tensions, saying that some venues are enthusiastic about hosting his events, only to face objections from people in the surrounding community.
The Bamboo Club opened in 1966 as a social hub for Bristol's Caribbean community
The young promoters' experiences echo a much longer history of black Bristolians having to create their own spaces for music and social life.

Many black people were turned away from existing clubs and bars in Bristol during the 1960s, which led to the creation of "blues parties", un-licensed house parties where people danced to genres such as ska, reggae and rocksteady.
In 1966, Tony Bullimore and his Jamaican-born wife Lalel, opened the Bamboo Club, which served as a cultural lifeline for the city's Caribbean community.
Glen Crooks, 70, who used to perform at the Bamboo Club when he was younger, remembers "sneaking in" with his friends when they were young.
"It was the only place that we could have," he recalls.
"Especially all the Caribbean people could go and really have a good time."
Rushtown aims to champion a variety of music genres from the African diaspora
Marti Burgess, who has been a co-owner of the nightclub Lakota since 1994, says although attitudes have changed over the years, some prejudices remain.
"There is a long history of treating a predominantly black audience as a concern, rather than recognising the audience, creativity and business that a promoter is bringing," she says.
"They should not have to keep proving that black audiences are welcome or commercially worthwhile."
Growing up, Marti was surrounded by music. Her parents went to the blues clubs and attended the Bamboo Club when it hosted artists such as Bob Marley, Desmond Dekker and Johnny Nash.
"It was through listening to the adults' conversations that I came to understand how much those spaces had grown out of exclusion from mainstream venues," she says.
"Creating somewhere of their own was both a necessity and a source of joy."
Lakota has expanded its programme to include genres including amapiano and Afrobeats
"St Pauls Carnival was hugely important for those of us growing up in the 1970s and 80s, and for our developing identities as Black British people."
Lakota is predominantly known to be a bass music venue, but over the years it has broadened its programme to include Afrobeats and amapiano events.
"Latino Fest this summer opened our eyes further to the audiences and musical communities we could welcome," says Marti.
"We want people across the different genres of black music to see Lakota as a venue that is open to them, where they can bring their music and their audiences."

items.title: These premium earbuds have a game-changing feature that Apple AirPods will never get
paragraphs: There are lot of wireless earbuds on the market today, from super budget options that don't tend to last very long to well-tuned audiophile IEMS. Apple's AirPods are among the most popular mainstream options, and they have a lot of selling points. But, if I know Apple, one thing they will probably never have is replaceable batteries.

That inevitably limits the lifespan of any earphone no matter how well it's designed. But the German audio specialist Sennheiser has now come along with the Momentum True Wireless 5, a premium inner-ear headphone with strong active noise cancellation, customisable sound and the ability to swap out the batteries in both the buds and the case using nothing more than a small screwdriver.

That could be a game changer when it comes to sustainability, allowing these to outlast rivals like the AirPods Pro 3, which retail at a similar price (for over-ear options, see our guide to the best wireless headphones).

Apple often gets called out for the lack of repairability of its products. The launch of an iPhone self-repair kit in 2022 did little to quell the accusations that it makes things intentionally difficult to fix, reducing tech sustainability. Three years ago in 2023, we reported on a hardware hacker who was determined to correct that by designing his own repairable homemade AirPods.

If you don't want to go to those lengths, the Sennheiser Momentum True Wireless 5 are an attractive alternative. They're one of very few mainstream inner-ear headphones with a replaceable battery – the component that most tends to limit the lifespan of wireless earphones.

The vast majority of earbuds are sealed with glue or solder, making the batteries difficult or impossible to change without destroying the device. Fairphone Fairbuds are one exception, packing fully modular, screw-based, user-replaceable coin-cell batteries.

The Momentum True Wireless 5 are a more premium option. They have high-fidelity TrueResponse transducers, 3D Dolby Atmos sound, adaptive active noise cancellation, AI-powered voice isolation, automatic wind reduction and a Lossless codec option for maximum fidelity. They also have a new ergonomic design.
Sennheiser cites up to 40 hours of playtime per charge with the case, while the Smart Control Plus app allows advanced sound personalisation, with customisable EQ.

items.title: Sam Fender calls out ticket prices ahead of tour
paragraphs: Sam Fender has called out the price of gig tickets ahead of his next tour, promising to lower the cost.
The 32-year-old announced his Proper Massive Stadium Tour earlier this week, which will visit Newcastle, Cardiff, London, Edinburgh, Dublin and Manchester in summer 2027.
While tickets are yet to go on sale, Fender responded to a post on social media which claimed to outline the expected ticket prices.
The Geordie musician also said standing would not be split into a front and back tier and he had "no idea how this was normalised at gigs".
Tickets are due to go on general sale at 09:30 GMT on Friday, with a pre-sale at the same time on Wednesday.
But Fender said he was "not happy" with the reported prices.
"They're getting changed," he said on Instagram.
"It got inflated well more than I'd had in mind, it should only be inflated in relation to the cost of putting the show on."
The North Shields singer also said he did not want there to be an option for fans to pay more money to be closer to the front.
"The standing will not be split as well, I had no idea about it," Fender said.
"I have no idea how this was normalised in gigs... it won't be happening on this tour."
He is not the first musician to raise concerns over ticket pricing.
Zara Larsson agreed with fans earlier this year that her tickets were too expensive.
The Swedish singer said while she did not have control over the prices, she hoped she would in the future.

items.title: The Atlanta Falcons 'Nazi' logo controversy strikes again
paragraphs: A couple of years back, a throwback Atlanta Falcons logo design was raising eyebrows due to an unfortunate resemblance. Although it was a revival of an old design that the NFL team had used in 1960s, the combination of black on red and the hard stylisation of the bird of prey motif reminded some of the aesthetic of a certain fascist regime from the 1930s.

It seems the team wasn't fazed by the controversy one iota. Two years on, it's doubled down with a remixed design that takes the Third Reich resemblance even further. The memes didn't take long to arrive.
@AtlantaFalcons Please explain how you missed this? https://t.co/noRcZcfBVGOctober 22, 2026
@AtlantaFalcons not a good look, meinami https://t.co/3qv6FNS4L1October 23, 2026

On social media, the Atlanta Falcons' new profile picture has been dubbed the "gridiron cross" and the "Bird Reich". "I read that the NFL wanted to conquer the world but I didn’t think they meant it so literally," one person comments on X.

The logo shows the previously used angular black falcon forming an 'F' shape over red, beige, black and cream vertical stripes. It's presumably intended as a temporary design just for this weekend, as the Falcons will play against the 49ers on Sunday wearing retro 1966-inspired uniforms, comprising red helmets, black jerseys and white pants.

To be fair to the Falcons, Nazi Germany never had a monopoly on birds of prey insignia (nor even the swastika, which had a long history before it was adopted by the Third Reich). The bald eagle is also a familiar piece of US iconography.

But after all the comments and ridicule during the last revival of the 1960s design two years ago, there's no way that the team didn't know what was coming this time around. And the addition of the vertical stripes only makes the resemblance to Nazi iconography more apparent, which it must have realised.

I'd be interested to hear from long-term Falcon fans about whether the same comparison was made when the team originally used this logo back in the 1960s. I guess that in those pre-social media days, people didn't pick apart graphic design in the same way they do today.

Even the best sports logos can generate controversy, and the Falcons logos aren't the most disturbing we've seen. That accolade goes to the old Red Sox logo. Meanwhile, the main Atlanta Falcons logo retains its place in our pick of the best NFL logos.

items.title: How Ben & Jerry's became a beacon of brand bravery
paragraphs: If any brand has become synonymous with activism over the years, it's Ben & Jerry's. From renaming its Chubby Hubby flavour Hubby Hubby to celebrate marriage equality, to campaigning to close a prison in St Louis and using its marketing to challenge racial injustice, the ice cream brand has always found creative ways to turn its values into action.

And the brand's founders, Ben Cohen and Jerry Greenfield, have also participated directly in protests. In April 2016, both were arrested at the US Capitol during the Democracy Awakening demonstrations against the influence of money in politics and restrictions on voting rights. More recently, Cohen was arrested in May 2025 during a US Senate protest over military aid to Israel and the humanitarian crisis in Gaza.

At this year's Paradigms conference in Croatia, in a talk exploring the power of brands to drive social change, chief marketing officer Jay Curley argued that businesses should do more than pay lip service to good causes. For the Vermont ice cream maker, activism is baked into the business, alongside the Cookie Dough.

But what happens when a brand gets it wrong, faces a backlash or risks alienating customers? And how do you choose which causes deserve your voice? We caught up with Curley to discuss why brands should stop sitting on the fence, why perfection shouldn’t stand in the way of progress, and how a little creativity can help change the world.
Peace, Love & Ice Cream | Ben & Jerry's - YouTube

I think traditional businesses are risk-averse. They have a traditional belief that it’s better to stay neutral and avoid polarising issues. For some businesses, that might be the right approach. But I feel that brands that stand for something, and have communities they value and connect with, have to show up. Ultimately, I think it’s a general aversion to risk that keeps businesses out of these issues.

Patagonia does a fantastic job. They’re a big inspiration for us. Lush Cosmetics is another company we’ve always considered a kindred spirit. There are also some less mainstream brands, such as Penzeys Spices in the US. They sell herbs, spices and other ingredients, and they’ve been unapologetically bold in standing up for what matters. I’d argue that this has also helped more people notice them.

Most people who work at Ben & Jerry’s are here specifically because of our values. But there’s no values test, and anyone is welcome to work here, so there are certainly times when people disagree. I think that’s okay.
What we try to do is educate and engage people internally on the issues, so they understand what we’re doing and why. If they still disagree, that’s fine.
It starts with our values, and then we look at where we can have an impact. Where could our presence and energy meaningfully contribute to action?

It’s about looking at our values, identifying emerging social movements that could benefit from what we have to offer, and considering what’s pressing in the world that relates to those values and requires our involvement.
We bring those factors together to decide where to focus. We can’t be everywhere at once, so we try to build campaigns where we believe we can make a meaningful difference.

In a way, even when we don’t get everything right, I usually feel that we did the right thing. It also takes a lot of courage to be imperfect. If we waited until Ben & Jerry’s was perfect in every aspect of racial justice as an organisation, we would never use our voice, because we’re never going to be perfect.

I look back at our Black Lives Matter statement from 2016, and there are things we could ideally have tweaked or expressed better. That said, I think it was really important that we spoke out when we did, rather than waiting until everything was perfect.
I’m grateful that we live in a free country where people can choose what they want to buy.

There are plenty of people who may not be deeply aligned with us on a values level but love Cookie Dough, so they buy it. I think that’s fine. Equally, some people decide not to buy our products, and that’s their choice.
My hope is that those people understand what we’re doing and why. If they decide Ben & Jerry’s isn’t for them, that’s fine with us.

Daniel John is Design Editor at Creative Bloq. He has interviewed leaders and designers at brands including Apple, Microsoft and Adobe.
