items.title: 6 Steam Next Fest demos to play if you love the art direction of Silver Pines
paragraphs: 1. The House Before: a body-horror game where you play the house
2. Derelikt: PS1-style sci-fi horror on a research station
3. The Road of Dust and Sorrow: anime-style pixel survival horror
5. Blighten: PS1-inspired survival horror shooter
6. Hyperarousal: psychological horror in Italy’s Camonica Valley

Before Steam Next Fest wraps up on 26 October, I thought I'd hunt down some demos for games with a bit of Silver Pines retro horror. One thing I loved about the 2.5D survival horror game Silver Pines when I reviewed it was how it looked: a mix of retro survival horror with comic book noir environment design and pixel art design that made it feel like a lost 16-bit game that was channelling aspects of Silent Hill and Metroid design made popular in indies like Hollow Knight and Mio: Memories in Orbit.

Silver Pines is one of the year's best games, and a reminder that you don't need another Unreal Engine 5 tech demo to make a game look good. With Steam Next Fest currently overflowing with upcoming indie games, I've been looking for demos with more personality and a bit of that Silver Pines blend of unique art, nostalgia, and fresh horror ideas, just in time for Halloween.
Below are some of the best upcoming indie games with demos worth trying before Steam Next Fest ends on 26 October.

Many horror games put you in a haunted house, but The House Before takes things a step further by making you the house. It's a weird, significant shift in perspective, the kind you find in indie horror movies like Presence.

This surreal body-horror adventure turns the building into something that resembles a living organism, with pipes becoming bones, tunnels acting like veins, and rooms taking on the qualities of internal organs. It's a wonderfully strange premise that gives the developers plenty of room to experiment with the game's visual language.

The art direction shifts as you play, which is another unique twist. Rather than sticking to a single visual style, the game uses those changes to make its world feel increasingly unfamiliar, and even the interface becomes part of the experience. It's the sort of idea that could easily become a gimmick, but when the visuals are doing so much of the storytelling, it makes sense to push them further.
The idea of playing as a house is odd enough to catch my attention, especially when the walls, pipes, and rooms are all part of the horror. I'd like to see how far the developers take it.
Download The House Before demo from Steam.
Formats: PC (Steam), PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S later

I have a soft spot for games like Derelikt (and the quirky Grease Trap '99) that feel like they escaped from the original PlayStation, back when 3D graphics were still a novelty, and developers were figuring out how to build a convincing world from a handful of polygons and that 'wobble' textures used to affect when it all moved.

Derelikt taps into that era with its retro sci-fi horror aesthetic, sending you to investigate a research station on a mysterious planetoid. Naturally, things don't go particularly well, and before long you're dealing with missing scientists, hostile environments and a growing understanding things are going to get bad before they get better.

There's also something refreshing about a game that understands how much you can do with lighting, composition and a few well-placed shadows, and this, along with Blighten, below on this list, offer that kind of unease simple but atmospheric design can deliver. You don't always need to see every little detail to be unsettled by what's lurking around the next corner.
If you grew up with PS1 horror games, or just enjoy the aesthetic of a lost 1990s sci-fi adventure, give this one a go.

I'm always interested in pixel art that gets the details right, like Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun 2, which nails that '90s shooter aesthetic, and The Road of Dust and Sorrow, which shows similar attention to detail and turns it into wonderfully grim places to explore. This upcoming survival-horror game follows Katherine and her daughter Ava through a post-apocalyptic world where a miracle crop has turned people into flesh-hungry creatures called Dusters.

The game's setting is filled with abandoned streets, ransacked buildings, and strange vegetation creeping back across the ruins. Katherine has bigger problems than the scenery, mind you, as she scavenges supplies, fights off Dusters, and tries to keep her daughter Ava safe.

That mother-and-daughter relationship is what sets the game apart from a straightforward 2.5D zombie adventure. Ava is more than someone to rescue at the end of a level; she's the reason Katherine keeps going, even when the world around them has become a pretty horrible place.

The game draws on '90s survival-horror classics like Resident Evil and Silent Hill, so it hits that Silver Pines DNA, but its detailed anime-like pixel art gives the ruined world its own character. The new Steam Next Fest demo is twice as long as the previous version and includes the entire first act, so there's plenty to get stuck into before the full game arrives on 3 December.
Download the The Road of Dust and Sorrow demo on Steam.

Retro horror has become a crowded corner of the indie scene, but Anomalith caught my attention for its Japanese period influences and use of liminal spaces, that in a way reminds me of the excellent Motorslice.

Anomalith follows a girl searching for her missing friend in a world warped by strange anomalies, drawing on Showa-era Japanese aesthetics to create something that feels caught between a familiar place and an unpleasant dream. The idea behind horror like this, and it's a reason Backrooms works so well, is the walls don't need to be covered in blood to make you feel uneasy – the sense of dislocation is what gives it an eerie edge.

Games that use a recognisable visual language and then start messing with it have a particular appeal. A corridor, a building, or an everyday object can become unsettling simply because it doesn't behave as you'd expect, it's why I loved aspects of Control Resonant so much, and the retro presentation gives Anomalith a distinctive identity of its own.

It's also a good fit if you enjoy horror that leaves you to work things out rather than explaining every little detail. Sometimes the most effective thing a game can do is give you a familiar place, then make you question everything you see.

Another PS1-inspired 3D world, Blighten embraces the way those technical limitations often forced developers to think carefully about what the player could see, and what they couldn't and explores how to redo that for modern gamers.

If you like your horror games with a bit of old-school grit and the kind of item juggling found in the Resident Evil games, Blighten is worth a look. It's a retro-styled survival horror shooter, with the sort of throwback presentation that will appeal to anyone who misses the rougher edges of the genre's PS1-era heyday.

Retro inspired graphics can give a game an immediacy that gets lost when everything is rendered in perfect detail, and there's a certain charm to seeing developers embrace that design idea. A rough texture, a blocky character model or an awkwardly lit room can become part of the experience and a way to build an uneasy atmosphere, one designed around nostalgia as much as horror imagery.

I'm always interested in games that understand this, particularly when the visual style has a purpose beyond making screenshots look nostalgic. Blighten is worth investigating if you're after another upcoming horror game that takes its cues from an earlier generation.

Hyperarousal has a nasty trick up its sleeve. This upcoming psychological horror adventure lets you stab tattoos on your own arm to reveal things hidden from ordinary sight, which seems a risky move when you're already dealing with ancestral nightmares (and if, like me, you hate needles and sharp, pointy things).

Set in Italy's Camonica Valley, a real place famous for its prehistoric rock art, the game follows Garlo as he returns to his family home looking for peace and quiet. That doesn't last long, as he becomes caught up in his ancestors' memories, travelling between the present day and different periods in the valley's history.

Hypervision, that bit where you stab yourself to see clues, is the game's strangest idea. By stabbing three ritual tattoos, Garlo can reveal hidden messages, sounds and routes through the world, but using them makes it harder to tell reality from memory and hallucination.

The real-life Camonica Valley has an estimated 8,000 years of human history etched into its rocks, making this Alps location an unusual, inspired setting for a horror game, giving Hyperarousal something more tangible to draw on than the usual abandoned hospital or haunted mansion.

items.title: Adrian Smith + Gordon Gill Architecture designs "fluid" skyscraper Lilli for Miami waterfront
paragraphs: US studio Adrian Smith + Gordon Gill Architecture has unveiled its latest skyscraper for Miami, designed to display “quiet refinement” on a slender site on the city’s waterfront.

Called Lilli, the residential skyscraper development is the latest in Miami from Adrian Smith + Gordon Gill Architecture (AS+GG). The studio is known for designing some of the world’s tallest buildings, including the world’s upcoming tallest skyscraper, the Jeddah Tower.
At 636 feet tall (193 metres), Lilli is planned for a narrow site in Miami’s Edgewater neighbourhood.
The luxury skyscraper will feature rounded edges and will have terraces on the water-facing side, with larger patios running up the opposite face.
Its design is characterised by rounded edges and large spans of glass interrupted by metallic floor plates.
“Our vision is for Lilli’s interior design to feel inseparable from its architecture,” said AS+GG design partner Juan Betancur.

“The fluidity of the building carries through the interior spaces, while a restrained palette of natural materials allows light, landscape, and views of Biscayne Bay to become part of the experience.”
“The result is a sense of quiet refinement that feels distinctly connected to its waterfront setting.”
The skyscraper will house 117 residences of varying sizes, spread across its 53 storeys, as well as amenities including lounges, pools and spas.
The ground floor will have a lobby for residents with large metallic columns and minimalist detailing.
At the top of the skyscraper, a pool will sit on the edge of a terrace underneath a bulkhead with the same reflective metal treatment seen elsewhere in the exterior.
Lilli is the latest in a series of residential skyscrapers being designed by the studio, which recently completed a “yacht-inspired” building in the city.
Residential skyscraper development has proceeded at a steady pace in Miami, with Bugatti recently unveiling its first branded skyscraper in the city.

items.title: Mystery over source of Ebola infection in Nigeria fuels concern about spread of virus
paragraphs: Health officials across Africa are racing to determine how Nigeria’s first Ebola patient ⁠in more than a decade ⁠became infected, amid fears ​the outbreak could spread further after reaching a fourth African country.

The Swiss foreign ministry said on Friday the patient in Nigeria, the Ugandan-born wife of a Swiss diplomat based in Abuja, had not travelled to the Democratic Republic of ⁠Congo, where the outbreak was first detected in mid-May before spreading to Uganda, Kenya and now Nigeria. The woman was believed to have contracted Ebola while travelling with her husband in Uganda, the ministry added.

The new information contradicts accounts from Uganda, which previously said the woman had travelled to eastern DR Congo, and will raise concerns about the ability of authorities to contain the outbreak, which is already the most geographically widespread in history.

The Ugandan government reported Ebola cases in May and June before WHO declared it Ebola-free in August. A Ugandan government spokesperson told Reuters on Thursday that Uganda had no ​Ebola cases and that, if ​it did, it would make that information ​public.
The World Health Organization said investigations were continuing to establish the likely source of infection for the Ebola patient in Nigeria.

The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention is investigating whether the patient may have come into contact with an Ebola patient in Kenya, as both travelled from Uganda’s Entebbe airport on 3 October, said Dr Wessam Mankoula, head of emergency preparedness and response at the organisation.

Catherine Smallwood, a WHO Ebola incident manager in DR Congo, told a UN briefing in Geneva via video ‌link on Friday that WHO staff in DR Congo had no information showing the patient in Nigeria had travelled to the country.

Smallwood said a link to the case in Kenya was possible, ​but added that officials would need to compare the timing with when the Nigeria patient’s symptoms began to tell whether the infection more likely happened at the Ugandan airport or elsewhere.

Marion Koopmans, a Dutch virologist and member of the WHO’s Ebola emergency committee, cast doubt on the theory. “I think that is very speculative unless there is evidence of sharing the same ​space in a manner that could explain that,” she said. “Random presence at the same location, a large airport, is not a supported epidemiological link by any standard of what we currently know.”

The Nigerian health minister, Muhammad Ali Pate, said Nigeria’s case remains contained and that contact-tracing was continuing. “We are trying to contain it so it doesn’t go out to the communities. Hopefully, it won’t get to that and we are working hard to ensure that,” Pate said.

Melaku Yirga, vice-president for Africa at Prosper Global (formerly Mercy Corps), said the confirmation of Ebola in Kenya and Nigeria reinforces the need for countries to work closely together to prevent further transmission.
“What matters most now is speed, sharing information across borders without delay and ensuring frontline health workers and local organiaations have the resources to respond quickly,” he said.

Ebola is a highly contagious and often fatal viral disease that affects humans and non-human primates. It spreads through body fluids or contaminated materials and causes organ damage, blood vessel impairment and sometimes severe internal and external bleeding.

The current outbreak is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has no approved treatment or vaccine. It was first announced on 15 May and has infected more than 9,500 people and killed nearly half of them.

The outbreak is the largest and deadliest in DR Congo’s history and second only ​globally to ​the 2014-16 outbreak in west Africa, which infected ​more than ‌28,600 people ​and ​killed more than 11,000.

items.title: Hammersmith Bridge is a symbol of our dysfunctional times. The money is there, the joined-up thinking isn’t | Simon Jenkins
paragraphs: London’s Hammersmith Bridge is a metaphor for all that is wrong with British government. Closed to motor traffic and inert for seven years, it is a victim of the anarchy that seeps into every tier of public administration. The bridge sits today on a sublime bend in the Thames, guarded by what looks like Checkpoint Charlie in iron curtain Berlin. With Albert Bridge also now closed, 37,000 extra vehicles seeking to cross the river have brought south London close to perpetual gridlock. No one cares.

London may be the richest, smartest, coolest place in Britain. Yet it is run like a high street vape shop. Its buses are ever slower, homeless people are ever more prevalent, waiting times in hospitals ever longer. No one can decide if they want an HS2 terminus or a Heathrow runway. A robotic Whitehall algorithm has just declared, ludicrously, that the borough of Kensington’s “housing target” must be 5,107 homes a year, up from a previous target of 1,381.

The first thing you notice about a city is its traffic. In other cities, it moves. In London, it crawls. Its congestion is officially rated the worst of any capital in the world. Efforts to improve the sclerotic traffic lights have failed. The recent installation of computer-assisted “smart” lights – the much-vaunted road time optimisers – has contrived to cut just 27 seconds off individual bus journeys. A Guardian investigation last month timed a series of trips, and found the average speed for a No 22 bus between between Putney Common and Oxford Circus was under 6mph, or 16% slower than a decade ago.

The principal reason for this appears to be London’s epidemic of roadworks. In most cities such infrastructure is subject to intense regulation and coordination. The reason is obvious: that the disruption can restrict movement and thus impose costs on third parties. There is no regulation worthy of the word in London.

In 2017 the Economist published what became a notorious map showing roadworks in Paris and London. The first had a scatter of sparse red dots; London’s map was a sea of blood. Estimates are that vehicles in London navigate 1,300 roadworks every day, with the total for 2024 at 490,893. There is no evidence of the slightest coordination of hold-ups.

The chief reason is that a quarter century of privatising utilities has given water and cabling companies virtually unlimited freedom to dig where and when they please. Streets in the most afflicted inner boroughs now awake each morning to what looks like an overnight blitz. A mass of road closures and detour signs have turned the London street into what looks like a permanent construction site. Seeing any work being done is rare and there is no sense of anyone being in charge.

Hammersmith Bridge is a tough case. It legally belongs to the local Hammersmith and Fulham council – not Richmond on the south bank – but it has decided it “cannot absorb” the cost of restoring its decaying structure, put at £300m. It merely allows pedestrians and cyclists to cross. Yet it claims to have spent £54m on it over seven years. Merely doing next to nothing costs millions of pounds a year.

The bridge’s predicament is serious. Built by Sir Joseph Bazalgette in 1887, it was one of the world’s first iron suspension bridges – and the iron’s life has expired. Repair could only be temporary, or over the longer term astronomical. As architecture it is a noble if rather ungainly structure, compared with graceful Albert Bridge downstream. A growing body of opinion is that it would be common sense to replace it.

Designing a new bridge should be a competitive challenge. It needs to respect the buildings and natural environment of Barnes and Hammersmith on either bank. A work of style and dignity should have nothing to do with the concrete gashes of the 20th century’s London and Waterloo bridges. It needs to be very special.

As for who should take the lead, in any other city a river crossing would be the responsibility of its mayor. British mayors spend their time trying for headlines or Downing Street. London’s Sadiq Khan appears to have no view on Hammersmith Bridge, any more than he does on the capital’s roadworks, building conservation or policy on tall buildings.

As for paying for a new bridge, there is an answer. The so-called City Bridge Foundation was formed in the middle ages to maintain London bridges and later City crossings. Its charter limits its responsibility to just five crossings: Tower, London, Southwark, Millennium, and Blackfriars bridges. However, its trustee, the City of London Corporation, could amend the charter so that it could reinvest in infrastructure. It is one of London’s richest charities – with assets in the order of £1.5bn. The foundation currently spends lavishly on causes that have nothing to do with bridges.

This needs changing. The City of London is an out-of-date relic of medieval local government. The legacy of London’s past wealth should be at the disposal of the whole metropolis. The money is there. A new Hammersmith Bridge should rise across the Thames’s most exquisite western reaches, and soon.

items.title: 'It's been relentless': IT workers scramble to fix PHP flaw described as worst crisis in years
paragraphs: Microsoft boss Satya Nadella says he has not seen anything like the PHP emergency "in a long, long time".

Referencing the ongoing global efforts to fix the critical cyber-security flaw in millions of websites, he told a conference "it was a long day and a long night, I know, for all the IT and security folks".

Other IT and cyber experts have told the BBC about their struggles in the last 48 hours, whose stories give us an insight into what it is like at the coalface of a major cyber emergency. But also highlight how misinformation and panic has made things a lot worse.
"It's been relentless," says UK-based system administrator Adam Mudd.
He said he had never had so many messages from people who were worried about their websites.
"The biggest challenge has been juggling clients who want their sites taken offline as a precaution, while trying to coordinate updates and fixes across countless different setups," he said.
"Sometimes it takes me longer to take a website down than to fix the PHP problem."
PHP is a very popular programming language which powers millions of websites.

But two critical flaws were found with the system that led to the emergency response, with national cyber-security authorities urging IT teams to download a security fix urgently or take websites and servers offline.
Mudd says since then he has been under enormous pressure and has lost a huge amount of sleep - working early and not finishing until 22:30 BST to secure his customers' systems.
In Mauritius, IT administrator Loganaden Velvindron said he too was flat out since his team realised just how much software relies on PHP.
"Many versions of php running are completely end-of-life, so we are having to rebuilding web apps and change code in some cases," he said.
He said part of the problem was the announcement about the security vulnerabilities in PHP came as a surprise, without much time to prepare for action.
Jon Jones, Technical director for a digital advertising company, was also spurred into action by the alerts.
"Seeing the warning drop was definitely eye-opening and a new experience we've not dealt with before," he said.
"But, in a way, it was exciting feeling like a bit of a Hollywood action scene."
The PHP Foundation, which manages the programming language, released its software fix and there was a scramble for people to download it.
Jones said it felt like "the race was on" when the patch launched at 15:00 BST on Wednesday.
"It was also a bit nerve-racking as anyone who has applied software updates before would know, there's always a chance than an update can cause other issues," he said.
The rush came as someone had leaked details of the PHP flaw early - and it was heavily rumoured that cyber-criminals were already trying to carry out attacks.
But cyber experts are also now questioning whether or not those rumours were real.
"We were flooded with rubbish intel about hackers being out there actively with working Proof of Concept (PoC) methods," said UK cyber expert Daniel Card.
He said he also been flat out since Tuesday when the rumours of PHP hacks began circulating.
"This isn't the first time we've had a situation like this but it feels like it's been on another dimension," he said.
He agreed that on paper the PHP vulnerabilities were very serious and should be taken seriously, but he and many others are frustrated with the misinformation about hackers being on the loose.
As well as the alerts from government agencies - even the Prime Minister of Japan - cyber-security companies also made errors which didn't help.
One major firm in this space issued warnings saying hackers had a working PoC - only to have to retract it.
In spite of warnings from Cloudflare and AWS that "millions of hacking attempts" had been made every hour, there is also no evidence of large scale data breaches or cyber-attacks.
It is true that hackers have been seen to use AI to attempt to build attack methods, but none of them seem to be working at scale at the moment - something that may well change soon.
AI was also used to find the PHP flaws which had been hidden from human researchers for decades.
The IT workers we spoke to all agreed that these kinds of serious flaws were going to be uncovered more frequently now that AI tools had become so good at hacking.
But some in the industry are concerned about how people were told about the critical vulnerabilities in PHP, as they fear improvements in AI will throw up more incidents like it.

"We're going to find scary vulnerabilities with the amazing capabilities that OpenAI and Anthropic are bringing online, but we need to calibrate the messaging," posted Mark Maunder, founder of Wordfence - a Wordpress security tool.
He said there was a risk of "alert fatigue" which could be a big problem if a fully exploitable and serious vulnerability arose.

items.title: How to design a winning 3D-printed headphone accessory: 5 tips from Bambu Lab
paragraphs: Got a clever idea for a 3D-printed headphone accessory? Bambu Lab and Nothing are back with another MakerWorld design challenge called Let's Make It: MakerWorld × Nothing Headphone Accessory Design Challenge, this time inviting makers to create add-ons for the Headphone (1) Pro, Headphone (1) and Headphone (a).

There’s a Nothing Headphone (1) Pro and a Bambu Lab A2L printer up for grabs for each category winner, but how do you make a design stand out from the crowd? Bambu Lab has shared five tips for getting your entry right, from coming up with an original idea to making sure other people can actually print and use it.

It's a good brand tie-up too, especially since I discovered in my CMF Speaker S review that Nothing is embracing 3D printing to enable device customisation. Bambu Lab has become a leading brand that makes 3D printing easier and builds some of the best 3D printers. Read Bambu's tips below, gather ideas, and enter this year's Let's Make It challenge.

Judges look for unique, eye-catching models, so go beyond the obvious. In the last contest we hosted with Nothing, the "Most Unexpected" winner, guysread's fly swatter for CMF Phone 1, folded out of the phone. The judge said it was "so unexpected that it made me laugh, but then I realised it's actually useful too." BuildyBryce's Brick Case, the "Best-looking" winner, works with toy bricks. The judge called it "a head-turner" with "endless customisation possibilities."

A great idea only wins if people can print it. Keep the design well-made, and share what works. The "Most Functional" winner, 3D Kimba's CMF RIG phone cage, lists recommended materials, layer height, infill and assembly tips. Kaburuk's popular foam dart launcher module needs only standard M3 screws and rubber bands. Test print first, so others get the same result at home.

Show your model from several angles and in use, and add close-ups of key details. Your cover image is often the first thing people see, so make it count. Good visuals help judges and the community grasp your idea quickly. For functional designs, a real-life GIF (not AI-generated) that demonstrates the idea is especially effective, because it shows people exactly what the accessory does.

Explain what your accessory does, what it needs and how to assemble it. Kaburuk's foam dart launcher, 3D Kimba's CMF RIG, and many other popular designs include pages that cover key features, print settings, magnet and screw advice, and safety information. Zile's foldable stand and card holder add a bill of materials and an iteration log, so people can see how the design improved. Clear pages make your model easier to print and trust.

Think about what others would find useful or fun. Zile's foldable stand and card holder works with both CMF Phone 1 and 2 Pro, and it fills a real gap: CMF phones have no NFC, so it gives contactless payers a way to carry a card. Kaburuk's launcher came from an office full of Nerf fans. BuildyBryce's Brick Case, the "Best-looking" winner, invites endless customisation. Solve a problem, or spark a smile.

items.title: Lowry kicks off, pop goes kinky and the wild man of Florence is tamed – the week in art

Sheep dung, snails and mouse brains are all beautiful … if you look closely enough. This artwork could be a newly discovered planet or an abstract piece by Stanley Donwood for Radiohead’s A Moon Shaped Pool, but the truth is tinier: this is the tip of a ballpoint pen, a winning entry from the Nikon Small World photography competition.

St Jerome and the Lion: Predella Panel by Fra Filippo Lippi and Workshop, 1455-60

Filippo Lippi was the wild man of early 15th-century Florentine art, if the stories told about him in the Renaissance are anything to go by. It was even said his patron Cosimo de’ Medici had to lock him in the Medici palace to stop his debauchery. There is a core of fact behind the tales, as Filippo – a friar – is known from legal records to have had children with an escaped nun, Lucrezia Buti. Their son Filippino also became an artist. But whatever his life was like, there’s no lack of piety in this painting of the early Christian Jerome, a real historical figure who translated the Bible into Latin. The lion tamely lets the holy man pull a thorn from its paw, in an intricately painted mountainous landscape with a pink church. Jerome concentrates on his work, as you would if you were de-thorning a dangerous big cat. This is just a small panel from the base of an altarpiece but it packs in the emotion and humanity that makes Lippi a great artist, in spite of, or because of, his sins.

items.title: Cliff Richard is having a revival, and it’s all thanks to GTA 6
paragraphs: British singer Cliff Richard is having an unexpected resurgence among gaming fans thanks to GTA VI. With his song 'Devil Woman' featuring in the game's soundtrack, a new generation of fans has been born – but I wonder how many are familiar with Sir Cliff's boomer legacy in the UK?

It's not a new phenomenon by any means, as games like Fallout have similarly revived classics like The Ink Spots' "I Don't Want to Set the World on Fire". It goes to show how the best video games have the power to influence pop culture way beyond the confines of the screen.

Released in 1976, Devil Woman is considered one of Cliff's 'edgier' tunes, which is why the sudden virality of the song amuses me. I suspect many new fans will be surprised to discover his wider discography, featuring the Eurovision hit "Congratulations" and the festive ballad "Mistletoe and Wine".

Devil Woman's sudden surge in popularity highlights the wider ways we discover new music. Whether it's a viral TikTok sound or a gaming score, these hits get new context, and suddenly a song once confined to the discomfort of an awkward family gathering becomes a mysterious (dare I say sexy?) soundtrack.

GTA VI is already permeating the cultural zeitgeist, taking over social media with viral memes – hey, we got a Cliff Richard revival before GTA VI... The excited response to its latest ad takeover in Miami proves that the game is the most hyped release we've seen in decades, and with graphics that good, it shouldn't come as a surprise.

Natalie Fear is Creative Bloq's staff writer. With an eye for trending topics and a passion for internet culture, she brings you the latest in art and design news. Natalie also runs Creative Bloq’s 5 Questions series, spotlighting diverse talent across the creative industries. Outside of work, she loves all things literature and music (although she’s partial to a spot of TikTok brain rot).

items.title: Loader Monteith expands red-brick bungalow within "remarkably compact footprint" near Manchester
paragraphs: Scottish architecture studio Loader Monteith has transformed a two-bed, red-brick bungalow into a four-bedroom family home in Prestwich, UK.

Described by the studio as “squeezing a quart into a pint pot”, the project involved expanding and reorganising the 69-square-metre home in the town near Manchester to accommodate a growing family and improve connections to a rear garden.
Loader Monteith designed a rear brick extension that opens up the home’s living spaces to the garden, while a new upper floor has been nestled beneath a dormer roof.
“The challenge was to maximise the space without compromising on architectural ambition,” studio co-founder Matt Loader told Dezeen.
“We developed the design in response to the existing house and its local context, creating appropriately scaled additions that respect the surrounding architecture,” Loader added.
“This delivers four bedrooms and two bathrooms within a remarkably compact footprint.”
The extension was designed by Loader Monteith for clients Matt and Angie Maurer, who took on much of the project’s construction themselves.

“Taking on so much of the work ourselves meant we also had to find the right contractors and suppliers who understood our vision and cared about the details in the same way we did,” Matt Maurer told Dezeen.
“Both clients were keen to embrace an ambitious architectural solution,” Loader added.
The home’s front elevation is marked by a green-toned, copper entryway that contrasts with its red-brick walls and clay roof tiles.
This is complemented by the angular red-brick extension at the home’s rear, which is also framed by copper detailing and topped with a sedum roof.
“We began by analysing the local architecture of Prestwich, where red brick predominates,” Loader said.
“We used brick for the new extensions, incorporating decorative corbelling and folded details inspired by local architectural patterns.”
At the front of the home, the living spaces have been relocated to accommodate two street-facing bedrooms, including one ensuite, along with a study, utility room and toilet.
Behind this, the kitchen, living and dining spaces are organised as a trio of interconnected spaces within the rear extension.
Steps between the spaces lead down to the sunken dining and living area, which sit level with the garden and open onto it through sliding doors.
“The challenge was fitting so much accommodation into such a small house while making it feel generous and improving its connection to the garden,” Loader said.
At the centre of the plan, a skylit staircase leads up to the newly-added first floor, where the primary ensuite bedroom and an additional bedroom and bathroom are located.
A pared-back material palette is used throughout the home, including concrete floors and white walls set off by exposed timber joinery.

Other UK home extensions recently featured on Dezeen include the expansion of a Grade II-listed rectory in the Cotswolds by Prest Vale Architects and the renovation of a terraced home in London by Polysmiths using “light as the primary material”.

items.title: Is a job guarantee the solution to mass AI unemployment?
paragraphs: In a preface to his book Capitalism and Freedom, the American economist Milton Friedman famously observed that a crisis can propel once-fringe ideas into the political mainstream.

“Only a crisis – actual or perceived – produces real change. When that crisis occurs, the actions that are taken depend on the ideas that are lying around,” he wrote. The job of intellectuals, thinktanks and economists, he argued, is to refine the quality of these ambient ideas, so that good ones are ready when disaster strikes.

A chorus of influential voices is now predicting that AI may trigger crises of vast magnitude. Bill Gates has declared that AI will advance so rapidly that within a decade, humans will not be needed “for most things”. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has warned that the technology could cause widespread unemployment within one to five years, eliminating many positions in law, tech, finance and other white-collar professions. Even if these predictions are wrong, investors who bet heavily on the technology may conclude that AI is a bubble, and this in itself could cause a recession and widespread job loss.

Whether a crisis of mass AI-related job loss turns out to be actual or perceived, one policy idea that is attracting growing attention and support could directly mitigate this problem: a job guarantee.

In its most ambitious form, such a program would ensure that anyone who wants work is guaranteed a meaningful, decently paid job. By creating a public option for employment, its supporters argue, a job guarantee could protect millions of people from the financial and psychological damage of joblessness and mobilize a vast labor force to tackle urgent societal problems, from infrastructure and climate adaptation to elder care and childcare.

The concept of a job guarantee has a long history, both as an ideal and an actual policy. Article 23 of the 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights states: “Everyone has the right to work, to free choice of employment, to just and favourable conditions of work and to protection against unemployment.” During the Great Depression in the 1930s, Franklin D Roosevelt established the Works Progress Administration (WPA), which employed millions of Americans in ambitious public works projects that constructed roads, bridges, sewers, playing fields and much more. More recently, France, India and Argentina are among the countries that have launched versions of a job guarantee.

Though a job guarantee and universal basic income (UBI) are often grouped together, a recent global survey found greater support for job guarantees than UBIs. Polling of Americans by the Democratic strategist David Shor also shows the same pattern, with greater support for the creation of well-paid jobs than for direct income support. This makes sense, the venture capitalist and civic activist Nick Hanauer said, because “jobs represent so much more than income in human societies. They represent connection and dignity and enfranchisement and participation.”

Algernon Austin, director for race and economic justice at the Center for Economic and Policy Research, agreed: “A job guarantee is significantly preferable to UBI because work is more than just income. When you have a job, you gain work experience and you gain skills and you gain a network.”

Calculating the cost of a job guarantee depends on a holistic assessment of its impacts. During a US Senate hearing on affordability in June, John Kennedy, a Republican senator for Louisiana, suggested that a job guarantee would cost trillions of dollars and was impossible. When Dr Julie Margetta Morgan, president of the public policy thinktank the Century Foundation, told Kennedy that she supported a federal job guarantee, he replied: “Do you believe in the Easter bunny?”

Economists who study job guarantees see the calculation of costs and benefits differently. Max Kasy, a professor of economics at Oxford who has studied a recent job guarantee experiment in Austria, said that while the wages a job guarantee pays participants comprise a cost, such programs also save money in multiple ways.

“The cost saving comes from the fact that you don’t have to pay unemployment benefits, or maybe disability benefits or early retirement benefits. Then people who are working pay taxes and make social insurance contributions, so that’s additional revenue for the state. And then they hopefully do something that’s actually useful for society,” he said.

Participants in the job guarantee experiment in Austria also experienced social and psychological benefits. While the monetary value of greater wellbeing may be hard to quantify, such intangibles are crucial, according to Pavlina Tcherneva, a professor of economics at Bard College.

“Providing a good job to a person is absolutely transformative,” she said. Factoring in the costs of health problems that come from precarious unemployment and long-term unemployment, she added, makes the policy even more attractive, saying: “It’s not only affordable, it’s an investment.”

In September, the US representative Ayanna Pressley, a Democrat from Massachusetts, reintroduced a congressional resolution calling for the creation of a federal job guarantee, something she first proposed in 2021. Her proposal would create a federally funded but locally administered job guarantee that pays participants at least $25 an hour, with regular adjustments to reflect the rising cost of living. The jobs would include a range of sectors, such as emergency preparedness, relief and recovery after natural disasters, care for children and seniors, and public art projects modelled on the WPA’s popular Federal Art Project.

Another recent proposal would directly tax AI companies to fund a federal job guarantee. The plan, which is supported by Democratic US representatives Greg Casar of Texas, Valerie Foushee of North Carolina and Sara Jacobs of California, would tax large AI companies on whatever was higher: the value of their “tokens” – units of data used in AI models – or their revenue from AI products.

If the unemployment rate rose, the tax rate would increase. “AI CEOs are openly predicting their technology could put millions of Americans out of work, and our government is doing nothing to save jobs and protect working people,” Casar said in a written statement.

In Cleveland, Ohio, a non-profit called Universal Basic Employment (UBE) is launching a small pilot study with a cohort of five workers who drive vans at a transportation company. Rather than create new jobs from scratch, the program subsidizes the wages of existing private-sector jobs in a way that benefits both workers and employers, according to Devin Cotten, founder and CEO of UBE.

Cotten and his team wanted workers to make what they call an autonomous wage – the pay level at which people are no longer eligible for most social safety net benefits. In Cleveland, that was just over $27 per hour. At a cost of almost half a million dollars for one year, UBE’s pilot will split that $27 figure with employers. The drivers currently make about $15 an hour, so the employer will save money, and the workers will get a sizable raise.

The program is not meant to replace other forms of assistance such as housing vouchers, Cotten said. But workers receiving more money as wages, rather than as a siloed benefit, can build their credit, perhaps qualify for a mortgage and also keep dollars circulating in the local economy, helping to revitalize poor neighborhoods.

Such a model may even attract a broader base of political support. “Work is a shared value across political lines,” Cotten said. “I think crafting a solution based on work allows us to be a bipartisan solution.”

items.title: Foster + Partners designs pair of skyscrapers connected by garden bridges in Armenia
paragraphs: A pair of skyscrapers joined by three bridge elements will form the centrepiece of World Trade Center Yerevan, a development by British studio Foster + Partners set to be built in Armenia.
Situated in the Armenian capital of Yerevan, one of the towers will house offices and the other will contain apartments and a hotel.
Foster + Partners plans to connect the skyscrapers with enclosed bridges that will provide amenities for occupants of both buildings, including landscaped terraces.
Wrapped in glazed facades, the pair of skyscrapers will have a concrete structural frame with steel bracing and a split core, catering for open, flexible interior spaces.

The towers will be angled to give views of notable landmarks, including the National Assembly of Armenia, the Armenian National Opera and Ballet Theatre, the Armenian Genocide Memorial and Mount Ararat.

The World Trade Center Yerevan development will also feature low-lying buildings at the base of the skyscrapers containing entertainment, hospitality and shopping spaces arranged around a public square.
“Our new development is in close dialogue with the country’s history and culture,” said Foster + Partners senior partner Niall Dempsey.

“The low-rise buildings seamlessly stitch into the wider urban fabric, while the towers are elevated above ground level, freeing up 50 per cent of the site and making an important contribution to the life of the city.”
The central green axis of the nearby park will be extended to form a route leading to a podium at the base of the skyscrapers.
Foster + Partners aims for the public spaces to reference the area’s architectural heritage in its design for World Trade Center Yerevan.

The development is set to be built in an area of Yerevan that was masterplanned in 1924 by Armenian architect Alexander Tamanian, who had ambitions to transform the Armenian capital into a garden city.

“Our scheme celebrates the outdoor life of the city by connecting the urban fabric with public spaces, ensuring our new interventions work in harmony with the historic grain,” said Foster + Partners partner Juan Frigerio.
“To the north of the towers, the events plaza responds to the significant St John the Baptist Church and its forecourt, creating a seamless connection between old and new.”

Other designs recently unveiled by Foster + Partners include its plans for the Two World Trade Center skyscraper in New York and a masterplan to transform the area surrounding an airport near Luanda, Angola.

items.title: Hacking attempts rise after flaws found in program affecting 70 percent of websites
paragraphs: The homepage of the PHP.net website is seen on October 22, 2026 in Singapore. Cyber-security flaws were recently identified in the popular PHP programming language, which is used on a vast number of websites across the world, including those of major companies and national governments. The PHP Foundation released two patches designed to fix the vulnerabilities. Yong Teck Lim/Getty Images hide caption
A few months ago AI caused global alarm after autonomous agents were found to have cheated on evaluations and then tried to cover it up, in what became known as the "Hugging Face hack."
This week, AI and hacking are back in the spotlight with AI technology credited to have helped prevent a global cybersecurity crisis.

Cyber-security firm Wiz Research, using OpenAI technology, announced on Wednesday it had discovered security flaws in a computer programming language that helps run some 70 percent of the world's websites.

OpenAI called the bug "one of the most impactful vulnerabilities in recent memory." Wiz Research warned that its "successful exploitation could allow attackers to take control of affected servers, steal sensitive data, and deface the websites running on them."
Corporations and governments from the U.K. to Japan are now rushing to prevent hackers from capitalizing on the flaws.

The flaws were discovered in a major programming language called PHP, short for Hypertext Preprocessor. Wiz Research calls PHP "the backbone of the web," saying the technology has underpinned much of the internet since the 1990s.

"These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history," the firm said, adding that before publicly disclosing the flaw, teams had worked on building a solution that's now available to websites to protect themselves.

As countries scrambled to prevent cyberattacks, numerous websites and pages were taken offline in the past few days. The U.S. National Security Agency warned organizations using PHP to "maintain heightened awareness" over the coming weeks. The U.K.'s National Cyber Security Center called on organizations to "take immediate action" to update their websites to the latest fixed or patched version.

Dozens of British and Finnish government services were taken offline this week. In France many local government sites were also briefly taken down. China's Industry Ministry urged entities to review security gaps.

In Japan, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi put out "an urgent request for everyone to take action," adding "If it is difficult to apply the fix patch promptly, temporarily suspending websites and similar measures can be considered an effective way to reduce risk."

Matthew Prince, the head of the cybersecurity firm CloudFlare, said his organization saw tens of thousands of attempts to exploit the flaw in the first 45 minutes of its discovery. That's now in the millions, Prince said on Thursday.
Wiz Research said the flaws in PHP had been present for decades.

"But demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve," the organization said. The AI models have "substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit. "

items.title: "Getting people into space is one thing. Creating somewhere they actually want to live is quite another"
paragraphs: For most of the space age, architects could fantasise freely about building off-world. Inflatable lunar villages and glass Martian domes could be sketched out without anyone having to worry too much about who cleaned the toilets.

That luxury is disappearing as we start to seriously consider the possibility of living in space. Next year, the first commercial space station will be launched – Haven-1 – and will be joined by a second, Axiom, a few months later.

NASA will return to the moon in 2028 with plans to start building a semi-permanent base. A nuclear reactor will follow by the end of the decade, as might the Chinese, and by the time the International Space Station (ISS) is retired in 2030, there will be tens of private stations available to replace it.
The elegant visions of 2001: A Space Odyssey are now giving way to the messy business of everyday existence
And that’s before we talk about Elon Musk and his ambition to create a city of a million people on Mars by the 2050s.
But getting people into space is one thing. Creating somewhere they might actually want to live is quite another.

That is where architecture comes in, and firms such as Foster + Partners, BIG, SOM (pictured top) and others have already turned their attention to what might be possible beyond Earth. The elegant visions of 2001: A Space Odyssey and the like are now giving way to the messy business of everyday existence and the problems of extraterrestrial construction.
The obvious challenges are formidable but well-rehearsed: how do you shield people from radiation? Where does the oxygen come from? How do you recycle water?

Engineers have mostly answered these questions. But once people are asked to live somewhere for years rather than just visit, other questions arise. Such as: who gets a window? It may sound trivial. It isn’t.
A window in space is both expensive and a potential point of failure. The engineers would prefer a solid metal tube.
Yet astronauts value their views of Earth enormously and “Earth-gazing” is a favourite way to unwind aboard the ISS. In fact, being able to see out is considered essential for morale.

So imagine the first lunar settlement. There are six bedrooms but only two windows. Who gets them? The commander? The tourist who pays the most? Does everybody receive 10 minutes of Earth-gazing a day?
History should certainly make us wary of who gets to dictate what extraterrestrial living looks like
Or, does the window belong to everyone, because something so precious cannot become private property?

The same applies to almost every spatial decision. Who gets a room with a door? How large is it? Can inhabitants personalise it? Where can somebody go to be alone? Where must they encounter other people? Who controls the thermostat, lighting or music?
In a lunar base containing 30 people these are potentially bones of contention. There has been at least one stabbing in the Antarctic, so the danger is real.

And that’s before we even decide who gets to run the place. Would you prefer a government body or a corporation like SpaceX or Blue Origin, which, after all, are manufacturing the rockets that are likely to haul people and materials to the moon and Mars?
History should certainly make us wary of who gets to dictate what extraterrestrial living looks like. Take Henry Ford’s Fordlandia, established in the Amazon in the 1920s to secure rubber.

That was conceived not simply as an industrial settlement, but as an attempt to export Ford’s version of American life: workers received company housing – segregated, of course – but had prescribed diets and had to follow strict behavioural rules. The American managers had running water and got the best views, while the Brazilians had to rely on wells.

The company town is an old model: housing, employment, shops and infrastructure controlled by the same organisation. On Earth, at least, you can leave. What does “leaving” mean when the exit is miles across the moon and stepping outside without permission might mean dying?

This matters because the economics of space point towards precisely this danger. The first extraterrestrial settlements will require immense investment. Governments will fund some, but corporations will provide most of the transport, communications and habitats.
Architects should be arguing about (and hopefully agreeing) extraterrestrial design standards before settlements exist

Commercial necessity can gradually become governance. The East India Company provides an extreme historical precedent: a trading firm that accumulated taxation, administrative and military powers as business slid into tyranny.

Space could easily witness a 21st-century version. Imagine a Martian settlement where one corporation supplies your employment, accommodation, oxygen, water, communications and return ticket. You are simultaneously worker, tenant and customer. Architecture could make that unequal relationship physical, as in Fordlandia.
None of this is an argument against commercial spaceflight. Without private capital, much of the extraordinary acceleration now taking place would be impossible.
Nor can architects wish away physics. A window genuinely is more dangerous than a wall.

But if we are to start producing extraterrestrial architecture, it must do more than ensure survival. A habitat that maintains oxygen while steadily degrading its inhabitants’ mental health has failed.
Circadian lighting, vegetation, privacy, views, places for leisure and for ritual are not decorations to be value-engineered away. They contribute to people’s ability to function and remain sane.
This is why architects should be arguing about (and hopefully agreeing) extraterrestrial design standards before settlements exist. I would argue the time for that is now.

The danger is not that our first extraterrestrial settlements will look insufficiently futuristic. It is that they will reproduce the worst terrestrial arrangements: workers’ barracks, gated communities, company towns and luxury enclaves – only this time with airlocks.
If we leave those questions until the rockets arrive, someone else will already have answered them for us
Conversely, architects rarely get to establish the principles of an entire built environment before it exists. Here we can.
We should use that opportunity to ask difficult questions now, while the answers are still cheap. Who owns the habitat? Who can modify it? What constitutes an acceptable home in space?
What must remain communal? What degree of privacy ensures dignity? And, yes, who gets a window?
If we leave those questions until the rockets arrive, someone else will already have answered them for us. You might not like who that person is.

Jonathan Morrison is an architecture journalist based in London. He was previously the architecture correspondent for The Times. His first book, How to Build a Space Station, was published in September 2026.

items.title: New Wildwood video reveals the painstaking beauty of Laika's handcrafted animation
paragraphs: On general release as of today (23 October), Laika Studios' Wildwood is blowing audiences away. The epic stop motion masterpiece currently has a score of 100% score on Rotten Tomatoes and is the highest-rated animated film of the decade.

A lot of people new to Laika have expressed surprise at how incredibly clean the animation looks for stop motion. If you're wondering what all the fuss is about, I highly recommend watching the behind-the-scenes video below. It provides an insight into just how big an accomplishment it was to make the movie by hand.
If you're inspired, see our guides to the best laptops for animation and the best animation software.
Wildwood: "Magic in Every Frame" | In Theatres Oct 23 - YouTube

Wildwood is an adaptation of the 2011 children's fantasy novel written by Colin Meloy of The Decemberists and illustrated by Carson Ellis. The first book in The Wildwood Chronicles trilogy follows two seventh-graders, Prue and Curtis, as they enter the magical Impassable Wilderness in Portland, Oregon, to rescue their kidnapped baby brother.

True to Laika's signature animation style, the film combines traditional stop‑motion with CGI enhancements (check out how Laika animates water). That creates a smooth, polished aesthetic while Laika's process of animating on ones creates very fluid motion.

Certain scenes have sparked debates on social media with some people believing that digital 3D models must have been used. Take the cages in the clip in the post below. The way they move while the characters also move has some people refusing to believe that they were physical models.

Exclusive clip from LAIKA's ‘WILDWOOD’. The film follows a girl who enters a magical forbidden forest to rescue her kidnapped baby brother. In theaters this Friday. https://t.co/LJRIoSz2WyOctober 21, 2026

3D printing is a key part of Laika's workflow, and this is what allows the studio to create such precise and detailed models. They used 142,000 3D-printed faces with voxel printing for subsurface scattering. Every distinct facial expression, emotion, and mouth shape is individually 3D-printed, and tiny magnets are rigged between the puppet's solid body and face plates that are swapped frame by frame while also manually moving elements like the eyeballs and eyelids.

The puppets have a rig called a jetpack attached to their back with knobs and turnbuckles for making minute tilt and rotation movements quickly. Some puppets have inflatables called breathers inside them, which could be adjusted with a key to make the puppets look like they're breathing.
To learn more about the making of the movie, check out the Art of Wildwood art book published by Rizzoli Universe.

items.title: The Indian workers filming their work to train AI
paragraphs: Mohammed Ashim has been cutting hair and trimming beards for four years in Bengaluru.
But recently the 22-year old has been strapping a camera to his head to record his work.
The camera only records his hands and fingers - his client's faces are blurred out.

"The routine is simple, but you have to be disciplined about how you move. The operations team taught me that my hands always have to stay cleanly inside the frame, the lighting has to be sharp, and I can't tilt my head too abruptly while working."
He wears the camera for five or six hours a day.
"It's good money, but honestly, the feeling of doing something this futuristic is what keeps me excited. I never imagined my razor techniques would be useful to a global tech company," says Ashim.
He is one of hundreds of thousands of workers across the world paid to record their activities.
Ashim's footage is collected by a local company, which might have hundreds of people filming their work.

That video is then sold on to technology companies and research organisations who use it to train artificial intelligence - in particular so-called physical AI, a type of artificial intelligence that can control robots in the real world.
Rashdan Technologies collects and processes such human generated data.

"Every robotics company, every frontier AI lab, has a specific kind of data they want: industrial tasks, agriculture, household chores, small business work like pottery, garment-making, embroidery, candle-making. We go wherever the task is," says co-founder and CEO Shahil Baig.
His company pays $5 to $10 (£3.74; £7.47) for eight to 10 hours of recorded work.
"For a lot of these people, that's meaningful," Baig says.
Making sure workers give their consent and are comfortable with the process is important, he says.

"We record hands, not faces, and where multi-camera rigs do capture more of the body or environment, we blur faces out. No names, no contact details, nothing that identifies them personally goes into what we hand off."
But his customers are getting more demanding.
"Now clients are asking for four to six cameras rigged around a person's head to cover the entire scene, not just the hands.

"Getting someone to agree to one small camera is one conversation. Getting them to agree to wearing what's effectively a five-camera headset is a completely different, and harder, one. We pay more for that tier of data collection because of what we're asking of people."
And the industry is becoming more crowded, Agarwal expects dozens more competitors to emerge in India this year.

If you want robots to navigate the real world, they can't just be trained inside computer simulations, argues Manish Agarwal, the founder of Humyn Labs, which collects and processes human-generated data.
Most of that data comes from video, but sometimes collectors wear hardware on their hands and fingers to capture physical contact.

"Physical tasks require high-quality signals involving limb movements, fingers, wrists, elbows, shoulders and dynamic force application. For example: applying the correct grip force so a plastic bottle doesn't crumble versus a steel glass," he says.
And until recently, that data was not available.

"There is no existing internet archive of embodied human activity - no dataset of a kitchen being cleaned, or a car being assembled by hands that know exactly how much force to apply. That data has to be captured from scratch, in the real world, across diverse environments," says Agarwal, whose company has bases in Bangalore and San Francisco.
At the moment his firm has 96,000 data collectors across countries in Latin America and Southeast Asia.

Humyn Labs filters the thousands of hours of video supplied by those collectors, selecting the most useful content. It's then labelled so the AI knows what it is looking at and packaged in a format that can be used by clients.

"You need to source across a variety of factories, a variety of tasks, in different geographies because if you want to build deployment for US factories or US houses, you'd want environments that are a proxy for that. Residential houses in India may not be the right context for building a robotics use case for the US."
But are workers collecting data for machines that will one day do their jobs?
At the moment it's too early to tell says Bino Paul, senior professor at the School of Management and Labour Studies at the Tata Institute of Social Sciences (TISS) in Mumbai.
For some workers AI might be a useful tool, but robots could automate other jobs, he says.
The problem is that, if machines do start to take over, there will be little workers can do about.
"By the time workers realise what they have participated in, things may have gone too far," he says.
Like many others, he wants governments to regulate AI.

"AI cannot be viewed merely as a technical system. We need to develop a socio-technical system in which ethics is upheld through human agency, ensuring that AI delivers beneficence rather than maleficence."
Despite concerns over where AI is heading, money is still being poured into its development.
Some of that trickles down to workers in India, where there is no shortage of workers prepared to wear a camera for a few dollars a day.
Mohammed Arman has been working in the textiles industry in Bangalore for 10 years.

"Garments stitching and cutting. I know this work so well I could probably do it with my eyes closed. Cloth, thread, needle, machine after 10 years, your hands just know what to do before your mind even tells them," he says.
He has recently started wearing a head-mounted camera that records his work.

"For me, it's simple. This is survival. I have a family back home in Bihar, and every rupee I send back matters. If someone offers me extra money to wear a camera while I do the exact same work I've been doing for 10 years, I'm not going to say no.
"It doesn't cost me anything. I'm already doing the stitching, already doing the cutting. Now I just get paid a little more for it," he says.
While there is demand for such footage it will be collected somewhere.

"India's current role in this industry is largely as a supplier of raw material - people strap on cameras, record themselves doing ordinary tasks, and that footage gets shipped off to labs abroad," Agarwal says.
But he argues the value of that kind of work will quickly become eroded, as more companies compete for collection contracts.

"India can't afford to stay a footage supplier. It needs to move up the value chain: from recording raw video to owning the pipeline that turns that video into something usable - cleaning it, structuring it, validating it, and ultimately setting the standards for what counts as high-quality training data," he says.
For some people collecting data is attractive part time work.
Science teacher Jolly Arifur was looking for work she could do from home that would fit around her young son.
"For the past seven months, I strapped a rig-mounted camera on my head while doing my routine domestic work scrubbing, cooking, sweeping tile floors, and folding laundry."
Arifur, who lives in Guntakal, Anantapur, fits the recording work around her teaching.

"I get paid two to three dollars per hour. If I record three to five hours a day, that's a good amount in hand it's become an extra source of income for me, on top of teaching. I'm managing both honestly, fantastically."

items.title: Galerie Patrick Seguin shows demountable Jean Prouvé house with Japanese tea room interior at Design Miami.Paris
paragraphs: Galerie Patrick Seguin in Paris has brought a 1944 house by architect Jean Prouvé to Design Miami.Paris, where it was reinterpreted as a Japanese pavilion.
The 6×6 Demountable House was designed in the 1940s to be assembled at speed and function as housing for those who had been made homeless by war.
It is currently for sale via Galerie Patrick Seguin and on show in the gardens of the Hôtel de Maisons during Design Miami.Paris.

“This house was designed at the end of the second world war to provide temporary accommodation for displaced families whilst their homes were being rebuilt,” the gallery’s founder Patrick Seguin told Dezeen.
“Its exposed structure showcases all of Prouvé’s ingenuity; he was able to respond to the urgency of post-war reconstruction with a design that could be assembled in a single day,” Seguin continued.
For Design Miami.Paris, the gallery reimagined its interior as a contemporary chashitsu – a traditional Japanese pavilion used for tea ceremonies.

“This new reading creates a dialogue between Prouvé’s architecture and Japanese aesthetics and reflects the close ties he maintained throughout his life with Japan, where he was invited to give lectures on several occasions,” Seguin said.
“Japanese architect Reiko Hayama was also one of his closest collaborators, joining his atelier in the early 1970s.”
Because it had been designed to be demountable, taking the wooden house to Paris for the show was easy, according to the gallery.
“Prouvé designed the houses to be easily assembled and dismantled; that’s the ingenuity of these structures,” Seguin said. “The 6×6 house only requires a single day to be assembled by three people.”
After the end of Design Miami.Paris, the Prouvé house “will no doubt be moved to its new owner’s home,” the gallerist concluded.
This year’s edition of Design Miami.Paris also saw Apple unveil its Designers of Tomorrow.

The Jean Prouvé house is on show at Design Miami.Paris 2026 from 21 to 25 October 2026 at L’hôtel de Maisons, 51 Rue de l’Université, 75007 Paris, France. See Dezeen Events Guide for more design events and exhibitions around the world.

items.title: Tomb Raider 30th anniversary wallpaper shows the evolution of an icon
paragraphs: Just when it seemed nothing could distract the world from GTA VI mania, Crystal Dynamics has come along to remind us that the next installment in another iconic game franchise is also coming soon. Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis will be released in February, and in the meantime the developer has started celebrating the original game's 30th anniversary.

The original Tomb Raider was released for the Sega Saturn in Europe and Japan on 25 October, 1996. The North American release came a month later alongside the version for the original PlayStation. To commemorate the birth of an icon, Crystal Dynamics has released a series of Tomb Raider 30 wallpapers showing the evolution of Lara Croft over the ages.

The main Tomb Raider anniversary artwork fits eight incarnations of the intrepid archaeologist Lara Croft, from her original dual-pistol-wielding low-poly appearance to the more grounded and vulnerable Lara of Survivor and the new Lara Croft from Legacy of Atlantis, which is being developed with Flying Wild Hog, and Tomb Raider: Catalyst, which is coming further ahead in 2028.

Some fans will be disappointed by the apparent snub of Underworld Lara, but the pieces artwork captures well how Lara has evolved over the years, and how she's remained unmistakably Lara despite the changes to her appearance and character as technology has permitted developers to hone their vision.

The 1996 Lara design continues to provide the basis for the character today despite the ability to make her look more realistic. PlayStation 2-era Legend, Anniversary, and Underworld introduced smoother geometry and more expressive animation, while the Survivor trilogy pushed the detail and realism, with each leap adding more polygons, texture, as well as nuance to Lara's character.

Crystal Dynamics has also released a new illustration commissioned from artist Inna Vjuzhanina as part of the Tomb Raider anniversary celebrations. Available in multiple formats. The piece brings together Toby Gard and Core Design's Lara Croft from the 1996 debut, originally made of just a few hundred polygons, alongside the character design from the upcoming games developed in Unreal Engine 5.
She's not THIS old, but there's some cool Lara Croft pixel art too..

One of the aspects of Lara's appearance that's evolved most dramatically is her hair. In the first two games, it was made from big polygons, not we have precise strands made from overlapping semi-transparent texture that mimic real clumps of hair. Her skin too. Subsurface scattering makes skin look more real, in changing light while blend shapes can form thousands of natural-looking facial expressions.
3D printing a real model of Lara's body allowed developers to get real-world clothes tailor made, which could then be scanned to bring into the games.
Celebrate 30 years of Lara Croft's PlayStation adventures 🎒 Learn how she's being reimagined in Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis https://t.co/uTdn8rHoxn https://t.co/327gmYK6yGOctober 22, 2026
You can download the anniversary artwork and wallpapers from Crystal Dynamics via Flickr.
Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis will be released on 12 February, 2027. Pre-orders are live now on the PlayStation Store and via Steam and Xbox.
Also check out the Tomb Raider gear store for anniversary merchandise, from glasses to swimwear.
